title: Arguments & Plots
section: Where does the history of data visualization begin?
text:
Where does the history of data visualization begin?

Does anyone recognize this visualization?

https://data-by-design.vercel.app/chapters/playfair gives a more detailed account of Playfair’s work and its historical context. William Playfair (1759–1823) was a Scottish engineer, political economist, writer, and sometimes political operative. He had trained as a draftsman and worked for the steam-engine designer James Watt before moving through a remarkably varied and often financially unstable career. That background matters because Playfair approached economic information as both an engineer and a public persuader: he wanted readers to see relationships in numbers rather than work through dense statistical tables.
His Commercial and Political Atlas, published in 1786, used engraved and hand-colored charts to represent British imports, exports, debt, revenue, and trade over time. Playfair is commonly credited with establishing the statistical line graph and bar chart as recognizable forms. His Statistical Breviary of 1801 later included the first published pie chart. The image here annotates some of the conventions he helped normalize: time moving horizontally, numerical magnitude moving vertically, labeled axes, lines connecting observations, color distinguishing series, and explanatory text embedded in the graphic. These choices now feel natural because they became conventions; they still had to be invented, taught, and learned.
I would be careful about calling Playfair the person who simply “invented data visualization.” People had long used maps, diagrams, timelines, tables, and other visual forms to organize knowledge, and historians have identified earlier examples resembling bar charts. Playfair’s importance is that he brought several techniques together into a reusable visual language for statistical and economic argument. His charts did not merely display neutral facts. They invited readers to compare nations, interpret trade balances, and form judgments about Britain’s political economy.
D’Ignazio and Klein describe a familiar history: European colonial mapping, the development of timelines and statistical charts, and the adoption of those forms by states seeking to know and govern populations.

“Its history is often traced from the explosion of European men mapping their colonial conquests in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, through the development of new visual typologies like the timeline and the bar chart in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, to the adoption of those forms by powerful nations as they amassed increasing amounts of data on the populations they sought to control.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 6)

They also challenge its progress narrative and predominantly white, male cast. This recalls our discussions of censuses, tabulating machines, and W. E. B. Du Bois. Visualization developed alongside institutions that counted, classified, governed, persuaded, and contested.
Playfair gives us several forms that later designers would adapt for different kinds of knowledge. The next examples broaden that history. Elizabeth Palmer Peabody uses visualization as a participatory method for learning chronology. Florence Nightingale uses it to compare causes of military death. Charles Joseph Minard combines geography, time, temperature, and quantity. W. E. B. Du Bois and his collaborators visualize Black social and economic life. As we move through them, ask how visual form turns recorded information into an experience and an argument.

title: Arguments & Plots
section: Who was Elizabeth Palmer Peabody and what is this chart?
text:
Who was Elizabeth Palmer Peabody and what is this chart?


This is Elizabeth Palmer Peabody’s chart of significant events in the seventeenth-century United States, published in A Chronological History of the United States. Peabody (1804–1894) was an educator, editor, publisher, and member of Boston’s Transcendentalist intellectual community. She is also associated with establishing the first English-language kindergarten in the United States. Her inclusion matters because the familiar history of visualization often moves among male inventors and treats finished charts as technical innovations. Peabody instead helps us see visualization as teaching, interpretation, memory, and labor.
Peabody adapted Józef Bem’s Franco-Polish chronology system rather than inventing the entire method herself. The grid assigns each year a location and uses smaller subdivisions, shapes, and colors to encode the types of events and nations involved. Students were expected to learn the key, connect the visual marks to a written chronology, and eventually construct their own mental or physical account of history.
She also worked with large “mural charts” that could be placed on the floor while students gathered around them. That makes the chart more than an image delivered by an expert to a passive audience. The act of navigating, discussing, remembering, and sometimes making the visualization was part of the production of historical knowledge.
D’Ignazio and Klein introduce Peabody alongside W. E. B. Du Bois and Shanawdithit to broaden the standard cast of visualization history. Peabody is especially useful here because she was an educator rather than a statistician or government administrator. Her chart belongs to a history of classrooms, textbooks, memory practices, and visual learning.
To read the chart, begin with its structure. The larger grid moves chronologically through a century. Each year is divided into smaller positions associated with different kinds of events, while colors identify the nations involved. The accompanying written chronology supplies the event that each mark represents. Neither the image nor the text is sufficient on its own; students move between them.
Lauren Klein’s later project digitally reconstructed Peabody’s charts and reimagined one as an interactive quilt. That reconstruction helps recover how the system worked, especially because Peabody’s large classroom mural charts have not survived. It also lets us compare the printed grid, a digital interface, and a tactile textile as three different ways of encountering the same chronology system.
This is our first historical opening into emotion and rhetoric. Peabody did not want students merely to retrieve dates. Color, pattern, bodily arrangement, and the labor of making a chart were intended to support memory and historical imagination. The chart’s difficulty is therefore not necessarily a design failure: learning how to interpret it was part of the pedagogical experience.
D’Ignazio and Klein write, “Each of these early visualization designers understood how their images could function rhetorically” (2020, p. 7). Here, rhetoric does not mean that the chronology is fabricated. It means that Peabody designed a particular encounter with historical information. The chart asks students to see a century as a pattern, to remember selected events through color and location, and to construct a historical narrative from those relations.
Ask: Does actively making and remembering the chart produce a different kind of historical knowledge than reading a list of dates? What emotions or associations might its colors and patterns attach to nations and events? Who decided which events deserved a place in the pattern?

title: Arguments & Plots
section: History of Data Viz: Who has seen these charts before?
text:
History of Data Viz: Who has seen these charts before?







These charts belong to both the history of visualization and the nineteenth-century history of information. Expanding states, militaries, hospitals, statistical societies, and engineering offices produced growing quantities of standardized records. Clerks counted, classified, summed, averaged, and arranged observations in tables long before tabulation became mechanized. Historians sometimes describe this period as an “avalanche of printed numbers.”
Printing helped those numbers travel. Government reports, statistical yearbooks, foldout plates, lithographs, and color printing allowed tables and graphics to circulate among administrators, reformers, engineers, and parts of the public. A visualization could condense pages of tabulated information into an image designed to be compared, remembered, and discussed.
Florence Nightingale (1820–1910) used military mortality records from the Crimean War in her 1858 Diagram of the Causes of Mortality in the Army in the East. Each wedge represents a month; its area shows the mortality rate. Blue indicates preventable disease, red wounds, and black other causes. The enormous blue areas make the central comparison immediate: disease killed far more soldiers than combat wounds.
Nightingale did not personally generate this entire information system. She worked with records produced through military administration and with collaborators who helped analyze and print them. Her achievement was to connect tabulation, visual design, publication, and political access. She had thousands of shorter printed summaries distributed because she knew few officials would read the Royal Commission’s dense tables and appendices.
Charles Joseph Minard (1781–1870) was a French civil engineer accustomed to records about roads, canals, railways, traffic, and movement. His 1869 map reconstructs Napoleon’s 1812 Russian campaign by combining geography, chronology, direction, temperature, and estimated troop strength. The tan band marks the advance, the black band the retreat, and the shrinking width turns attrition into a visible historical process.
Both charts transform tabulated records into visual rhetoric. Nightingale organizes mortality by time and cause to argue that deaths were preventable. Minard organizes historical estimates into a narrative of movement and catastrophic loss. Neither merely replaces a table with a picture: each selects variables and gives them a visual relationship that directs interpretation and feeling.
D’Ignazio and Klein remind us that “any communicating object that reflects choices about the selection and representation of reality is a rhetorical object” (2020, p. 7). Their desire to persuade does not automatically make these charts inaccurate. It prompts us to inspect the chain from recordkeeping and tabulation to printing, design, circulation, and argument.
Ask: What can each chart communicate more quickly than a printed table? What administrative records had to exist before it could be made? Whose deaths were counted, and whose remain outside the frame?

title: Arguments & Plots
section: History of Data Viz: Who remembers the author of these charts?
text:
History of Data Viz: Who remembers the author of these charts?


This chart is by W. E. B. Du Bois (1868–1963), whose work we discussed earlier in the semester. Du Bois was a sociologist, historian, civil-rights activist, and one of the founders of the NAACP. He was also committed to empirical social research. At Atlanta University, he and his collaborators assembled surveys, government records, and community data to study Black life under the conditions created by slavery, Reconstruction, segregation, and racial violence.
The chart was created for the Exhibit of American Negroes at the 1900 Paris Exposition. Du Bois helped lead the production of the Georgia materials as part of a larger collaborative exhibit. The visualizations addressed an international audience and directly contested racist claims that Black Americans were incapable of social, educational, or economic advancement. This is important context: the charts were not simply descriptive sociology. They were evidence created within a political struggle over who had authority to represent African American life.
This particular chart is titled Income and expenditure of 150 Negro families in Atlanta, Ga., U.S.A. It organizes families into income brackets and shows how much they spent on rent, food, clothing, taxes, and other expenses. Ask students to look closely at what happens as income rises. The chart makes household budgeting and material constraint visible, but it also presents Black families as economic actors whose lives could not be reduced to the racist stereotypes circulating at the exposition and in American social science.
Du Bois used saturated color, strong diagonals, unusual geometry, and hand lettering. These visual choices distinguish the charts from the statistical graphics we have already examined and connect them to the modern visual culture of an international exposition. Their production also involved a team of students and collaborators at Atlanta University, reminding us that famous visualizations are often collective work.
The design refuses the idea that empirical seriousness requires visual restraint. Color and composition command attention, but they do not replace the data. Instead, they help Du Bois and his collaborators assert Black modernity while presenting statistical evidence about Black social and economic life. The charts communicate both through measured quantities and through an expressive visual identity.
This gives us a useful comparison with Nightingale. Both transform administrative or survey data for audiences beyond the institutions that originally collected them. Nightingale works with military mortality records; Du Bois and his collaborators assemble evidence about Black social and economic life for an international exposition. Ask what each team had to collect, calculate, and compare before a visualization could be made.
I would use this to ask: What did the Atlanta University team want an international audience to learn and feel about Black life? Which measurements did they consider necessary? How do the charts relate to Du Bois’s larger program of empirical sociology? Would a conventional monochrome chart have made the same argument to visitors at the exposition?
D’Ignazio and Klein use Du Bois to challenge a visualization history whose “cast of characters … is predominantly white and male” (2020, p. 6). Recovering these charts changes more than the list of important designers. It also expands what we recognize as rigorous visualization: collective research, political purpose, aesthetic experimentation, and emotional force can coexist with empirical evidence.
The Library of Congress catalog describes the object as a bar graph showing expenditure by families in different income brackets and notes that it was prepared for the 1900 exposition to demonstrate African American economic and social progress after emancipation.
For more on the visualizations, see Jason Forrest, “W. E. B. Du Bois’ Staggering Data Visualizations Are as Powerful Today as They Were in 1900”, and the Library of Congress collection.

title: Arguments & Plots
section: History of Data Viz: Who decides what is a “good” visualization?
text:
History of Data Viz: Who decides what is a “good” visualization?







https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1400/0*go-VEeiqfSwLKBrg.png data ink ratio?
These books do not mark a single moment when visualization became digital. Tukey deliberately designed many techniques for pencil-and-paper use, while Tufte published a carefully designed print book. What changes here is that visualization becomes more explicitly codified as both a method of analysis and a field with standards for judging graphics. Machine-readable data and computing would make these practices easier to repeat and scale.
John W. Tukey (1915–2000) worked at Princeton and Bell Laboratories, connecting statistics to science, engineering, and computing. His 1977 Exploratory Data Analysis argued that researchers should look at distributions, relationships, and unusual cases before settling on a formal explanation. A visualization could help discover the question, not merely illustrate an answer already known.
Tukey’s standard for a good chart is therefore discovery: does it help us notice something unexpected? This is the foundation for the technical work we will do with notebooks. Plotting missing values, distributions, and outliers is part of thinking with data. But it also raises cultural questions: is an outlier an error to remove, or a historically significant case that challenges the categories?
Edward Tufte’s 1983 The Visual Display of Quantitative Information helped establish a different set of criteria: clarity, graphical integrity, high information density, and visual economy. His concepts of the data-ink ratio and chartjunk ask designers to remove marks that do not communicate data and to avoid effects that exaggerate differences. D’Ignazio and Klein summarize his position: “a visualization designer should strive to use ink to display data alone” (2020, p. 5).
Tufte’s rules remain useful for identifying misleading axes, unnecessary three-dimensional effects, and decoration that obscures evidence. But the charts we just examined complicate the idea that minimalism is automatically better. Color helps Peabody organize memory, Nightingale demand reform, and Du Bois assert Black modernity. Removing those choices would change the argument rather than reveal untouched data underneath.
This brings us to Alberto Cairo and the question of what makes a chart good. Is it enough for a visualization to be factually accurate? Must it also make its assumptions and persuasive purpose visible? Cairo worries about audiences mistaking a deliberately shaped argument for an automatic or neutral product of the data. D’Ignazio and Klein push further: all charts are shaped, including minimalist ones.
“Edward Tufte. Back in the 1980s, Tufte invented a metric for measuring the amount of superfluous information included in a chart. He called it the data-ink ratio” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 5)
“Indeed, psychologists have called it a master stereotype and puzzled over how it endures even when certain emotions—even extreme ones, like anger and pride—are simultaneously associated with men.9 A central focus of feminist scholarship has been to challenge false binaries like this one between reason and emotion and to point out how they establish hierarchies as well. (” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 6)
“For now, the important thing to note is how false binaries work to benefit a single one of Haraway’s partial perspectives: that of the group already at the top—elite white men.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 6)
“Two additional questions help challenge this reductive way of thinking and the oppressive hierarchies that it supports. First, is visual minimalism really more neutral? And second, how might activating emotionleveraging, rather than resisting, emotion in data visualization—help us learn, remember, and communicate with data? Exploring these questions helps get us closer to the third principle of data feminism: embrace emotion and embodiment.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 6)
“Its history is often traced from the explosion of European men mapping their colonial conquests in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, through the development of new visual typologies like the timeline and the bar chart in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, to the adoption of those forms by powerful nations as they amassed increasing amounts of data on the populations they sought to control. But feminist scholars are increasingly challenging this simple narrative of progress, as well as its cast of characters, which is predominantly white and male.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 6)

title: Arguments & Plots
section: Should a visualization make us feel something?
text:
Should a visualization make us feel something?



US Gun Deaths visualization



Periscopic’s U.S. Gun Deaths project visualizes each victim’s age at death and a statistically projected lifespan. The orange line marks years lived; the gray arc represents estimated years “stolen.”
The project uses demographic data and statistical methods, but it leads with loss, grief, and mourning. Alberto Cairo asked whether audiences understood that designers had actively shaped the data to support a cause.

“The visualization uses demographic data and rigorous statistical methods to arrive at these numbers, as is explained in the methods section on the site.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 2)


“At root for Cairo was the question of how detached and ‘neutral’ a visualization should be. He wondered, Should a visualization be designed to evoke emotion?” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 4)

Ask: Does emotion make this less accurate? What assumptions are embedded in estimating a life that did not happen? Is calling the years “stolen” analysis, persuasion, or both? The useful distinction is between argument and deception, not between persuasion and neutrality.
“In the wake of this unconscionable tragedy, and of the additional acts of gun violence that followed, the design firm Periscopic began a new project: to visualize all the gun deaths that took place in the United States over the course of a calendar year.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 2)
“The visualization uses demographic data and rigorous statistical methods to arrive at these numbers, as is explained in the methods section on the site.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 2)
“This message was clearly received, as was the project overall. It was featured in Wired magazine, and even won an Information is Beautiful award. But it also caused some stewing on the part of the visualization community. Alberto Cairo, the author of the visualization book The Truthful Art, expressed his concerns about the use of emotion and persuasion in the project: “Is it clear to a general audience that what they see is the work of professionals who actively shape data to support a cause, and not the product of automated processes?”1 At root for Cairo was the question of how detached and “neutral” a visualization should be. He wondered, Should a visualization be designed to evoke emotion?” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 4)
“This embrace of multiple perspectives and positionalities helps to rebalance the hierarchy of reason over emotion in data visualization.24 How? Since the early 2000s, there has been an explosion of research about affect—the term that academics use to refer to emotions and other subjective feelings—from fields as diverse as neuroscience, geography, and philosophy.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 13)
“Once we embrace the idea of leveraging emotion in data visualization, we can truly appreciate what sets Periscopic’s “US Gun Deaths” graphic apart from the Washington Post graphic or from any number of other gun death charts that have appeared in newspapers and policy documents. The Washington Post graphic, for example, represents death counts as blue ticks on a generic bar chart. If we didn’t read the caption, we wouldn’t know whether we were counting gun deaths in the United States or haystacks in Kansas or exports from Malaysia or any other statistic. In contrast, the Periscopic visualization leads with loss, grief, and mourning—primarily through its rhetorical emphasis on counting “stolen years.”” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 13)

title: Arguments & Plots
section: How did Jonathan Stray detail these two graphics? What is the argument of this example?
text:
How did Jonathan Stray detail these two graphics? What is the argument of this example?


https://data.journalism.columbia.edu/sites/data.journalism.columbia.edu/files/content/curious-journalist-s-guide-to-data.pdf gives a more detailed account of the New York Times graphics and their context.
A data visualization of the September 2012 jobs report from the perspective of Democrats (a) and Republicans (b). The New York Times data team shows how simple editorial changes lead to large differences in framing and interpretation. As data journalist Jonathan Stray remarks on these graphics, “The constraints of truth leave a very wide space for interpretation.” Images by Mike Bostock, Shan Carter, Amanda Cox, and Kevin Quealy, for the New York Times, as cited in The Curious Journalist’s Guide to Data by Jonathan Stray.
“But in more recent history, many of data visualization’s theorists and practitioners have come from technical disciplines aligned with engineering and computer science and have not been trained in that most fundamental of Western communication theorie” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 7)
“Any communicating object that reflects choices about the selection and representation of reality is a rhetorical object. Whether or not it is rhetorical (it always is) has nothing to do with whether or not it is true (it may or may not be).” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 7)
“This includes visualizations that do not deliberately intend to persuade people of a certain message. It especially and definitively includes those so-called neutral visualizations that do not appear to have an editorial hand. In fact, those might even be the most perniciously persuasive visualizations of all!” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 7)
“Either of these graphics, considered in isolation, appears to be neutral and factual. The data are presented with standard methods (line chart and area chart respectively) and conventional positionings (time on the x-axis, rates expressed as percentages on the y-axis, title placed above the graphic). There is a high data-ink ratio in both cases and very little in the way of ornamentation. But the graphics have significant editorial differences.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 7)
“So neither graphic is neutral, but both graphics are factual. As Jonathan Stray says, “The constraints of truth leave a very wide space for interpretation.”16 When visualizing data, the only certifiable fact is that it’s impossible to avoid interpretation (unless you simply republish the September jobs report as your visualization, but then it wouldn’t be a visualization).” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 9)
“Fields very close to visualization, like cartography, have long seen their work as ideological.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 9)
“Other aspects of data visualization also work to displace viewers’ attention from editorial choices to reinforce a graphic’s perceived neutrality and “truthiness.” After doing a sociological analysis, Helen Kennedy and coauthors determined that four conventions of data visualization reinforce people’s perceptions of its factual basis: (1) two-dimensional viewpoints, (2) clean layouts, (3) geometric shapes and lines, and (4) the inclusion of data sources at the bottom.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 11)
“These conventions contribute to the perception of data visualization as objective, scientific, and neutral.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 11)
“So if plain, “unemotional” visualizations are not neutral, but are actually extremely persuasive, then what does this mean for the concept of neutrality in general? Scientists and journalists are just some of the people who get nervous and defensive when questions about neutrality and objectivity come up.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 11)
The chapter compares factual graphics that use conventional forms but make different choices about framing. Start dates, scales, comparisons, titles, and annotations direct attention toward different explanations.
As Jonathan Stray writes, “The constraints of truth leave a very wide space for interpretation.” A visualization can be factual and rhetorical at the same time.

“So neither graphic is neutral, but both graphics are factual. As Jonathan Stray says, ‘The constraints of truth leave a very wide space for interpretation.’” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 9)

Ask what an audit would inspect: source data, exclusions, derived measures, scales, categories, annotations, uncertainty, audience, and intended action.

title: Arguments & Plots
section: What is the problem of distance in data visualization? What is the god trick?
text:
What is the problem of distance in data visualization? What is the god trick?








Quantification is a technology of distance.
Theodore Porter Porter’s phrase explains why numbers acquire institutional authority. Standard measures can travel without requiring personal trust in their makers.


“As historian of science Theodore Porter puts it, ‘Quantification is a technology of distance.’ And distance, he explains, is closely related to objectivity because it puts literal space between people and the knowledge they produce.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 5)

But distance can separate a number from the people, judgments, and institutions that produced it. D’Ignazio and Klein connect this history to the gendered hierarchy of reason over emotion. Detachment is itself a stance, not the absence of one.
This recalls Rosenberg’s history of data as a “given.” Visualizations often make selected and transformed observations feel given rather than made.
“They’re not the first ones to posit this belief. In the field of data communication, any kind of ornament has long been viewed as suspect. Why? As historian of science Theodore Porter puts it, “Quantification is a technology of distance.”3 And distance, he explains, is closely related to objectivity because it puts literal space between people and the knowledge they produce. This desire for separation is what underlies the nineteenth-century statistician Karl Pearson’s exhortation, echoed in Cairo’s comments about the Periscopic visualization, for people to set aside their “own feelings and emotions” when performing statistical work.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 5)
Who is Donna Haraway?
Donna Haraway is a feminist scholar of science and technology and Distinguished Professor Emerita at UC Santa Cruz. Her work joins feminist theory, history of science, biology, and science and technology studies.
Her 1988 essay “Situated Knowledges” rejects both an impossible universal view and a relativism in which every claim is equally valid. Every observer occupies a partial position. Better knowledge comes from recognizing the limits and responsibilities of that position and placing partial perspectives into relation.

“It’s not just data visualization but all forms of knowledge that are situated, she explains, meaning that they are produced by specific people in specific circumstances—cultural, historical, and geographic.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 12)

What is the “god trick”?
Haraway calls the disembodied claim to complete vision the “god trick.” In visualization, it occurs when a chart hides who gathered the data, which records are missing, how categories were defined, which transformations were applied, and why one view was selected.
What appears universal is often the partial perspective of a dominant group presented as the default. Naming a position does not weaken knowledge. It makes the claim more accountable.

“She described data visualization, in particular, as ‘the god trick of seeing everything from nowhere.’” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 5)


“What appears to be everything, and what appears to be neutral, is always what she terms a partial perspective.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 5)

“Donna Haraway’s idea of the god trick comes from a larger argument about the importance of developing feminist objectivity. It’s not just data visualization but all forms of knowledge that are situated, she explains, meaning that they are produced by specific people in specific circumstances—cultural, historical, and geographic.19 Feminist objectivity is a tool that can account for the situated nature of knowledge and can bring together multiple—what she terms partial—perspectives. Sandra Harding, who developed her ideas alongside Haraway, proposes a concept of strong objectivity. This form of objectivity works toward more inclusive knowledge production by centering the perspectives—or standpoints—of groups that are otherwise excluded from knowledge-making processes.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 12)
“Linda Alcoff has introduced the idea of positionality, a concept that emphasizes how individuals come to knowledge-making processes from multiple positions, each determined by culture and context.21 All of these ideas offer alternatives to the quest for a universal objectivity—which is, of course, an unattainable goal.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 12)
“The key to fixing this problem is to acknowledge that all science, and indeed all work in the world, is undertaken by individuals. Each person occupies a particular perspective, as Haraway might say; a particular standpoint, as Harding might say; or a particular set of positionalities, as Alcott might say. And all would agree that research by only men and about only men cannot be universalized to make knowledge claims about all other people in the world.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 12)
“Linda Alcoff has introduced the idea of positionality, a concept that emphasizes how individuals come to knowledge-making processes from multiple positions, each determined by culture and context.21 All of these ideas offer alternatives to the quest for a universal objectivity—which is, of course, an unattainable goal.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 12)
“The key to fixing this problem is to acknowledge that all science, and indeed all work in the world, is undertaken by individuals. Each person occupies a particular perspective, as Haraway might say; a particular standpoint, as Harding might say; or a particular set of positionalities, as Alcott might say. And all would agree that research by only men and about only men cannot be universalized to make knowledge claims about all other people in the world.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 12)
“Disclosing your subject position(s) is an important feminist strategy for being transparent about the limits of your—or anyone’s—knowledge claims. Thus, for example, we (the authors) included statements about our own positionalities in the introduction in order to disclose the gender, race/ethnicity, class, ability, education, and other subject positions that informed the writing of this book.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 12)
“This embrace of multiple perspectives and positionalities helps to rebalance the hierarchy of reason over emotion in data visualization.24 How? Since the early 2000s, there has been an explosion of research about affect—the term that academics use to refer to emotions and other subjective feelings—from fields as diverse as neuroscience, geography, and philosophy.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 13)

title: Arguments & Plots
section: What is data visceralization? How does it relate to feminist objectivity?
text:
What is data visceralization? How does it relate to feminist objectivity?


Whether a visualization is rhetorical is separate from whether it is true. It is rhetorical because someone selected and represented reality through it.

“Any communicating object that reflects choices about the selection and representation of reality is a rhetorical object. Whether or not it is rhetorical (it always is) has nothing to do with whether or not it is true (it may or may not be).” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 7)

The dataset supplies evidence, analysis transforms it, and visualization organizes attention. The apparent absence of an editorial hand can be especially persuasive because it encourages viewers to mistake conventions for inevitability.

“It especially and definitively includes those so-called neutral visualizations that do not appear to have an editorial hand.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 7)

In 1989, the Guerrilla Girls compared the small share of women among artists in the Met’s modern art galleries with the large share among nude subjects.

“The graphic makes a data-driven argument by comparing the gender statistics of artists collected by another New York museum, the Metropolitan Museum of Art (the Met), to the gender statistics of the subjects and models in the artworks.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 14)

The operations are simple: count, group, compare. The argument comes from deciding what to count together and placing those counts in tension. Computational complexity alone does not produce a meaningful claim.
Ask what an audit would still need: Which galleries and date? How were gender and nudity classified? Who counted? Can the result be reproduced?
The chapter discusses Ekene Ijeoma’s A Sort of Joy. Its underlying operations are counting and grouping, but the audience experiences names one at a time and only gradually constructs the whole.
This reverses Ben Shneiderman’s influential mantra: “Overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand.” Sequence is an argument. Beginning with the aggregate supports comparison but can turn people into an immediately consumable total. Beginning with records preserves specificity, time, and emotional weight.

“In this data performance, we do not see the overview first. We hear and see and experience each datapoint one at a time and only slowly construct a sense of the whole.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 16)

title: Arguments & Plots
section: How can a visualization communicate uncertainty?
text:
How can a visualization communicate uncertainty?

Is uncertainty something we see, calculate, or feel?

Visualization is rhetorically associated with certainty. Probability bands can be mistaken for vote shares, ignored, or reduced to whichever line is on top.
D’Ignazio and Klein discuss the New York Times election needle. Its movement gave viewers a perceptual and emotional experience of uncertainty. The discomfort communicated something mathematically important: probability is not a settled outcome.

“It gave people the perceptual, intuitive, visceral, and emotional experience of uncertainty to reinforce the quantitative depiction of uncertainty.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 20)

Missing records, disputed categories, OCR errors, uncertain dates, and ambiguous classifications should not simply disappear during cleaning. We need to preserve and communicate these limits.
“As it turns out, visceralizing data may help designers solve one particularly pernicious problem in the visualization community: how to represent uncertainty in a medium that’s become rhetorically synonymous with the truth. To this end, designers have created a huge array of charts and techniques for quantifying and representing uncertainty.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 17)
“. The underlying problem was not the failure of data but the difficulties of depicting uncertainty in visual form. People are just not sufficiently trained to recognize uncertainty in graphics such as this. Rather than interpreting the gradient bands as probabilities (e.g., Trump had a 20 percent chance of winning at 6 p.m.), people may interpret them as votes (e.g., Trump had 20 percent of the vote at 6 p.m.). Or they may ignore the gradient bands altogether and look only at the lines. Or they see Clinton on top and assume she is winning.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 19)
“At the top of the page was a gauge (figure 3.8) that showed the New York Times’s real-time prediction of who was likely to win the race, with a gradient of categories that ranged from medium blue (“Very Likely” that Clinton would win) to medium red (“Very Likely” that Trump would win). But the needle did not stay in one place. It jittered between the twenty-fifth and seventy-fifth percentiles, showing the range of outcomes that the New York Times was then predicting, based on simulations using the most recent data.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 19)
“t gave people the perceptual, intuitive, visceral, and emotional experience of uncertainty to reinforce the quantitative depiction of uncertainty. The fact that it unsettled so much of the New York Times readership probably had less to do with the ethics of the visualization and more to do with the outcome of the election. So score one for emotion in the task of representing uncertainty” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 20)

title: Arguments & Plots
section: How do we select what to visualize?
text:
How do we select what to visualize?


Margaret Pearce’s Coming Home to Indigenous Place Names in Canada adopts the projection and visual authority of an official map to challenge a colonial view of the land.
The map deliberately does not reveal everything. Names were treated as Indigenous cultural property, permissions were sought, and communities could decline translations. Pearce insists that the place names are not simply a dataset but cultural property shared through relationships with the map.

“The place names aren’t datasets. The place names are cultural property being shared with the map that come from people.” (Margaret Pearce, quoted in D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 21)


“Cartography, then, becomes not a straightforward representation of ‘what is’ in some absolute sense. Rather, Coming Home is a map of relations, conversations, and shared investments across difference in the landscape.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 24)

This recalls Mukurtu. An audit must distinguish data lost through neglect, data never collected because of bias, and knowledge intentionally withheld according to community protocols.
“The answer to these questions may surprise you: definitively no! If there is any single rule in design, it’s that context is queen. A design choice made in one context or for one audience does not translate to other contexts or audiences.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 20)
“Coming Home to Indigenous Place Names in Canada leverages the authority of the god’s-eye view to challenge the colonizer’s view, to advocate for a “reseeing” of the land under terms of engagement that recognize Indigenous sovereignty and respect Indigenous homelands. The extent of geographic territory included and the sheer number of names asserts the Indigenous presence as major, originary, and ongoing. This is by design. Pearce intentionally created the map with the same paper size, fold, scale, and projection as the map published by Natural Resources Canada, the country’s geographic authority.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 21)
“There is actually another twist on top of its intentionally authoritative view: the map does not reveal everything.53 As the cartographer, Pearce proceeded with the Indigenous methodologies of respect, responsibility, and reciprocity.54 What this meant in practice was caring for each name as Indigenous cultural property—securing the permissions for each name and respecting when communities did not want to share English translations of the name. She is definitive about the fact that the names are not data: “The place names aren’t datasets. The place names are cultural property being shared with the map that come from people.”” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 21)
“Cartography, then, becomes not a straightforward representation of “what is” in some absolute sense. Rather, Coming Home is a map of relations, conversations, and shared investments across difference in the landscape.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 24)
“The third principle of data feminism, and the theme of this chapter, is to elevate emotion and embodiment. As we have shown, these are crucial if often undervalued tools in the data communication toolbox. They help avoid inadvertently conveying the view from no body: the view from an imaginary and impossible standpoint that does not and cannot exist.” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 24)
“Rather than making universal rules and ratios (think: data-ink) that exclude some aspects of human experience in favor of others, our time is better spent working toward a more holistic and more inclusive ideal. All design fields, including visualization and data communication, are fields of possibility. Black feminist sociologist Patricia Hill Collins describes an ideal knowledge situation as one in which “neither ethics nor emotions are subordinated to reason.”57 Rebalancing emotion and reason opens up the data communication toolbox and allows us to focus on what truly matters in a design process: honoring context, architecting attention, and taking action to defy stereotypes and reimagine the world.58” (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020, p. 25).

title: Arguments & Plots
section: “Isn’t It Obvious?” & Lincoln Mullen: What makes a finding feel inevitable?
text:
“Isn’t It Obvious?” & Lincoln Mullen: What makes a finding feel inevitable?





Lincoln Mullen



Historian of American religion
Director, Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media
Creator of America’s Public Bible


Lincoln Mullen is a historian of American religion and nineteenth-century U.S. history at George Mason University. America’s Public Bible identifies biblical quotations in nineteenth-century newspapers.
Mullen begins with a recurring response to digital history: even when computational work presents an interpretation, someone claims that the result was already obvious. He asks what visual clarity does to our memory of what we knew before seeing the evidence.

“There is a particular form that this claim sometimes takes which I think is mistaken: the idea that even when interpretations or arguments from digital history work are presented, they do not tell us anything new.” (Mullen, 2018)
digital history failed to make an argument

A common response to digital history research is that has failed to make an argumentative or interpretative payoff commensurate with the amount of effort that has been put into it. Broadly speaking, I’m sympathetic to that claim. But there is a particular form that this claim sometimes takes which I think is mistaken: the idea that even when interpretations or arguments from digital history work are presented, they do not tell us anything new. Scott Weingart has written perceptively and more generally about the problem that “digital history can never be new.” I want to add only a small piece to that discussion.
“claim sometimes takes which I think is mistaken: the idea that even when interpretations or arguments from digital history work are presented, they do not tell us anything new.”
Section A annotations

Hong Ju Jin: I think visualization communicates so fast that viewers mistake quick comprehension for prior knowledge
Hong Ju Jin: Showing blank axes first proves audiences cannot actually predict the curve or scale before seeing the data.
Jack Goby: Very interesting to see this visualization come together. The fact that all 3 items shown in this visualization drop juristically between the years 1840-1850 is quite interesting. Very good thing to put a picture to the story here by the author!
Jack Miller: This is something that I see people talk about a lot with regards to studies and research. When research proves something that is already “common knowledge,” is it still worthwhile research? Answering this is really complicated actually, because it hinges on very complex issues, such as whether or not western science should be considered the final authority on defining our reality. However, completely disregarding all scientific process can lead to a lack of credible sources to cite in future research. It’s a complex back and forth of not devaluing the lived experiences of people (particularly indigenous and marginalized people), while upholding (western) standards of research. Because, like it or not, the dominant structure that we live in is a western one, which means that research needs to meet those western standards in order to be considered valid by the system at large, even if the phenomenon the research is proving is something widely known and accepted. It’s important to keep in mind that, while this can be a good system for standardization and ensuring validity of findings, it can also lead to the oppression, silencing, and/or assimilation of voices that fall outside of this system (this is especially true for indigenous cultures, which often approach and manage information very differently than we do in the west). This is a REALLY long way to say: the enforcement of western research standards is a very complicated subject, but researching “common knowledge” can still be important.
Mason Le: I think this is really good. It shows that a lot of us take the research done for granted without actually seeing how much work was needed to do it. Nobody truly knows for sure until something is researched.
Rachel Tam: This stood out to me because digital history can be built off previous historical information but wouldn’t using digital methods help find new patterns and information that was never recognized online?

title: Arguments & Plots
section: Why does Mullen show a blank chart?
text:
Why does Mullen show a blank chart?


Pause and have students predict the trend. The exercise records what they actually knew before the answer became visible.
Mullen would have guessed something “vaguely downwards,” but could not predict the scale or detailed pattern. His audiences could not reliably predict it either.

“Before showing the audience a visualization, I first show them a blank visualization with just the axes and title, and ask them to sketch out what they think the trend will be.” (Mullen, 2018)


“Before I made the visualization, I couldn’t predict the trend. I would have said something like ‘vaguely downwards.’ I certainly could not have predicted the scale.” (Mullen, 2018)

audiences claim they already know visualization
“The sense that a visualization is immediately explainable is the result, I think, of the ability of visualizations to rapidly and persuasively communicate large amounts of information.”
Matthew Lincoln has written about the “confabulation” or “just-so stories” that readers of visualizations can come up with in order to explain them. And it’s not just the audiences for visualizations who do this; I do it myself whenever I create visualizations for my own consumption. The sense that a visualization is immediately explainable is the result, I think, of the ability of visualizations to rapidly and persuasively communicate large amounts of information.

title: Arguments & Plots
text:
Was the result obvious?


Compare the result to students’ predictions. Visualization communicates information so quickly and persuasively that viewers can collapse learning into recognition.

“The sense that a visualization is immediately explainable is the result, I think, of the ability of visualizations to rapidly and persuasively communicate large amounts of information.” (Mullen, 2018)

Mullen focuses on how visual clarity makes unknown results feel familiar. Matthew Lincoln’s experiment, which we will examine next, raises the stakes by showing that historians can produce plausible explanations for opposing results.
Knowing that a phenomenon exists is not the same as knowing its timing, magnitude, structure, or relationships. Scholars knew newspapers reprinted one another before Viral Texts, but mapping the specific reprinting networks produced different knowledge.
The problem is that often it is not possible to know what a visualization would look like in advance, and so it should not be possible immediately after seeing it to explain it as something that we already know. To convey this point, I’ve been trying a new technique when giving talks. Before showing the audience a visualization, I first show them a blank visualization with just the axes and title, and ask them to sketch out what they think the trend will be. For instance, here is a blank visualization of the trends in the rate at which the Bible was quoted in nineteenth-century U.S. newspapers, from my America’s Public Bible project.
Before I made the visualization, I couldn’t predict the trend. I would have said something like “vaguely downwards.” I certainly could not have predicted the scale. When I have given this talk to various audiences, no one has been able to predict what the actual visualization should look like. Nor for that matter could anyone guess what the top ten most frequently quoted Bible verses were with any degree of accuracy—certainly not me.
A project need not discover a wholly unsuspected phenomenon. It may specify chronology, magnitude, distribution, relationships, exceptions, or change.

“Knowing that there is a network and knowing what the network is are two different kinds of knowledge.” (Mullen, 2018)

But scale and precision do not automatically produce an argument. Students should identify what their structured evidence makes newly knowable and why that difference matters for a humanistic question.

title: Arguments & Plots
section: How did America’s Public Bible turn newspapers into evidence?
text:
How did America’s Public Bible turn newspapers into evidence?


America’s Public Bible is an interactive scholarly work about how Americans used the Bible in public life during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Newspapers printed sermons and Sunday-school lessons, but biblical language also appeared in jokes, advertisements, election coverage, arguments about slavery, wartime commentary, and debates in which opposing sides invoked the same text.
The project begins with Chronicling America, the Library of Congress collection created through the National Digital Newspaper Program. The original project searched OCR text from roughly eleven million newspaper pages dated from 1836 through 1922. That scale makes manual reading impossible, but the OCR is also noisy: damaged paper, unusual layouts, and historical typefaces can turn text into gibberish.
Mullen’s workflow moves through several representations:

Newspaper page images are transformed into OCR text.
The text is searched for passages resembling verses from the King James Bible.
A supervised classification model estimates whether each candidate is genuinely a biblical quotation rather than a coincidental string match.
Identified quotations are aggregated by verse and date to produce trends.
Readers can move from a trend back to the matching newspaper pages to interpret who quoted a verse, in what context, and for what purpose.

The output is not simply a count of the word “Bible.” It links particular passages to particular pages and dates. The original interface let readers explore approximately 1,700 frequently quoted verses. Mullen found, for example, different temporal patterns for verses associated with nationalism, war, children, politics, and humor.
This is important methodologically. The visualization discovers patterns at a scale no individual could read, but the links back to page images allow close reading and error checking. Quantification proposes where to look; it does not replace interpretation.
The method also creates limitations we should audit:

Chronicling America is a large collection, not every U.S. newspaper.
OCR quality varies by newspaper, year, typography, and scan quality.
Beginning with the King James Version privileges one translation and may miss paraphrases or other versions.
A probability threshold determines which candidate passages become “quotations.”
Frequency cannot by itself tell us whether a verse was endorsed, criticized, parodied, or merely reprinted.

Mullen later described the project as an interpretive pyramid: source quotations form the base; aggregated trends and tables organize them; verse histories and longer essays build historical interpretation above them. That is useful for the semester project because it models how data, visualization, examples, and argument can remain connected.

“By identifying and studying quotations in American newspapers, America’s Public Bible offers a commentary on how the Bible was used in public life, uncovering trends and patterns that would be invisible to a single scholar’s reading of these documents.” (Mullen, 2023)

Sources: Mullen’s introduction to the original project; discussion of the classifier and visualization choices; published project.

title: Arguments & Plots
text:
Confabulation & Matthew Lincoln




Digital art historian
Research software engineer
Network analysis and visualization


Matthew Lincoln is a digital art historian and research software engineer whose scholarship examines networks of artistic production, especially early modern printmaking.
The post grows from dissertation research powered by network analysis. It deepens Mullen’s question: after a visualization makes a pattern legible, can historians distinguish a result that sounds reasonable in retrospect from one they actually knew in advance?

“It’s a tale as old as the ‘digital humanities’ itself: skeptics rightly asking whether or not we are actually learning anything new by using quantitative approaches to historical questions.” (Matthew Lincoln, 2015)

Section A annotations

Hong Ju Jin: just because an explanation makes sense in hindsight doesn’t mean we actually knew it before
Hong Ju Jin: this stood out to me that historians can easily make two completely opposite trends sound totally believable using the exact same background.
Jack Goby: Wondering why scholars have this outlook on quantitative approaches. I think this could possibly be because they are part of an older generation that sometimes is against technology helping to make conclusions about history. If anyone has any insight let me know.
Jack Miller: :)
Mason Le: This shows that it WAS beneficial that they began to reach out to more connections that were global/abroad!
Min Kim: Seems like this pinpoints why confabulation is so dangerous in research. Our ability to construct a convincing post-hoc narrative is essentially limitless. When we mistake that narrative fluency for actual prior knowledge, we devalue quantitative analysis and trick ourselves into believing we never needed empirical verification in the first place.
Min Kim: The problem with relying solely on retrospective framing is that historical facts are vast enough to serve whatever storyline we want to substantiate. When both an outcome and its exact opposite feel entirely expected, our standard for what constitutes an explanation needs to be reassessed.
Min Kim: also wanted to define confabulation. it is misinterpreted memories about oneself without any conscious intention. It is genuinely believing their false recollections are true.
Min Kim: I think it is possible because not every single historical dataset has been analyzed using quantitative approaches, and new knowledge can be created as technology grows and enables new analysis
Min Kim: good example of how computational methods complement qualitative history. I think translating collaboration into concrete graph properties can give us a reliable baseline to test our historical theories against, rather than just guessing

title: Arguments & Plots
section: What do these plots appear to show?
text:
What do these plots appear to show?







dutch print making → internationally vs domestic
I’ve run in to an odd version of this in presenting my own research. In my dissertation, I explore how the organization of artistic print producers (including designers, plate cutters, and publishers) in the Netherlands shifted between 1500 and 1700, and what these changes may have meant for individual artists and for their works of art. I have powered this research, in large part, though computational network analysis of a large database of prints from this period. Without getting bogged down in the details, this essentially involves measuring how certain network properties, such as overall centralization, or density, or transitivity, change over time. Let’s take a look at two examples.
reasonable vs already knew
PLOT 1: This plot visualizes the changing balance of domestic vs. international connections made by Dutch printmakers. A value of 0 indicates an even balance of connections; positive values indicate majority international connections; negative values indicate majority domestic connections. → What are we seeing? Between 1570–1580, Dutch printmakers shifted very rapidly from making the majority of their connections internally, to now making more than half of them to international collaborators. […] Thus, it is not surprising to see that Dutch printmakers also turned outward in this period.
PLOT 2: This plot visualizes the changing balance of domestic vs. international connections made by Dutch printmakers. A value of 0 indicates an even balance of connections; positive values indicate majority international connections; negative values indicate majority domestic connections. → What are we seeing? Around 1575, Dutch printmakers shifted very rapidly from making the majority of their connections internationally, to now making more than half of them to domestic collaborators […] Thus, it is not surprising to see that Dutch printmakers turned inward in this period.
“Neither results seems particularly surprising, once we’ve constructed a just-so story to rationalize the answers. You’ll have to go look at my actual presentation on this to see the “real” answer (or, at least, the answer as actually derived from my dataset — whether or not this is representative of true historical trends is a fair and fascinating question :)”
“coming up with post-facto historical explanations to contextualize any given observation, that we are particularly susceptible to confabulating these post-facto rationalizations with the idea that we somehow knew the results of this quantitative work already (and, implicitly, that we didn’t need to waste our time doing it.) I”
What did Lincoln change?

One plot is the result. The other is the same result multiplied by -1.

Why can we explain both?
The plots show opposite trends, yet Lincoln constructs a persuasive explanation for either. He calls these “just-so stories”: post-hoc narratives that make an observed result sound inevitable.

“Neither result seems particularly surprising, once we’ve constructed a just-so story to rationalize the answers.” (Matthew Lincoln, 2015)

Historians are trained to contextualize. That strength becomes a weakness when contextualization is mistaken for prior knowledge or causal proof. Interpretation needs friction: alternative hypotheses, comparison cases, recorded expectations, robustness checks, and evidence beyond the pattern.

title: Arguments & Plots
section: How does a museum record become a network?
text:
How does a museum record become a network?


Lincoln builds his analysis from two digitized museum collections: the British Museum in London and the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam. Both contain extensive European print holdings and detailed curatorial metadata. He analyzes them separately rather than merging them. Agreement between the collections makes it less likely that a result is merely an artifact of one museum’s acquisition and cataloguing history; disagreement becomes a reason for caution.
The scale is substantial but uneven. For Dutch artists, for example, the British Museum data include 682 artists associated with 14,399 prints, while the Rijksmuseum data include 730 artists associated with 30,738 prints. The British Museum has far more English prints than the Rijksmuseum, which affects how confidently Lincoln interprets the English results. A museum database records what survives, what entered a collection, and what curators described—not every print or working relationship that once existed.
Lincoln then operationalizes those object records as a production network:

A node represents a person involved in print production, including designers, plate cutters, and publishers.
A surviving print is treated as evidence of a direct or indirect professional relationship among the people credited with producing it.
An edge connects two people who co-produced at least one print during a given span of time.
Dated records allow him to construct successive time slices rather than collapsing two centuries into one static network.

For example, a 1587 print designed by Bartholomeus Spranger and engraved by Hendrick Goltzius produces a dated connection between them. Repeating that transformation across many records generates the networks pictured here.
This is a deliberately partial representation. It does not include family, friendship, finance, guild membership, religion, or physical distance unless those relationships also appear through print co-production. Lincoln compares it to an X-radiograph: some information is removed so that a particular structure becomes easier to see.
Source: Lincoln, 2017, fig. 3, pp. 28–29.

title: Arguments & Plots
text:
How does Lincoln measure internationalization?


Lincoln groups people using the national or regional classifications already assigned by museum cataloguers: Dutch, Flemish, British, French, German, and Italian. He stresses that these are modern, retrospective categories, especially unstable for the Low Countries during the Eighty Years’ War. He therefore treats nationality as a category to test rather than a foundational historical truth.
For each regional group, he calculates an external/internal index, or EI index:
[ EI = ]

+1 means every measured connection crosses the group’s boundary.
0 means an equal balance of external and internal connections.
-1 means every measured connection remains within the group.

The figure illustrates why group size and structure matter. Group A has mostly internal connections and therefore a negative index. Group B makes slightly more external connections and has a positive index. Group C connects only internally and reaches -1. Calculating this measure across successive time slices produces the trend lines in Lincoln’s plots.
The measure does not prove why collaboration changed. It describes the balance of ties created by Lincoln’s data model. Its meaning still depends upon museum coverage, attribution practices, dating, the treatment of repeated collaborations, and the imposed national categories.
Source: Lincoln, 2017, fig. 4, pp. 28–30.

title: Arguments & Plots
text:
What did Lincoln actually find?


The real Dutch result is the inward turn: Dutch print producers moved rapidly in the 1570s from mostly foreign connections to a roughly even balance and then came to favor domestic collaborators. The inverted outward turn in the blog post was the fabricated result.
Lincoln’s larger answer is more interesting than simply choosing the correct plot. He calls it continuity within disruption. The black lines are the patterns observed in the British Museum data. The red ribbons show the range produced by simulated networks with the same regional population sizes and overall connectivity. An EI index above zero indicates more external, international connections; below zero indicates more internal, domestic connections.
Much of the black line falls within the red simulated range. This means that many apparently sudden changes did not require a story centered on one famous artist, national school, war, or political turning point. Gradual changes in the relative size of regional printmaking communities could themselves produce abrupt-looking shifts in collaboration.
To create that comparison, Lincoln generates networks with the same number of people, the same regional group sizes, and comparable overall connectivity as the observed museum network. The simulation begins with regional clusters and then adds internal and international connections probabilistically. New ties preferentially attach to already well-connected people, reflecting a print industry in which reputation, expertise, and established professional connections could attract further collaboration. He repeats this process to produce the red range rather than one alternative line.
The mismatches still matter. Lincoln uses the places where the black line leaves the red range to identify periods requiring more specific historical explanation. These include unusually domestic Dutch connections after the end of the Dutch Revolt, unusually international Flemish connections around the Spanish invasion of Antwerp and artist migration, and the prolonged inward orientation of Italian production following plague and economic collapse.
The methodological lesson is not that historical events do not matter. It is that we should first ask how much of an observed pattern can be explained by broader structural conditions. Model failure then becomes evidence: it directs attention toward the moments when demographic structure is not enough.

“This paper has shown that what appeared as dramatic, discontinuous changes in one register of these print production networks … can, by in large, be explained as the results of gradual, continuous changes in another (the relative populations of each community).” (Lincoln, 2017, p. 40)

Source: Matthew D. Lincoln, “Continuity and Disruption in European Networks of Print Production, 1550–1750,” Artl@s Bulletin 6, no. 3 (2017), fig. 7, pp. 35–40. https://docs.lib.purdue.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1120&context=artlas

title: Arguments & Plots
section: Data Biographies & Heather Krause: How do we get to know a dataset?
text:
Data Biographies & Heather Krause: How do we get to know a dataset?




Data scientist
Founder, Datassist and We All Count


Heather Krause is a data scientist and founder of Datassist and We All Count. Her work focuses on data equity and supports journalists, nonprofits, and policy organizations.
Mullen and Lincoln identify two dangers at the point where patterns become arguments: a new result can look obvious, and almost any result can acquire a plausible story. Krause now takes us backward in the analytical chain. Before interpreting a pattern, how well do we understand the data that produced it?
The piece emerged from NICAR, the Investigative Reporters and Editors conference devoted to computer-assisted reporting. Journalists evaluate the interests, credibility, and limits of human sources. Krause asks them to bring the same skepticism to datasets.

“When I’m introducing students to the world of data analysis and visualization, I’m often asked what the most important step in working with data is, and my answer is always the same: developing data biographies.” (Krause, 2017)

What is a data biography?
Krause defines a data biography as the background or origin of data. You would not publish a human source without learning who they are and why they might know or say something. Data deserves the same investigation.

“You’d never write a story without researching the person who supplied your information—why treat data any differently?” (Krause, 2017)


“For every piece of data you’re going to include in your story, you need to create a data biography—the background, or origin of your data.” (Krause, 2017)

Where includes institution, jurisdiction, platform, file, and chain of custody. Who includes collectors, funders, subjects, and maintainers. How includes sampling, instruments, definitions, cleaning, and aggregation. Why includes administrative, commercial, advocacy, scientific, or political purposes.
Section A annotations

Hong Ju Jin: I see that treat data like a human source by thoroughly vetting its background before trusting the numbers.
Jack Goby: Interesting thought here. Giving a explanation to our data analysis and visualization does probably help the viewer a lot. On the same idea with that, giving a user a method to your projects most definitely helps when the user wants to do something like going deeper into whatever topic you are analyzing.
Mason Le: This example definitely helps understand the above bullet points and how they are important to us as readers/consumers of data.
Min Kim: Numbers are not objective facts; they represent human records with embedded motivations, limitations, and blind spots.
Min Kim: A rise in reported numbers often signals improved reporting safety or institutional trust rather than an actual increase in violence. Conflating administrative reporting rates with true incidence misunderstands the dynamics of sensitive data.
Rachel Tam: This reminds me of how we interact online and how often we underestimate the amount of data we give away. Something small (like our names) can reveal a lot about us. This makes me wonder how much information can be learned about someone just from the data they share online.

title: Arguments & Plots
section: What did the first plot seem to show?
text:
What did the first plot seem to show?

Is this a change in the world, or a change in the data?

Krause’s team used United Nations data on violence against women. Quick plots appeared to show surprising changes in several countries.

“Trends in some countries were surprising and indicated unusual changes in the rates of violence against women. We wondered what was happening.” (Krause, 2017)

This is when exploratory visualization is valuable but dangerous. A plot reveals an anomaly worth investigating; it does not yet tell us what generated it. Did the phenomenon change, or did the process of observing, defining, or recording it change?

title: Arguments & Plots
section: What was hidden inside one variable?
text:
What was hidden inside one variable?


The same variable combined observations about all women, particular age groups, and particular marital statuses. Documentation also revealed different collectors, purposes, and methods. A shared column name made unlike evidence look comparable.

“All this data was lumped together in the same variable—the same name, the same label, and no hint as to the differences in the data sources.” (Krause, 2017)


“All of our data, collected using different methods and for different reasons, was presented in the same table, with the same variable name and the same labels.” (Krause, 2017)

A tidy table can conceal heterogeneous evidence. Consistent labels are not proof of consistent meaning. An API can likewise return uniform fields whose records were generated under changing rules and institutional purposes.

title: Arguments & Plots
section: Did violence change, or did collection change?
text:
Did violence change, or did collection change?







Some apparent changes were differences in collection. Rwanda was different because collection appeared reasonably consistent, allowing the team to investigate the spike more seriously.

“Once we had completed our data biography, it became clear that some of the trends we had seen that looked like significant changes in violence rates were actually variations in the data collection.” (Krause, 2017)

Even then, provenance did not supply causation. Was there backlash against political change, or did reporting increase because women had more recourse? A data biography determines what a pattern might mean; it does not eliminate interpretation.

title: Arguments & Plots
section: What should a dataset audit produce?
text:
What should a dataset audit produce?




Layer
Questions




Provenance
Who, where, when, why?


Structure
What does each row, field, and identifier represent?


Transformation
What was cleaned, merged, inferred, or excluded?


Coverage
Who or what is present, absent, or incomparable?


Interpretation
Which claims can this evidence support?





An audit should leave evidence, not merely produce caution. Useful outputs include source notes, a data dictionary, missing-value and duplicate checks, comparisons across time or groups, records of cleaning decisions, and examples of ambiguous cases.
The goal is not a perfectly objective dataset. It is enough understanding to make bounded claims and show future users how those claims were reached.
