title: Platforms & Popularity
section: Who Are Melanie Walsh and Maria Antoniak?
text:
Who Are Melanie Walsh and Maria Antoniak?





Melanie Walsh



Read her Public Books piece last week
Remember Cultural analytics from the Manovich reading?
Also her textbook Introduction to Cultural Analytics & Python





Maria Antoniak



Assistant Professor at the University of Colorado Boulder in CS, affiliated with Information Science and the Boulder NLP Group
Specializes in natural language processing for culture, language, and social systems
Directs the Culture, Language, and Systems (CLS) Lab.



Melanie Walsh works across literary studies, cultural analytics, media studies, and library and information science. Her research asks how data and computational methods shape culture and how those methods can help us understand cultural life in turn.
Maria Antoniak is a computer scientist whose work connects natural language processing with cultural and social questions. She directs the Culture, Language, and Systems Lab at the University of Colorado Boulder.
Their collaboration matters because the Goodreads essay is neither simply a statistical analysis nor simply an interpretation of reviews. They assemble more than 120,000 reviews and use computational methods to examine reader activity at scale, but they also interpret the platform, its ownership, and its categories.
This is a useful example of the methodological combination we have been discussing throughout the course: computation expands what they can observe, while humanistic questions determine what those patterns might mean.

title: Platforms & Popularity
text:
What Is Goodreads?

Why might we want to study Goodreads as a cultural platform? How much do we understand about this platform? What is a social media platform even?

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: Where do social media platforms come from?
text:
Where do social media platforms come from?
What is web 2.0?


We will return to the technical history of Web 2.0 and APIs on Thursday, so here I only want enough context to understand the reading’s institutional setting.
The term Web 2.0 became popular in the mid-2000s as a way of describing sites organized around participation, user-generated content, and networked interaction. The earlier web was never entirely passive, but platforms increasingly made profiles, posting, tagging, rating, commenting, and sharing central to the experience.
Every one of these actions creates data. A book review is cultural expression, but its star rating, tags, likes, comments, timestamp, and relationship to a user profile can also be stored and analyzed. Participation is therefore both the experience offered to users and a source of value for the platform.
This recalls our discussion of GitHub and data labor: the platform becomes valuable partly because users fill it with content, classifications, relationships, and activity.

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: How Did Reading Become Social Media?
text:
How Did Reading Become Social Media?








Year
Platform development




2005
LibraryThing launches as a personal and social catalog


2006
Shelfari launches with virtual bookshelves and reader communities


2007
Goodreads launches around finding, tracking, and discussing books


2008
Amazon acquires Shelfari


2013
Amazon acquires Goodreads


2016
Shelfari is folded into Goodreads





“Though Goodreads data is a boon for literary criticism and a potentially trans­ formative development for literary culture, it is also a boon for corporations. Amazon’s looming shadow over Goodreads data helps bring into focus a more financially minded definition of a classic” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 3)
Goodreads was part of a wider mid-2000s rise of social cataloging. LibraryThing launched in 2005, Shelfari in 2006, and Goodreads in 2007. These sites let people construct virtual bookshelves, describe books, compare collections, join groups, and receive recommendations.
Books work particularly well for social cataloging because they already have titles, authors, editions, ISBNs, covers, publishers, and established descriptive metadata. Platforms could import or reuse bibliographic data and then add a new layer of user activity.
The history also shows consolidation. Amazon acquired Shelfari in 2008 and Goodreads in 2013; Shelfari was later folded into Goodreads. Amazon’s 2013 announcement described Goodreads as a community for discovery and discussion, while also emphasizing its connection to Kindle.

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: How did we study readers before the digital era?
text:
How did we study readers before the digital era?


This is the cover of Janice Radway’s Reading the Romance, first published in 1984. Radway combined interviews, questionnaires, and ethnographic observation to study a community of women who read romance novels. Rather than treating meaning as something contained entirely within a book, she examined reading as a social practice shaped by readers’ lives, relationships, and uses for literature.
Before Goodreads, scholars could study readers and literary taste through several kinds of evidence:

Publishing records, sales figures, and bestseller lists documented which books were purchased or commercially prominent, but purchasing a book does not necessarily tell us whether or how it was read.
Library circulation records documented borrowing within particular institutions and communities. These records could show patterns of access and selection, while rarely preserving readers’ interpretations.
Reviews, letters, diaries, marginalia, and fan publications preserved richer responses, but only for readers whose writing was published, collected, or archived.
Surveys, interviews, focus groups, and ethnographies could ask readers directly about their practices and interpretations, although these studies generally involved smaller, researcher-defined groups.
Book clubs, reading societies, schools, critics, publishers, and prize committees did not simply measure taste. They also helped define and organize it.

These methods did not produce an incomplete version of Goodreads data. They asked somewhat different questions and often supplied forms of social context that a rating or digital shelf cannot capture. Radway, for example, could ask why readers selected romance novels and what reading enabled them to do in their everyday lives.
Goodreads changes the scale, continuity, and granularity of the available record. Readers routinely leave ratings, reviews, shelves, friendships, and other traces without first entering a formal research study. Those activities become machine-readable data that can be aggregated across millions of accounts.
That shift creates the transition into Walsh and Antoniak: Goodreads gives scholars unprecedented access to everyday reader responses, but those responses are recorded through categories and interfaces designed by a commercial platform. Does Goodreads merely reveal literary taste, or does it also organize and produce taste through its shelves, rankings, recommendations, and ownership?

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: How Do The Authors Study Goodreads?
text:
How Do The Authors Study Goodreads?
What is the value of scale? How do we transform reviews into data? How do they get this data?


The tensions between democratic potential and corporate exploitation that we observe in the Goodreads classics are characteristic of many social networks and Web 2.0 platforms, which fundamentally rely on user-created content. These dynamics have been studied extensively by scholars of fandom, new media, and digital culture, among other fields.10 Yet how social network dynamics and the internet economy are reshaping literary culture, in particular, is still a relatively new conversation, led by critics such as Murray, Aarthi Vadde, Lisa Nakamura, and Mark McGurl.11
“For the twenty-first century, we might update Van Doren’s definition and say that a classic is simply a book that continues to make money in whatever form it takes, whether as a print book, audiobook, e-book, screen adaptation, or as the subject of millions of online book reviews. In fact, it is clear, based on the Goodreads reviews that we analyze in this essay, that indus­ tries such as film, television, publishing, e-commerce, and tech not only profit from the classics but profit from each other in a circular loop, benefiting from the reinforcement of works as classics in other mediums and domains. Considered together, this classics industry,” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 3)
“we hope to contribute to this emerging conversation. We also hope to add a quantitative, data-driven perspective to the discussion by curating a collection of more than 120,000 Goodreads reviews and by using computational methods to study some of the most salient trends. We believe that digital literary culture is an area that especially rewards the convergence of digital humanities meth­ ods and contemporary literary criticism. The massive number of Goodreads ratings and reviews is part of what makes the platform worthy of study and fi­ nancially lucrative, but also what makes Goodreads difficult to understand in broad strokes. Digital humanities and cultural analytics scholars have demon­ strated, however, that computational methods can help us better understand cultural phenomena at scale. By employing these methods on Goodreads data in particular, we build on previous Goodreads-related DH research” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 4)
“Scale is not our only motivation for using computational methods. The contem­ porary book world, including but not limited to Goodreads and Amazon, is in­ creasingly governed by algorithms and data, which presents a number of chal­ lenges for contemporary literary scholars.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 4)
“To provide one answer to Murray’s ur­ gent question, we believe that computational methods can supply a way of doc­ umenting, understanding, and critiquing algorithmic culture and its effects. By collecting and analyzing Goodreads data with computational methods, we are able to see, for example, that Goodreads only publicly displays a small fraction of its data. We are also able to detail some of the specific social effects of the platform’s default sorting algorithm, which prioritizes the most liked and most commented on reviews. This digital infrastructure produces a feedback loop among Goodreads reviews, in which reviews that receive attention continue to receive more attention ad nauseam. This feedback loop is a fitting metaphor for the consecration of the classics on Goodreads more broadly. Though Goodreads users technically define the clas­ sics for themselves, their definitions are clearly shaped by a reciprocal system of reinforcing influences — old institutions like high schools, universities, and publishing houses as well as new institutions like Amazon. The result is a read­ er-produced vision of the classics that is surprisingly less diverse, in terms of” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 4)

“This essay understands Goodreads users to be readers as well as ‘amateur critics.’” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 5)
“The digital platform of Goodreads similarly allows amateurs to perform acts of literary criticism, to publish their own analyses and judgements of literature, without formal training and without access to traditional publishing venues.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 5)
“The three main ways that Goodreads users act as amateur critics are by rating books between one and five stars, by reviewing books in 15,000 characters or less, and by ‘shelving’ books into categories.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 5)
“To close this introduction, we foreground our own approach to Goodreads data, since the exploitation of user data is a central subject of this essay. We have chosen not to publicly share our dataset of Goodreads reviews, though we have shared the code that we used to collect data from the Goodreads website, and we have obtained explicit permission from each Goodreads user who is directly quoted in this essay. 14 We believe that ethical approaches to user data will con­ tinue to be one of the most important conversations for digital humanities and cultural analytics research, and we expand on our choices further in the Appendix.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 5)
The authors call Goodreads users “amateur critics.” Amateur does not mean unserious or unskilled. It distinguishes these readers from professional critics and academics while recognizing that they interpret, evaluate, categorize, and publicly debate literature.
The interface formats those critical acts. A star rating compresses judgment into a number. A review permits extended language but imposes a character limit. A shelf classifies a book while potentially mixing genre, value, mood, identity, reading status, and personal memory.
Each action is expressive for the user and useful as structured or semi-structured data for Goodreads. This dual function is central to the essay.
“The first telling clue about these shelves is that the Goodreads website fluidly refers to them as ‘shelves,’ ‘genres,’ and ‘tags.’ This slippery relationship points to a significant evolution of genre among readers and amateur critics in the twenty-first century: genre is being subsumed and reshaped by tagging.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 6)
Walsh and Antoniak treat Goodreads users as readers and amateur critics. Users evaluate books through ratings and reviews, but they also classify books through shelves. Goodreads fluidly calls these categories shelves, genres, and tags. This slippage matters because a personal organizational practice becomes part of a collective classification system.
The platform therefore produces a folksonomy: a bottom-up taxonomy generated through user tags. That sounds democratic because readers can create categories beyond those used by publishers, libraries, or universities. Yet Goodreads aggregates this labor into its own enormous library and turns shelves into advertising categories.
This lets me reconnect the article to our earlier conversation about data labor. Readers are not only expressing opinions. Their activity organizes books and readers for a platform owned by Amazon.
“Shelves are also financially lucrative for Goodreads and Amazon, the classics shelf particularly so. Each time a Goodreads user shelves a book in their personal library, that user simultaneously shelves the same book in the platform’s massive library of more than two billion books.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 7)
“By shelving books, Goodreads users also (more unsettlingly) organize themselves into coherent audience categories that can be effectively targeted by advertisers.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 8)
Goodreads users collectively classify an enormous catalog without being paid as catalogers. Their shelves make books discoverable, generate recommendations, define audiences, and supply advertising keywords.
This connects directly to our earlier discussion of data labor. The activity does not have to feel like work to create economic value. Users may shelve books for themselves or their communities, while Goodreads and Amazon benefit from the aggregated result.
Walsh and Antoniak compare this system to Netflix’s microgenres. Netflix paid people to tag films, then combined those tags with viewing behavior. Goodreads instead crowdsources much of its classification labor to readers. In both cases, classification becomes a competitive asset.
This does not invalidate the pleasure or community readers gain from Goodreads. It asks us to hold user benefit and corporate extraction together.

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: How does the platform shape the data? How do the authors try to get around these constraints?
text:
How does the platform shape the data? How do the authors try to get around these constraints?


“authors’ race and ethnicity, than those represented by U.S. literature syllabi, though more diverse in terms of genre, including more genre fiction, young adult fiction, and adapted fiction.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 5)
“The first telling clue about these shelves is that the Goodreads website fluidly refers to them as “shelves,” “genres,” and “tags.” This slippery relationship points to a significant evolution of genre among readers and amateur critics in the twenty-first century: genre is being subsumed and reshaped by tagging. Tagging is a common system for classifying and organizing content on the in­ ternet, in which users tag digital content with their own free-form descriptions, keywords, and metadata (think hashtags on Twitter). The shelf system on Goodreads is a social or collaborative tagging system because users can apply different tags to the same content, essentially crowdsourcing book categoriza­ tion. Prior computational social science and natural language processing re­ search has explored how these collaborative tagging systems produce “folk taxonomies” or folksonomies, classification systems built by communities from the ground up. 17 Literary genre, in the hands of internet users equipped with tagging systems, has similarly blossomed into a grassroots taxonomy that in­ corporates conventional genres but also splinters into new genres, microgen­ res, publishing industry categories, reception metadata, hashtags, and more.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 6)
““users” are mostly authors, who mold genre to create their own literary works, the ambiguous term suggests that others can use genre, too, including readers and amateur critics. Thus, “classics” emerges as an important contemporary genre for readers in addition to a label of literary value and publishing category.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 6)
“Shelves are also financially lucrative for Goodreads and Amazon, the classics shelf particularly so. Each time a Goodreads user shelves a book in their per­ sonal library, that user simultaneously shelves the same book in the platform’s massive library of more than two billion books.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 7)
““Goodreads turns the reader into a worker,” as Lisa Nakamura observes” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 7)
“Though “classics” is just one Goodreads shelf among thousands, it is one of the most important and foundational. In the website’s earliest days, the company used “classics” as their first anchoring example to introduce and explain the shelving system: “You can create your own personal bookshelves. From classics to canadabooks, to childrenslit and geek, you can create any category that suits your personal taste.” 22 Ten years later, the classics remained Goodreads go-to example: “Shelf names range from classics and coffee-table-books to childrens-lit and sci-fi — you can create any category that suits your personal taste.” 23 Because “classics” supposedly represents the oldest and most tradi­ tional literary category, it serves as an effective foil for any unconventional lit­ erary category a Goodreads user might dream up, and it also invites a mass of readers and amateur critics to participate in a seemingly elite conversation. The classics thus make the entire shelf system legible and appealing.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 7)
“crowdsources the enormous work of organizing two billion books to the masses. 25 By shelving books, Goodreads users also (more unsettlingly) orga­ nize themselves into coherent audience categories that can be effectively tar­ geted by advertisers. The same shelves that Goodreads users invent are sold as advertising target keywords, as Goodreads’ informational material for advertis­ ers shows in figure 2.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 8)
“This digital infrastructure produces a feedback loop among Goodreads reviews, in which reviews that receive attention continue to receive more attention ad nauseam.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 4)
The reading gives us a concrete algorithmic feedback loop. Goodreads defaults to displaying reviews that already have the most likes and comments. Reviews that become visible therefore have more opportunities to receive additional engagement, which helps keep them visible.
The platform is not merely recording which reviews are popular. Its sorting system participates in producing their popularity. Walsh and Antoniak use this as a metaphor for the Goodreads classics more broadly: established books receive institutional and platform attention that can reinforce their established status.
This is where I want to distinguish an algorithm from a neutral calculation. An algorithm applies rules, but those rules determine which signals matter and what users encounter. We can observe some effects of the default sort without having full access to every detail of Goodreads’ recommendation systems.


Democratic potential

Readers publish criticism
Communities form around books
Users challenge established value
New genres enter “the classics”


Corporate extraction

Readers provide unpaid metadata
Shelves become advertising categories
Algorithms concentrate attention
Amazon controls the resulting data


“It is not possible to ‘make a blanket case for or against the emancipatory potential of participatory culture on the Internet.’” (Vadde, quoted in Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 34)
“We believe this framing is helpful for teasing out how Goodreads users sometimes explicitly resist Goodreads and produce remarkably interesting amateur criticism all while being exploited by Goodreads.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 34)
The essay’s strongest claim is not that Goodreads is secretly bad or purely liberating. Participatory culture is already commercialized, industrialized, and plural. Users can experience genuine community and critical agency inside a system that extracts value from their activity.
Treating users only as exploited workers would erase their creativity and relationships. Treating Goodreads only as democratization would erase ownership, advertising, algorithmic amplification, and Amazon’s broader position in publishing and media.
The authors maintain this tension because both dimensions are empirically present. This is also a model for studying platforms: avoid allowing either corporate power or user agency to become the whole story.

“For these reasons, we have chosen not to publicly share our dataset, though we have shared the code that we used to collect data from the Goodreads website.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 37)
Walsh and Antoniak explicitly connect their research ethics to the subject of the essay. Because corporate exploitation of user data is central to their argument, they do not want to reproduce that extraction by releasing a large collection of reviews for unrestricted reuse.

This gives us an important distinction among open methods, open data, and ethical research. Transparency does not require making every piece of human-generated data maximally open. The choice connects back to our discussion of Christen and relational access.

They shared collection code, but not the review dataset
They requested permission from every user quoted
Public availability did not automatically equal ethical reuse
The research critiques the same extraction it might otherwise reproduce

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: What is the difference between genre and tagging?
text:
What is the difference between genre and tagging?
Where have we seen folksonomies before? What is the problem of an algorithmic echo chamber?


“The shelf system on Goodreads is a social or collaborative tagging system because users can apply different tags to the same content, essentially crowdsourcing book categorization.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 6)
“Literary genre, in the hands of internet users equipped with tagging systems, has similarly blossomed into a grassroots taxonomy that incorporates conventional genres but also splinters into new genres, microgenres, publishing industry categories, reception metadata, hashtags, and more.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 6)
Walsh and Antoniak focus first on shelves because Goodreads itself moves fluidly among the terms shelves, genres, and tags. A shelf can describe an established genre, a reading status, an affective response, a subject, or an intensely personal category.
When many users apply these free-form labels, their individual descriptions become a collaborative tagging system or folksonomy. This can produce classifications that are more flexible than a controlled vocabulary designed by experts.
But the platform does not merely host these categories. It aggregates them. A user who places a book on a personal shelf also contributes to the classification of that book in Goodreads’ platform-wide database.
The sensitive examples matter. Categories related to mental illness or abuse might help readers organize meaningful experiences, but they can also become market segments. Classification changes meaning when it moves from personal expression to advertising infrastructure.

title: Platforms & Popularity
text:
Why Focus on Classics?
What is the Classics Industry?


In fact, it is clear, based on the Goodreads reviews that we analyze in this essay, that industries such as film, television, publishing, e-commerce, and tech not only profit from the classics but profit from each other in a circular loop, benefiting from the reinforcement of works as classics in other mediums and domains. Considered together, this classics industry, as we call it — a formulation inspired by and indebted to Simone Murray’s “adaptation industry” as well as Pierre Bourdieu’s theories of cultural production9 — proves to be one of the strongest influences on Goodreads users’ perception of the classics.
“This flood of Goodreads classics content represents an excitingly large archive of amateur criticism and reader responses, an opportunity for scholars to hear nonacademic readers’ voices in ways that were difficult if not impossible before the internet” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 2)
“Yet the question — what is a classic? — remains surprisingly powerful in the twenty-first century because the classics are alive and thriving on the internet, in the marketplace, and among readers, even if not in universities or among academics. Contemporary readers not only use the term ‘classic,’ they use it a lot and often have strong feelings about it.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 2)
These quotations establish the two reasons for studying Goodreads. First, the platform preserves an enormous archive of reader responses from people who are usually absent from published literary criticism. Second, it shows that the category “classic” remains culturally active even though literary scholars have largely shifted toward the language of canons and canon formation.
“Perhaps most glaringly outdated is the word ‘classic.’ Literary scholars don’t often use the term anymore, at least not as a serious label for literature ‘of the highest rank or importance.’ In 1991, John Guillory declared that the term classic was ‘all but retired.’” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 1)
“Instead, in academic conversations, the ardent language of the ‘classics’ has largely been displaced by the more critical vocabulary of the ‘canon,’ which frames literary significance more carefully as a product of cultural selection.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 1)
Walsh and Antoniak begin with a vocabulary problem. Literary scholars have largely moved away from “classic” because it can make literary value sound natural, universal, and timeless. “Canon” more clearly names a process: people and institutions select, preserve, teach, publish, and repeatedly discuss particular works.
Yet “classic” remains extremely active outside academic literary criticism. Goodreads users apply it as a shelf, genre, judgment, aspiration, complaint, and marketing category. The term has not disappeared; it has migrated into platforms, publishing, adaptations, and everyday reader discourse.
This opening establishes why Goodreads matters as a cultural archive. If scholars only study academic criticism, they miss where many contemporary discussions of literary value actually occur.
This feedback loop is a fitting metaphor for the consecration of the classics on Goodreads more broadly. Though Goodreads users technically define the classics for themselves, their definitions are clearly shaped by a reciprocal system of reinforcing influences — old institutions like high schools, universities, and publishing houses as well as new institutions like Amazon. The result is a reader-produced vision of the classics that is surprisingly less diverse, in terms of authors’ race and ethnicity, than those represented by U.S. literature syllabi, though more diverse in terms of genre, including more genre fiction, young adult fiction, and adapted fiction. Though Goodreads users seem strongly influenced by traditional institutions and the capitalist marketplace, they nevertheless demonstrate enormous creativity in finding ways to make this critical conversation their own — parodying and panning different literary styles, reliving and reimagining high school English classes, pushing back against the perceived arbiters of literary authority, and publicly changing their minds.

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: What do we learn about Goodreads’ Classics vs. AP and Open Syllabus?
text:
What do we learn about Goodreads’ Classics vs. AP and Open Syllabus?


Top 100 most shelved as classics across 2006–2019
+
Top 100 most read classics during one week in September 2019
= 144 unique titles
How does this combine accumulated status with current activity?
“When Goodreads users shelve books, they supposedly classify books on their own terms without direct intervention from the academy, the publishing industry, or Amazon.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 11)
“Yet when we collate the books that Goodreads users have collaboratively consecrated as classics, we find the strong influence of school curricula and what we call the classics industry, the interrelated network of businesses that generate and profit from the classics such as publishing, film and television, and internet corporations like Goodreads itself.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 11)
The Goodreads classics do not arrive as a ready-made research object. Walsh and Antoniak construct the collection through two platform-defined signals.
The most-shelved list captures accumulated classification across Goodreads’ history. The “Most Read This Week” list captures a more immediate and platform-promoted form of activity. Because the lists overlap, combining one hundred titles from each produces 144 unique works.
This choice is an example of operationalization. The authors define a Goodreads classic through observable platform actions rather than assuming they can identify all classics in the abstract.
It also means the dataset inherits Goodreads’ interface and counting systems. “Most read” is based on what users report through Goodreads, not direct observation of reading. “Most shelved” depends on how users employ the classics tag.
“First, the Goodreads classics are considerably less di­ verse in terms of the race and ethnicity of their authors. Race is extremely com­ plex and difficult to reduce to data, especially because racial categories differ across different societies. However, if we acknowledge this reduction and use racial categories from the U.S. to reflect the perspective of the majority of Goodreads users, 33 then almost 94% of the Goodreads classics authors are white, which makes them whiter than both the AP recommended authors (70%) and the Open Syllabus authors (86%). The Goodreads classics include works by six Black writers: Alexandre Dumas, Frederick Douglass, Chinua Achebe, Zora Neale Hurston, Toni Morrison, and Alice Walker. There are also works by Laura Esquivel and Gabriel Garca Marquez, who would likely be read as Latinx from the perspective of U.S. racial logics, and Kahlil Gibran, who would likely be read as Middle Eastern or North African from the same perspective. There are no works by Asian, Asian American, or Indigenous authors. Further, there are few texts written by authors beyond North America and Europe, with notable ex­ ceptions including Achebe’s Things Fall Apart, Gibran’s The Prophet, and Marquez’s One Hundred Years of Solitude” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 13)
“Their publication dates noticeably skew toward the late-nineteenth and twenti­ eth centuries. More than a third were published after 1945. While the dominant form of literature in these Goodreads classics is fiction, there is also a small amount of poetry, drama, and non-fiction” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 13)
“Many texts labeled as classics by Goodreads users seem to overlap with English literature curricula from U.S. grade schools, high schools, and colleges. Though the Goodreads platform has an increasingly global audience — with notable emerging userbases in India and the UK — most of its users have historically hailed from the U.S. and still make up an estimated 40% of sitewide traffic. 31 For two rough estimates of how much the Goodreads classics overlap with school syllabi, we consulted a recommended reading list from the Advanced Placement (AP) English program — a common literature curricula in U.S. high schools — as well as a compilation of college-level English literature syllabi from the Open Syllabus Project, which draws on syllabi from many countries but predominantly from the U.S. 32 More than a third of the Goodreads classics au­ thors are specifically recommended by the AP English program, and about half rank within the top 200 most assigned college-level authors.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 13)
“the user demographics of Goodreads. Beyond the platform’s U.S.-centrism, the racial demographics of its user base skew overwhelmingly white—at least ac­ cording to Quantcast, one of the ad industry’s leaders for measuring online traf­ fic and user demographics. As of June 2020, according to Quantcast, Goodreads users were 77% Caucasian, 9% Hispanic, 7% African American, 6% Asian, and 1% other. 34 It is crucial to note, however, that Quantcast uses statis­ tical modeling techniques to predict demographic characteristics such as gen­ der, age, ethnicity, and income, and, as sociologist Ruha Benjamin argues, com­ panies that “create racial-ethnic data to be sold to others” deserve intense scrutiny. 35 Quantcast data is nevertheless used by many companies, including Goodreads, which makes it important to consider. 36 With these purported user demographics in mind, the predominantly white Western makeup of these read­ er-produced classics is not shocking but it is nevertheless startling, and it cau­ tions any outsized faith in crowdsourced technologies as necessarily or pre­ dictably democratizing tools.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 14)
“Goodreads users have not, on the whole, disrupted or remade the traditional canon of classics in any clearly radical ways via their crowdsourced shelving practices — save perhaps for the incorporation of genre fiction. From the per­ spective of race and ethnicity, Goodreads users in fact seem to be reinforcing an even whiter and less diverse canon of classics than one would find in a typi­ cal high school or college classroom today. By analyzing Goodreads reviews in addition to shelf classifications, we hoped to better understand the forces and influences shaping this perception of the “classics” — who and what “is respon­ sible for maintaining them in their preeminent position,” as Jane Tompkins once put it. 38” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 14)

144 books classified as Goodreads classics
More than 120,000 reviews
Shelving and reading activity
Ratings, likes, comments, and review position
Author demographics and publication history
AP and Open Syllabus comparisons

Their evidence combines platform data with contextual data. Goodreads provides classifications, ratings, reviews, and engagement. Outside sources help the authors ask whether this user-produced collection differs from institutional reading lists and how its authorship is distributed.
This is important methodologically. Platform data can describe activity inside Goodreads, but it cannot explain itself. The comparisons with AP recommendations and Open Syllabus data connect the platform to schools and universities.
The review dataset also exposes limits in public access. Goodreads publicly displays only a fraction of all reviews. For each book, the authors collected approximately nine hundred reviews, which were generally those elevated by the default sorting system rather than a random sample of all reader responses.

Almost 94% of represented authors were classified as white
No represented authors were classified as Asian, Asian American, or Indigenous
More than one-third appeared on AP English recommendations
About half ranked among the 200 most assigned college authors
Genre fiction, young adult fiction, and adapted fiction gained visibility

What changed, and what remained surprisingly stable?
“First, the Goodreads classics are considerably less diverse in terms of the race and ethnicity of their authors. Race is extremely complex and difficult to reduce to data, especially because racial categories differ across different societies.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 13)
“Goodreads users have not, on the whole, disrupted or remade the traditional canon of classics in any clearly radical ways via their crowdsourced shelving practices — save perhaps for the incorporation of genre fiction.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 14)
The answer is not simply that nothing changed. Goodreads broadens what can count as a classic by incorporating more genre fiction, young adult fiction, and recently adapted works.
But the collection does not radically disrupt the traditional literary canon. By the authors’ necessarily reductive demographic coding, almost 94 percent of authors in the Goodreads classics collection were white. They found no Asian, Asian American, or Indigenous authors in the set. The collection was less racially diverse than the AP and Open Syllabus comparisons they used.
The authors are careful about the difficulty of reducing race and ethnicity to data. Their categories reflect U.S. racial logics and cannot capture the complexity of identity across different national contexts. This caveat is part of the finding, not a footnote we should ignore.
The broader interpretation is that crowdsourcing can reproduce the histories brought to the platform by its users, institutions, and available books. A crowd is not outside history.

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: What is the difference between the classics and the canon? How do they relate to each other?
text:
What is the difference between the classics and the canon? How do they relate to each other?
Who determines the canon? Why does it matter?
Can we separate reader choice from the institutions that shaped what readers encountered?



High school and college reading
Publishing and continuous reprinting
Film and television adaptation
Audiobooks and celebrity narration
Goodreads rankings and recommendations
Amazon’s retail ecosystem

“Many texts labeled as classics by Goodreads users seem to overlap with English literature curricula from U.S. grade schools, high schools, and colleges.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 13)
“Popular conceptions of school syllabi and required reading shape readers’ habits long after their school days, and readers even self-assign books in order to belatedly join these communities.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 31)
Walsh and Antoniak describe a “classics industry”: an interdependent network of education, publishing, film, television, e-commerce, and technology.
School reading is especially influential. Readers often begin their Goodreads history by rating books they remember from high school or college. Required reading supplies a shared cultural starter pack even for users whose current tastes differ significantly.
Publishing keeps established works available through repeated editions. Adaptations return selected books to public attention. Audible and AmazonClassics connect Goodreads to other Amazon-owned services. These systems create what the authors call, drawing on adaptation scholarship, circular affirmation: works are repeatedly confirmed as classics across different media and institutions.
The platform is therefore not replacing older institutions. It is recombining and monetizing their accumulated effects.

School memories remain central
Adaptations and audiobooks shape encounters
Readers debate race, gender, style, pace, and character
Negative reviews often require extended justification
Criticizing a classic can create confidence and community

“We use the topic model not only to identify broad patterns in the collection but also to draw specific and noteworthy examples to the surface and to our critical attention.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 23)
The review analysis complicates the structural critique. Goodreads users do not merely reproduce institutional judgments. They argue with them, reinterpret them, and sometimes gain confidence from seeing other readers reject celebrated books.
Negative judgments can require especially long explanations because readers feel pressure to justify disagreement with a classic’s reputation. Community can make that dissent feel possible.
At the same time, criticism produces additional attention. A long takedown keeps the book visible, contributes data, and participates in its continued circulation. Love and hate can both sustain a classic as a commodity and object of discussion.
This paradox helps explain the durability of classics. Their value does not depend on universal admiration. It depends partly on remaining available, assignable, adaptable, and debatable.

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: What is Topic Modeling? How do they use it to analyze reviews?
text:
What is Topic Modeling? How do they use it to analyze reviews?


“Looking at the list of most popular Goodreads classics and analyzing liking patterns can only tell us so much about how Goodreads users perceive, define, and discuss the classics. To know more, we needed to listen to readers’ own critical voices.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 19)
Topic modeling is a family of methods rather than a single technique. Walsh and Antoniak use latent Dirichlet allocation, usually shortened to LDA.
The model begins from patterns of word occurrence across documents. It does not know in advance that a review concerns gender, war, school, adaptations, or writing style. It identifies groups of words that repeatedly occur under similar conditions.
The word “topic” can be misleading. The output is a probability distribution over words, not a concept understood by the computer. Researchers interpret the group by examining its most strongly associated words and the documents in which that pattern is prominent.
This connects to our earlier distinction between data, information, and discourse. The model calculates patterns in data. Researchers turn those patterns into meaningful information and arguments.
How Do Walsh and Antoniak Use Topic Modeling?
120,000 reviews cannot be read in the same way as twelve reviews.
Their 30-topic model helps surface recurring discussions of:

Literary themes
Literary qualities
Linguistic styles
The classics industry

Does the model discover topics, or help researchers construct interpretations?
“The number of topics that we decided on was a significant and subjective decision. The topic model is not an objective magic wand but an interpretive tool.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 22)
Walsh and Antoniak use an LDA topic model to identify recurring patterns across the review collection. The method groups words that tend to appear in similar documents. It does not understand a topic in the human sense or automatically provide a meaningful label.
The researchers choose the number of topics, inspect the associated words and reviews, assign interpretive labels, and organize the results into larger categories. They explicitly describe choosing thirty topics as a subjective decision reached through experimentation.
The model supports movement between scales. It can identify broad patterns across thousands of reviews and help bring particular reviews back to the researchers’ attention for close reading. This is why they treat topic modeling as an interpretive tool rather than an objective answer machine.
The exercise also raises a critical question: if researchers can derive information about reader interests and responses from reviews, what might Amazon infer using a much larger collection and more powerful infrastructure?

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: LDA Topic Modeling: How do we turn patterns of words into meaningful topics? How do we interpret the results?
text:
LDA Topic Modeling: How do we turn patterns of words into meaningful topics? How do we interpret the results?


How Does LDA Represent a Review Collection?
Each topic is a mixture of words
women · men · society · female · life · writing
Each review is a mixture of topics
gender & sexuality + school + literary style
Where does interpretation enter this process?
LDA makes two linked assumptions. Each topic can be represented as a probability distribution across words, and each document can be represented as a mixture of topics.
A review does not have to belong to only one category. It might combine discussion of gender, a memory of reading the book in school, and an evaluation of the author’s prose. This mixed representation can be useful for cultural material that does not fit exclusive categories.
Interpretation enters at many points: preparing the text, defining what counts as a document, selecting the number of topics, deciding whether the results are coherent, labeling them, and choosing which patterns matter to the argument.
Walsh and Antoniak also use an “Authorless Topic Model” workflow to reduce patterns tied only to individual literary authors. Their goal is to foreground themes that recur across reviews of different books rather than simply rediscovering vocabulary distinctive to Shakespeare or Austen.
“For Goodreads and Amazon, a classic is a prominent advertising target value, a marketing tool, and a source of lucrative adaptation material.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 36)
“Yet for Goodreads users, a classic is also an invitation to become amateur critics and creative writers, a chance to reflect on their lives and relationships to power, a conduit for connecting to others, and an opportunity to enter a critical conversation that has long excluded them.” (Walsh and Antoniak, 2021, p. 36)
The conclusion returns to the opening question but gives multiple answers rather than a universal definition.
For Goodreads and Amazon, classics are commercially useful: they organize audiences, remain continuously marketable, and supply material for editions, audiobooks, films, and television. For readers, the category is lived and contested. It can name a school assignment, a beloved book, an overrated book, a screen adaptation, or an entry into public literary discussion.
This prepares the transition to TikTok. In both cases, popularity is neither only imposed from above nor spontaneously generated from below. Platforms structure how user activity becomes visible, measurable, and profitable.

“Born digital culture requires a born digital approach.” (McNulty, 2023, p. 2)
Tess McNulty studies born-digital and viral culture by bringing together cultural criticism and computational methods. Her larger project assembles datasets of highly engaged content across major platforms and asks what viral content reveals about cultural form.
“What’s on Top of TikTok?” begins from an evidence problem. Billions of people spend substantial time on platforms, but researchers cannot readily identify what they collectively view, like, share, or comment on most often.
This is different from studying a predefined hashtag, creator, or controversy. McNulty wants a broader top-down account of popular culture, but the platform’s technical and governance choices make that difficult.

What has happened to public APIs for platforms? Why is it difficult to study what people see on social media?







But further catalogs are challenging, if not impossible, to locate outside of industry settings (and especially without paying high premiums). Put another way: today, billions of global citizens peruse popular platforms for hours per day. And yet, as academics—and by extension, the general public—we don’t know what they are actually consuming: the types of content that they are viewing, liking, sharing, or commenting on in the largest quantities. At first, this may seem a familiar story. It’s well-known—at least among techcritical types—that the platforms are stingy with their data. And it’s generally agreed that this is a problem, not only for scholarly inquiry, but for democratic society. When Elon Musk, for example, recently announced that he would close down free access to Twitter’s academic and public data source (or “API”) he did not simply disrupt multiple active scholarly research projects (and by extension, academic careers). He made it easier for the platform, moving forward, to conceal its role in ongoing crises, like misinformation or cyberharassment. But the issue that I describe is more specific, and less regularly discussed in public fora. Even where social media companies have been more forthcoming with their data—opening their APIs and sharing their data with researchers more freely5 6 7” (McNulty, 2023, p. 4)
“But the issue that I describe is more specific, and less regularly discussed in public fora. Even where social media companies have been more forthcoming with their data—opening their APIs and sharing their data with researchers more freely” (McNulty, 2023, p. 4)
“Here, therefore, I’d like to take you through the details of this transparency problem: what it is, why it’s worrisome, and what we can do about it. We can’t easily compel the platforms to release more data, although that political fight wages on, with at least a few potential victories on the horizon. But we can more deliberately attempt to discover and consider the web’s most widespread content, and we can scrounge together the relevant data through our own devices. This project is essential for the health of our media cultures; in the year 2023, it’s some of the most crucial work that cultural critics can do. GOOD DATA ABOUT (POPULAR) CONTENT IS HARD TO FIND To grasp the problem, it’s necessary, first, to understand a few basics of social media research. Currently, this research emerges from a broad array of mostly socialscientific disciplines (political science, communications, rhetoric, and many more), in a near-infinite variety of forms (network analyses, ethnographies, et cetera). For our purposes, two facts are relevant: First, only some of these scholars take a general sort of interest in the most popular or viral content. Instead, most—insofar as they address content at all—focus in on case studies involving narrower subtypes of content, like fake news, COVID misinformation, #MeToo tweets, or makeup tutorials. Second, where these scholars do more data-driven research, they often find it particularly useful to use the above-mentioned tools that are called APIs (or “Application Programming Interfaces”). These programmatically accessible tools can be hosted by the platforms in academically accessible versions (there are also other, less research-oriented types of APIs). Moreover, they curate “back-end” platform data—that is, data beyond what you can see on your tailored feed—in easily manipulable formats (think spreadsheets, not newsfeeds). But those who want to use these APIs face a simple but pernicious obstacle: the platforms, one by one, have shut them down. Traditionally, Meta was the major villain in this story. In 2021, the company suddenly disbanded the team that ran its research-oriented API, which was called CrowdTangle; in 2022, they then paused new user applications for the tool. Since then, CrowdTangle has been reportedly glitchy for those who already had access, and unavailable to those—like myselfwho did not. Researchers in search of free, back-end Facebook data, therefore, have 9” (McNulty, 2023, p. 5)
“To grasp the problem, it’s necessary, first, to understand a few basics of social media research. Currently, this research emerges from a broad array of mostly socialscientific disciplines (political science, communications, rhetoric, and many more), in a near-infinite variety of forms (network analyses, ethnographies, et cetera).” (McNulty, 2023, p. 5)
“focus in on case studies involving narrower subtypes of content, like fake news, COVID misinformation, #MeToo tweets, or makeup tutorials. Second, where these scholars do more data-driven research, they often find it particularly useful to use the above-mentioned tools that are called APIs (or “Application Programming Interfaces”). These programmatically accessible tools can be hosted by the platforms in academically accessible versions (there are also other, less research-oriented types of APIs). Moreover, they curate “back-end” platform data—that is, data beyond what you can see on your tailored feed—in easily manipulable formats (think spreadsheets, not newsfeeds). But those who want to use these APIs face a simple but pernicious obstacle: the platforms, one by one, have shut them down. Traditionally, Meta was the major villain in this story. In 2021, the company suddenly disbanded the team that ran its research-oriented API, which was called CrowdTangle; in 2022, they then paused new user applications for the tool.” (McNulty, 2023, p. 5)
“Twitter and Reddit, meanwhile, throughout the late-2010s, were often called “Petri dishes” for social media research, because they hosted freely accessible research-oriented APIs (YouTube did, too; but researchers often found it easier to work with text-based platforms). Recently, however, as mentioned—and thanks to Elon Musk’s takeover of Twitter—they have both cut off access to these APIs and announced that they will charge expensive fees for their future use. TikTok has recently opened a new academic API; but the tool remains largely untested in published research, due to foreboding terms of service.” (McNulty, 2023, p. 6)
How does this relate to previous readings?
“problem with API data is slightly more specific, and, arguably, more acute. Such scholars, at least in theory, have more reason to ask general questions about the most popular content, rather than focusing on narrower case studies (e.g., tracking the spread of vaccine misinformation or conducting ethnographies of Estonian teens involved in Game of Thrones fan cultures). But this type of general data can be still harder to acquire. Even where the APIs have been open—making it easy to collect data concerning predefined subtypes of content (e.g., by user or keyword)—they’ve made it harder to survey content more unboundedly. Take, for example, Twitter’s recent academic API. In its official documentation, the API offered clear methods for searching through past tweets by hashtag, keyword, or creator; but it provided no simple function for conducting wider searches of content, from a particular past-tense period, sorted by numbers of likes or retweets (There were workarounds—but not that could allow users to produce the desired “top” datasets, without first surpassing their tweet quotas). Or take YouTube’s Data API, which remains accessible and free of charge. The documentation for this API does include one function that allows users to call up lists of vaguely defined “most popular” videos in a region, at the present moment. But when it comes to searching through larger stores of content from past periods, the suggested queries are narrowed down, for example by keyword, channel, or other subcategories (again, workarounds prove imperfect). Instagram’s regular tier Graph API, meanwhile, though it’s not oriented toward academics, does curate some data. But while it allows users to search for photos tagged with a particular hashtag, for example, it doesn’t allow them to turn up all top hashtags more broadly. (TikTok’s new academic API, if it becomes commonly used in published 10” (McNulty, 2023, p. 6)

section: What are recommendation systems? How do they shape what users see and do?
text:
What are recommendation systems? How do they shape what users see and do?





Collaborative Filtering






Content-Based Filtering




https://knightcolumbia.org/blog/tiktoks-secret-sauce Possible signals include:

Books a user rated, shelved, or reviewed
Similarities among books
Activity from supposedly similar users
Overall popularity and recent engagement
Commercial or editorial priorities A recommendation system is not one algorithm or one universal technique. It is a system for selecting and ordering possible items based on signals about users, items, and prior activity.

On a reading platform, signals might include a user’s ratings and shelves, similarities among book descriptions and categories, patterns among users with overlapping tastes, or general popularity. Platforms may also include editorial, promotional, or commercial objectives that are not visible in the interface.
The output is not simply a prediction of what exists in the world. It is a decision about what receives visibility. Once a recommendation changes what someone encounters, it can also change later behavior and future training data.
Arvind Narayanan’s 2022 essay, “TikTok’s Secret Sauce”, challenges the popular idea that TikTok succeeded because it invented a uniquely advanced AI system. Based on TikTok’s descriptions, leaked documents, independent studies, and reverse engineering, he argues that its underlying recommender resembles systems used across major platforms. What feels distinctive is the larger sociotechnical system: the recommendation model works together with short vertical videos, continuous swiping, creator tools, and a feed organized around individual pieces of content rather than primarily around accounts a user follows.
The swipe interface changes how users experience an imperfect recommendation. On a platform where I must choose a video, a poor choice creates noticeable effort: I have to leave it, inspect alternatives, and select again. On TikTok, rejecting a recommendation takes one quick gesture. The system can therefore make many mediocre predictions while still feeling uncannily accurate, because the cost of a miss is nearly invisible. The same design also reduces deliberate choice. A person may continue watching something they would never have consciously selected, so watch time cannot be treated as a transparent statement of preference.
Narayanan frames recommendation as a tradeoff between exploitation and exploration. Exploitation shows users material similar to content that has already performed well for them. It is safer but can become repetitive. Exploration introduces less certain material so the system can discover new interests and test whether unfamiliar creators or topics might find an audience. TikTok appears to emphasize exploration more heavily than many competitors: a new video can be tested with a small audience and then shown to progressively larger groups if it performs well.
This helps explain both TikTok’s “long tail” of niche content and its ability to make videos from relatively unknown creators visible. The feed evaluates videos more independently from follower counts than older subscription-centered platforms do. That is not simply a technical choice. Instagram and YouTube already have powerful creators whose audiences and livelihoods depend on follower relationships, so radically deemphasizing subscriptions could provoke resistance from the people who supply those platforms with content.
The essay therefore gives me a more precise answer to the question on the slide. Recommendation systems shape behavior not only through model predictions but through the interfaces, metrics, defaults, labor relations, and business decisions surrounding those predictions. The model selects what enters view; the interface determines how easy it is to accept or reject; the resulting watch, swipe, like, and creation activity becomes new data; and those data influence later recommendations. Preference is not merely detected. It is continually elicited, recorded, and reshaped.
This is also a useful caution against treating an algorithm as a mysterious autonomous force. Narayanan’s larger claim is that design, data, and institutional choices often matter more than small differences in algorithmic sophistication. Asking only “How does the algorithm work?” can obscure equally important questions: What behavior does the interface make effortless? What does the platform count as success? Whose content receives an initial test audience? Who benefits from the resulting visibility, and who is responsible for its harms?

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: Ranking Is Not the Same as Recommending
text:
Ranking Is Not the Same as Recommending




Ranking
Orders a known collection
Which review appears first?

Recommendation
Selects items for a user
Which book should this reader encounter?

How can both systems turn past attention into future attention?
The article gives us strong evidence about Goodreads’ default ranking of reviews. The platform appears to prioritize reviews with more likes and comments. That is not identical to the less visible system that recommends books to particular users.
Both systems nevertheless govern visibility. Ranking decides which items within a collection appear first. Recommendation decides which subset of a much larger collection enters a user’s field of view at all.
Both also create feedback. A review shown first can receive more likes. A book recommended more often can receive more ratings. Those new interactions can then justify continued visibility. The measurement and production of popularity become difficult to separate.

Bot Traffic and Studying the Internet


“For example, in the late-2010s, the journalist Kevin Roose started to publish weekly tweets listing the most-linked domains on Facebook (using what he called a “kludgey workaround” in CrowdTangle). In so doing, he revealed that new, alt-right news sources like Breitbart were more prevalent on the platform than many had imagined. Facebook, soon after, disbanded the CrowdTangle team. Such control allows them to steer cultural production in their favor. Where new streaming services like Netflix, for example, refuse to release their shows’ ratings, they do so because it generates hype: better for potential advertisers, in some cases, to guess—rather than know—the audience numbers. title: Platforms & Popularity
section: How does our dataset define popularity?
text:
How does our dataset define popularity?



OCLC and WorldCat library holdings
Editions and translations
Goodreads ratings and reviews
Author metadata from VIAF
Publication data from Wikipedia
Public-domain texts from Project Gutenberg

When does “widely held” become “popular,” “canonical,” or “great”?
OCLC compiled the original Top 500 list from holdings recorded in WorldCat. Preus and Sheth expand that list with additional information so they can compare institutional holdings with other measures, especially Goodreads activity.
The source of each column matters. WorldCat describes library collections. Goodreads records activity by platform users. VIAF and Library of Congress authority records impose standardized biographical categories. Wikipedia supplies publication dates. Project Gutenberg determines which full texts can be incorporated from its edited public-domain collection.
The resulting dataset is therefore an assembly of institutions rather than a single view of literary value. Each source has different users, purposes, categories, and omissions.

section: Who Are Anna Preus and Aashna Sheth?
text:
Who Are Anna Preus and Aashna Sheth?







Anna Preus studies twentieth-century literature and data science in the humanities, especially how historical print cultures move into digital resources. Aashna Sheth studied computer science and comparative history and previously researched metadata in the Chronicling America newspaper dataset.

Literary studies and digital humanities
Historical print culture
Humanities data science
Project director for Responsible Datasets in Context
Computer science and comparative history
Cultural and historical metadata
University of Washington B.S. and M.S. in Computer Science Their essay is part of Responsible Datasets in Context, a project that pairs datasets with detailed accounts of their provenance, construction, limitations, and ethical stakes. The dataset is not treated as a transparent input waiting for analysis. Its history is itself part of the research.

Preus and Sheth begin with OCLC’s claim that literary greatness can be measured by how many libraries hold a novel. They then ask what institutional histories and technical decisions are hidden inside that apparently simple measure.

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: What Does the Top 500 Dataset Measure? How did they collect the data?
text:
What Does the Top 500 Dataset Measure? How did they collect the data?


https://www.oclc.org/en/worldcat/library100/faq.html The Top 500 list represents a massive data extraction and analysis effort on the part of OCLC. While they do not provide detailed information on how the list was compiled, they do offer a brief explanation of the process that went into creating the list on their FAQ page (written in the context of the top 100, but also applies to the top 500):
Materials in libraries are described and tracked in WorldCat in two ways. Any specific work of literature, music, art, history, etc., has an associated catalog record. This describes the item in a general sense. Every copy of the same book, for example, shares the same record. WorldCat also tracks library holdings, which indicate that a specific library has (or holds) at least one copy of that item.
The Library 100 is based on the total number of holdings for a specific novel across all libraries that have registered that information in WorldCat. When a library tells OCLC, “We have a copy of that book available,” that counts as a holding, and in the case of The Library 100, counts as +1 toward its ranking on the list.
This process initially sounds straightforward: to create the Top 500 list, the OCLC team presumably searched the title of a work, counted the number of libraries that held each title, and published the first 500. But when we dug into the database, we found it was actually much more complicated than that. The list is influenced by a range of factors, including which libraries’ collections are represented, what kinds of books are considered, and how holdings are totalled across different editions and translations of individual titles
According to OCLC, “WorldCat holdings information represents the collective inventory of OCLC member libraries” (“WorldCat Holdings” 2021). But who are these member libraries? And where are they? OCLC publishes some summary data about WorldCat, revealing, for example, that it currently holds over 548 million bibliographic records representing over 3.3 billion library holdings in 490 languages. But while OCLC stresses its position as “The worldwide catalog of library resources” and emphasizes the membership of libraries in over one hundred countries, it doesn’t provide much specific information on where these libraries are located or what kinds of institutions they are (“WorldCat Holdings” 2021).
In order to get a general sense of the geographic distribution of OCLC member libraries, we dug into the organization’s directory and conducted filtered searches for libraries in each country. We found that over 70% of OCLC’s members are in the U.S., followed by 7% in Germany, 4% in Australia, 2.6% in Canada, and 1.5% in the U.K. Clearly, OCLC is most well represented in the U.S., where it is based, and the fact that three of the other top four countries in terms of membership have English as a national language helps to explain why English-language materials are disproportionately represented in the catalog and in the Top 500 List.
We used a similar approach to look at what kinds of institutions are represented in WorldCat, this time filtering by “Library Type.” We found that most OCLC members are school libraries (29%), public libraries (29%), or academic libraries (25%) and that membership is fairly evenly distributed across these categories. The prominence of school libraries and academic libraries raises the issue of which patrons have access to these libraries–and thus whose conception of popularity is being represented in the holdings data. It also points to the influence of educators on this picture of the Top 500 novels.
Number of libraries in OCLC’s member database by institution type Which books are represented? Since the list focuses specifically on novels in these libraries’ collections, it is also narrowed by genre. OCLC discusses its process for identifying novels on its FAQ page, noting that they began with “everything in WorldCat that counts broadly as ‘fiction’” and then winnowed the list down through the removal of known categories like “children’s books, poetry, drama, folklore, comics,” and “short stories.” The final list was later “reviewed by an editorial team.”
Importantly, the Top 500 List is also based only on holdings of physical books, and it “does not include e-books, audiobooks, children’s adaptations, film adaptations, etc.” This exclusive focus on print books puts emphasis on the choices of librarians, since libraries have limited shelf space and periodically have to cull their print collections. As OCLC puts it, “libraries offer access to trendy and popular books. But, they don’t keep them on the shelf if they’re not repeatedly requested by their communities over the years.” By contrast, they suggest that ebooks are often incorporated via “automatic links to free collections on the web,” which do not “represent a specific decision to add a particular novel to a library’s collection” (“The Library 100” 2023). While this may be the case, given the popularity of eBooks (Zhang and Kudva 2013), a focus on print must have influenced the overall makeup of the list, and, again, whose idea of popularity or “greatness” it represents.

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: How do they explore popularity? What is the relationship to Goodreads?
text:
How do they explore popularity? What is the relationship to Goodreads?


Because we were interested in whose opinions are represented on the list, we wanted to bring in an alternate measure of popularity, and we decided to use information from Goodreads. Goodreads was appealing because of its prominence online (over 130 million users), which we hoped might help us consider the opinions of a somewhat different set of readers than those theoretically represented through the physical holdings of libraries. Melanie Walsh and Maria Antoniak, for example, have drawn on Goodreads reviews to analyze how social media users define the “Classics.” Drawing on this work, we compare the ranking of novels on OCLC’s original list of Top 500 novels to the rankings of those same novels based on Goodreads ratings and number of reviews. Through this comparison we aim to consider how social media users engage with “classic” and “popular” novels and to interrogate the relationship between canonicity and popularity, using information from different data sources.
To unpack the differences between the Goodreads data and the Top 500 rankings, we first need to think about how we want to compare the two lists. Given that we have recorded Goodread rankings by average star rating and total number of ratings, which metric would be better to use? Would we want to create another metric?
For our purposes, we decided to use total number of ratings instead of average rating, since it seemed most closely related to how OCLC measures popularity–by number of holdings, not how much patrons say they enjoy reading the books.

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: What is OCLC? What is WorldCat? How did they get started?
text:
What is OCLC? What is WorldCat? How did they get started?







https://librarytechnology.org/mergers/oclc/ | Year | Development | |—|—| | 1967 | Ohio College Library Center founded as a nonprofit cooperative | | 1971 | Ohio University librarians add the first records to the online union catalog | | 1979 | The shared catalog passes five million records | | Later | OCLC expands beyond Ohio and the catalog becomes WorldCat |
OCLC began in 1967 as the Ohio College Library Center. Its initial purpose was practical: participating libraries wanted to share cataloging work and reduce costs through a computerized network.
In 1971, librarians at Ohio University’s Alden Library entered the first records into the OCLC Online Union Catalog. Within eight years, it contained more than five million records. As participation expanded beyond Ohio and then internationally, the organization became the Online Computer Library Center and the catalog became known as WorldCat.
The important historical point is that WorldCat was not originally built to rank literary greatness. It was built to support cataloging, discovery, resource sharing, and interlibrary loan. The Top 500 ranking repurposes traces produced by that infrastructure for a different question.
This returns us to our earlier discussion of catalog cards, MARC records, and the history of library metadata. Libraries have long needed to describe materials consistently enough for people to discover and retrieve them.
Before computerized cooperative cataloging, institutions could duplicate substantial amounts of descriptive labor. A union catalog brings records from multiple collections into a shared system. Libraries can reuse records while adding information about their own holdings.
Cooperation reduces duplicated labor and makes collections discoverable across institutions. It also creates dependencies on shared standards, identifiers, governance, technical systems, and membership structures.
This is why OCLC belongs in a class about platforms. It coordinates participants and data through common infrastructure, even though its history and nonprofit cooperative model differ from commercial social-media platforms.
OCLC began in 1967 as the Ohio College Library Center. Its original purpose was to support cooperative library cataloging, allowing participating libraries to share bibliographic records rather than independently cataloging every item. It later expanded internationally and became the Online Computer Library Center.
WorldCat aggregates catalog records and holdings from OCLC member libraries. A bibliographic record describes an item or edition. A holding indicates that a particular member library reports possessing that item. This makes WorldCat extraordinarily valuable infrastructure for discovering materials and studying library collections.
But holdings are not readership. They reflect acquisition, preservation, cataloging, available budgets and shelf space, curricular demand, publishing history, and the composition of OCLC’s membership. Preus and Sheth found that more than 70 percent of listed OCLC member institutions were in the United States. Editions and translations also complicate aggregation: works published and republished in many editions can accumulate more records and holdings.
OCLC offers a different kind of platform from Goodreads or TikTok, but it still organizes data through membership, standards, identifiers, interfaces, and aggregation rules. Its infrastructure makes some comparisons possible while shaping what those comparisons mean.

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: What data do the authors compile? What is the problem of translations and editions?
text:
What data do the authors compile? What is the problem of translations and editions?


How are editions and translations counted? One further complication is that in WorldCat, records are stored by edition, meaning that each edition of a particular novel has its own catalog record. An individual title may have been released in hundreds or thousands of editions since its initial publication. Miguel de Cervantes’s Don Quixote, for example, has over 9,000 editions listed in WorldCat.
This means that when developing the list, the OCLC team actually had to find all the editions of a specific title and sum the number of libraries that hold that edition across all editions. Thus the top 500 list is not only a representation of how many libraries carry the work, but a representation of how many times a book has been re-edited and re-issued; the more editions a book has, the more records are created and the more copies of a book a library may hold. Often, there are duplicate records for individual editions, which may affect the overall count of copies tallied by OCLC. And when a work is translated into different languages, all the editions of all the translations are also recorded in WorldCat, which also figures into the count of total holdings for each novel.
The combined influence of these different factors can be seen in the representation of works in languages other than English, which make up around 14% of the list. The non-English-language texts that are at the top of the list–Don Quixote, Crime and Punishment, Madame Bovary, The Three Musketeers, and War and Peace–have all been widely translated into English, a trend that continues as you go down the list.
Our curated dataset: We chose to contextualize the Library Top 500 List by compiling additional information on each novel from a range of other sources. We focused on gathering three main categories of information: information that could help us understand what types of works–and whose works–were included on the list, data that could potentially provide alternate measures of popularity or canonicity, and the full text of each novel that was in the public domain. We collected information from the following sources:
WorldCat: we used the now-shuttered OCLC tool Classify to gather data from WorldCat based on an OWI (OCLC Work ID) for each of the 500 novels on the list.3 We recorded total physical and eholdings for this work. The Top 500 list only considers physical holdings. The number of holdings in our curated dataset is not perfectly descending as the top 500 rank decreases, as one would expect. This is likely due to complications with the OWI number and with the inclusion of translations; the top 500 list uses multiple OWIs to calculate total holdings, while we only use one. Which OWIs the top 500 curators use for each work is unclear.
VIAF: The Virtual International Authority File is an OCLC-run database that contains structured records–called “name authority files”–for individual authors and creators. We used VIAF to gather information on authors whose novels were included on the list, including their birth and death dates, nationalities, genders, and occupations.
image_tooltip
Example of Toni Morrison’s authority record in VIAF Wikipedia: We used Wikipedia, the popular, free, volunteer-authored encyclopedia, to identify the year of first publication for each novel on the list.
Goodreads: Goodreads, which is owned by Amazon, is the largest social networking site related to books, with over 150 million members. It allows users to rate, review, and discuss a huge range of texts. We drew on data from Goodreads as a potential alternate indicator of texts’ popularity, collecting total number of reviews, total number of ratings, and average overall rating for each novel on the list.
