Project Gutenberg: We used Project Gutenberg to access the full-text of all novels on the list that are currently in the public domain, or in other words, out of copyright. We chose Project Gutenberg because their eBooks are edited by volunteers, whereas many larger content repositories, like Internet Archive and HathiTrust, only make available machine-generated transcriptions of historical texts, which tend to be less accurate.
Our work creating this dataset not only builds on the work of the OCLC team who compiled the Top 500 list, but on the labor of the thousands of librarians who created records held in WorldCat and VIAF, of the volunteers who transcribed texts for Project Gutenberg and wrote articles for Wikipedia, and of the social media users who reviewed and rated books on Goodreads.

title: Platforms & Popularity
section: How do they approach the impact of platforms or databases on their data?
text:
How do they approach the impact of platforms or databases on their data?


The top 500 list: The OCLC’s definition of “literary greatness” is biased based on the libraries that OCLC represents, the list’s exclusive focus on physical books, and its emphasis on raw number of holdings, which is influenced by number of editions. OCLC acknowledges potential biases in their claims, noting that “The [top 500] list emphasizes many books that we tend to think of as ‘classics,’ because those are the novels most often translated, retold in different editions, taught and widely distributed in library collections. Because of this, the list tends to reflect more dominant cultural views.”
A key reason we decided to collect additional data related to the list was to explore what kinds of works, and especially whose works, it represents. Drawing on author data gathered from VIAF, we can calculate some overall descriptive statistics for the list.
Looking at the AUTHOR_GENDER column, we can count the number of authors identified as male and the number identified as female (VIAF only includes options for binary genders, which is discussed further below), and we can see that over 70% of the novels were written by men.
Drawing on slightly more complex techniques, we can see that there is a strong positive correlation (p=1.1165e-73, r=0.6985) between the current ranking of the Top 500 List and a ranking based on the total number of editions for each novel. This suggests that the more editions a novel has, the more likely it is to be higher on the list, which is relevant because European and American editing practices have long favored authors occupying dominant social positions. Historically, works by White authors and male authors are more likely to have been re-edited and re-issued and to be considered literary classics (Gates; Mandell).4

title: Openness & Organization
text:
Who Is Kimberly Christen?





Scholar of digital technology, archives, and Indigenous knowledge
Founder of Mukurtu CMS
Co-director of Local Contexts

How does her work connect technology to relationships and responsibility?


Kimberly Christen is a scholar of digital technologies, archives, cultural heritage, and Indigenous knowledge systems. Her work developed through sustained collaboration with Warumungu people in Tennant Creek, Australia.
That collaborative history matters. Mukurtu was not designed as an abstract technical solution and then delivered to a community. It emerged from a specific community’s existing protocols for storing, circulating, and caring for cultural materials.
Christen later helped develop Mukurtu CMS as a free and open-source platform adaptable to the needs of Indigenous communities. She also co-directs Local Contexts, which develops Traditional Knowledge and Biocultural Labels and Notices.

title: Openness & Organization
section: Why Does Christen Begin With Slashdot?
text:
Why Does Christen Begin With Slashdot?


In January 2008, Slashdot framed the Mukurtu Wumpurrarni-kari archive as an “Aboriginal Archive” using a new form of digital rights management. The post produced a large debate that often misunderstood both the archive and the community protocols that shaped it.
Christen explains that the project, after two years of development and with several goals, was suddenly reduced to the familiar language of DRM. Some responses treated any technological control as inherently oppressive. Others romanticized Indigenous people as “ancient.” Both responses obscured the contemporary Warumungu collaborators and the specific relationships behind the archive.
The opening gives us the article’s central problem: the vocabulary of open versus closed, free versus proprietary, is too narrow to describe every form of knowledge circulation.

title: Openness & Organization
text:
What Is Mukurtu?


The first Mukurtu Wumpurrarni-kari community archive was installed at the Nyinkka Nyunyu Art and Culture Centre in Tennant Creek in 2007. Mukurtu CMS launched in 2010 as a free, open-source, standards-based content management system for cultural heritage.
Christen writes that mukurtu translates to “dilly bag” in Warumungu, but the Warumungu elders working on the project defined it as a “safe keeping place.” That definition holds together protection and circulation. The goal is not to hide everything or expose everything. It is to keep materials safely while sharing them through appropriate relationships.
The platform itself is open-source. Openness at the software layer does not require every cultural item inside an installation to be universally available.

title: Openness & Organization
section: What Problem Was Mukurtu Built to Solve?
text:
What Problem Was Mukurtu Built to Solve?


What if access depends on relationships rather than a universal public?

Mukurtu begins with existing social relationships and information circulation routes. Access can be shaped by family, clan, community, gender, age, ceremonial responsibility, or other protocols defined by the community using the system.
Christen describes consultations with communities whose needs differed: kin-based networks, family structures, exchange with the Library of Congress, and distinctions between material intended for commercial use and material intended only for internal circulation.
The important point is not that every Indigenous community uses the same rules. It is precisely the opposite: the software must support communities in defining their own protocols rather than making one institutional idea of the public universal.
Student annotations to raise:

Abhi P. (arp14, Section B) wrote that he normally understands restriction as harmful, but that it operates differently here because it respects community traditions and is based on trust. Open annotation
Jack G. (jgoby2, Section A) asked how an archive with culturally differentiated access decides who receives access to each record. This gives me an opening to distinguish technical permissions from the social process of assigning them. Open annotation Can Access Be Relational?
Family and kinship
Community membership
Gender or age
Ceremony and responsibility
Conditions for reuse and circulation This diagram helps make the architecture visible. A record is not simply marked public or private. Communities, cultural protocols, and categories create intersecting conditions for circulation.

This is also an ontology: a model of what kinds of people, materials, relationships, and permissions exist in the system. A conventional repository might imagine a generic user and a generic item. Mukurtu treats relationships as part of the data model.
The design raises a question for us: what social assumptions are embedded in a platform’s categories? If a system only supports “public” and “private,” what forms of relationship has it made impossible to represent?
This connects to our Data Feminism discussion of classification. Facebook could present many gender choices to users while translating those identities back into a binary system for advertisers. The visible interface and the underlying ontology did not represent people in the same way. Mukurtu offers a different model: the categories and permissions represent community relationships and authority rather than only administrative convenience.
It also anticipates Rawson and Muñoz’s argument from our curation class. They ask whether communities can construct their own authority structures while still participating in larger information networks. Mukurtu gives us a concrete example of local authority and interoperability being designed together rather than treated as opposites.

title: Openness & Organization
text:
Does Information “Want” to Be Free?

“On the one hand information wants to be expensive, because it’s so valuable. … On the other hand information wants to be free, because the cost of getting it out is getting lower and lower all the time.”
— Stewart Brand, 1984


Christen recovers the longer version of Stewart Brand’s statement from the first Hackers Conference in 1984. The slogan usually survives only as “information wants to be free,” but Brand articulated a tension between information’s value and the falling cost of distributing it.
More importantly, information does not literally want anything. People, institutions, and communities make decisions about circulation. Treating openness as information’s natural condition can hide those decisions and the power behind them.
Christen argues that the slogan acquired moral force through free-software movements, critiques of corporate copyright, and American narratives about individual liberty. Those histories are important, but they do not produce a universal rule for every kind of knowledge.
Student annotations to raise:

Drew B. (drewbowen, Section A) connected this slogan to contemporary concern about private information being collected without meaningful consent and then stored insecurely. Open annotation
Eric C. (ecampos3, Section B) asked whether increasingly open but decontextualized information—especially LLM answers without visible provenance—can produce less trust rather than more knowledge. Open annotation

title: Openness & Organization
section: Is Privacy the Opposite of Sharing?
text:
Is Privacy the Opposite of Sharing?

“What people care most about is not simply restricting the flow of information but ensuring that it flows appropriately.”
— Helen Nissenbaum, quoted by Christen


This is the point where privacy becomes more than secrecy. Nissenbaum’s concept of contextual integrity asks whether information moves in ways appropriate to a particular relationship and context.
Christen argues that privacy and secrecy can be necessary parts of sociality and knowledge production. Sharing does not have to mean universal circulation. A person might share something with family but not a corporation; a community might share knowledge internally but not permit commercial reuse.
The better question is not only whether information flows, but who sends it, who receives it, under what conditions, and with what obligations.

title: Openness & Organization
text:
Why Was Copyright Created?


Modern Anglo-American copyright is usually traced to the Statute of Anne in Britain in 1710. The first U.S. federal Copyright Act followed in 1790 and protected maps, charts, and books for fourteen years, with a possible fourteen-year renewal.
The U.S. Constitution gives Congress power to secure exclusive rights for “limited Times” in order to “promote the Progress of Science and useful Arts.” Copyright is therefore not an eternal natural ownership right in U.S. law. It is a statutory system intended to balance incentives and public benefit.
Over time, copyright expanded to more kinds of works, more rights, and much longer terms. That history helps explain why debates over mass digitization and machine learning turn on copying at a scale the eighteenth-century system could not have anticipated.
We first encountered this history through Project Gutenberg and Public Domain Day. Gutenberg can distribute plain-text books because copyright has expired or never applied to those editions. Every January 1, another group of works enters the U.S. public domain as its term expires. The technical simplicity of downloading Pride and Prejudice was therefore built on a legal history, not just a convenient URL or file format.
This also returns to the distinction we made in the libraries class: digitization does not itself create access. A library may possess a physical book, Google may scan it, HathiTrust may preserve the resulting files, and users may still receive only metadata or search results because the work remains copyrighted.

title: Openness & Organization
text:
Why Did Creative Commons Emerge?


Creative Commons emerged from a late-twentieth-century conflict between expanding copyright and the rapidly falling cost of digital copying and distribution.
The U.S. Copyright Term Extension Act of 1998, often called the Sonny Bono Act, extended existing copyright terms by twenty years. For many individual works, the standard term became the author’s life plus seventy years. Eric Eldred, who published public-domain literature online, challenged the extension with attorney and Stanford law professor Lawrence Lessig. In 2003, the Supreme Court rejected that constitutional challenge in Eldred v. Ashcroft.
Critics also called the law the “Mickey Mouse Protection Act.” Disney and other major copyright industries supported term extension while valuable works from the 1920s were approaching the end of their existing terms. Mickey Mouse was a memorable symbol of the debate because the character first appeared in the 1928 films Steamboat Willie and Plane Crazy. The nickname can oversimplify the law—the extension affected an enormous range of works and rights holders—but it makes the political economy visible. Copyright terms are created through legislation, and organizations with commercially valuable catalogs have strong incentives to influence when works enter the public domain.
The extension delayed the U.S. public-domain release of covered works for twenty years. After that pause, works from 1923 began entering the public domain on January 1, 2019. The 1928 versions of Mickey and Minnie depicted in Steamboat Willie and the silent version of Plane Crazy entered the U.S. public domain on January 1, 2024. The Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain uses this case to explain both what became available and what remained protected.
The qualification matters: the public-domain event did not make every version of Mickey Mouse free to use. Copyright expiration applies to the expression contained in those particular 1928 works. Later visual designs, later films, and newly added expressive elements retain their own copyright terms. Disney also continues to hold trademarks associated with Mickey. Copyright and trademark answer different questions: copyright limits copying of creative expression for a limited term, while trademark protects consumers against confusion about the source or sponsorship of goods and services. Someone may draw on the 1928 depiction without thereby gaining permission to suggest that Disney produced or endorsed the new work.
This is a useful case for returning to our distinction among access, public domain, and permission. A digitized copy of Steamboat Willie could circulate online before 2024, but technical access did not end its copyright. Once the 1928 film entered the public domain, people gained much broader rights to reproduce and adapt that particular work, while separate legal and ethical questions still remained.
Creative Commons grew alongside that litigation. Lessig, Eldred, Hal Abelson, and collaborators founded the nonprofit in 2001. The first Creative Commons licenses appeared in 2002. Their intervention was practical: copyright applies automatically, so a creator who wants broad circulation still needs a reliable way to grant permission.
Aaron Swartz, whom we previously discussed in relation to Markdown, JSTOR, and open-access activism, was one of Creative Commons’ early technical architects. As a teenager, he helped design the machine-readable code layer for the licenses. His original RDF data model and metadata strategy made it possible for software and search engines to recognize licensing information rather than treating a license only as prose on a webpage.
This is an important connection to Markdown. Swartz’s projects repeatedly joined human-readable formats to machine-readable infrastructure. Markdown sought source text that people could read while software converted it into HTML. Creative Commons combined human-readable license deeds, formal legal code, and machine-readable metadata. Both projects imagined an open web where technical design could lower barriers to publishing, discovery, and reuse.
Swartz later worked on the Internet Archive’s Open Library and became a prominent open-access activist. In 2011 he was arrested after downloading a very large corpus of JSTOR articles through MIT’s network. JSTOR settled its civil dispute and asked that the criminal case not continue, but federal prosecutors pursued charges under computer-crime law. Swartz died by suicide in January 2013 while the case was pending. His life links the apparently separate histories we have studied: web standards, Markdown, structured metadata, libraries, licensing, scholarly publishing, and conflicts over access to knowledge.
Creative Commons changed the default vocabulary from a binary choice between “all rights reserved” and abandoning copyright to “some rights reserved.” A creator retains copyright but grants the public specified permissions in advance. This reduces the need for every potential user to locate the rights holder and negotiate separately.
The license elements can be combined:

BY requires attribution.
SA requires shared adaptations to use the same or a compatible license.
NC limits licensed uses to noncommercial purposes.
ND permits redistribution but not the sharing of adaptations.

The licenses have three interconnected layers: legal language enforceable in court, a human-readable summary, and machine-readable metadata that search engines and platforms can interpret. That last layer made licensing part of the architecture of the web rather than only a notice printed inside a book.
Creative Commons released CC0 in 2009. CC0 is not another restrictive license; it is a public-domain dedication and fallback license designed to waive copyright and related rights as fully as a jurisdiction permits. It is commonly used for data and metadata when rights holders want to maximize reuse. Version 4.0 of the CC licenses, released in 2013, was designed for international use and explicitly addresses database rights that exist in some jurisdictions.
There are several limitations to emphasize. A person can license only rights they actually hold. A CC license does not eliminate privacy, publicity, trademark, contractual, or culturally grounded obligations. Once granted, a CC license generally cannot be revoked for people already using the work under its terms. Applying CC0 to a dataset also does not mean that every record is ethical to release.
This is where Creative Commons and Christen’s argument meet. CC provides an important standardized vocabulary for copyright permission. Mukurtu and Traditional Knowledge Labels address relationships, authority, and responsibilities that copyright licensing alone cannot express. Open licensing answers “What legal reuse has the rights holder authorized?” It does not necessarily answer “Who should have had authority over this material in the first place?”
I should explicitly remind students of our earlier three-part comparison. Project Gutenberg distributes works whose copyright has expired. Creative Commons lets current rights holders authorize reuse before expiration. JSTOR usually provides access through subscriptions and contractual licenses that do not authorize users to redistribute its full holdings. These are three different infrastructures of access, even when all three deliver a PDF or text file through a browser.

title: Openness & Organization
section: Why do we need Traditional Knowledge Labels?
text:
Why do we need Traditional Knowledge Labels?




Copyright often assumes:

An identifiable creator
A fixed work
Exclusive rights
A limited term


Community protocols may concern:

Collective authority
Inherited responsibility
Relationships and context
Continuing obligations


Christen calls copyright one social and legal solution to tensions among creators, consumers, and distributors. It is not a complete theory of knowledge circulation.
Western copyright law often privileges identifiable authors, fixed works, exclusive rights, and limited terms. Indigenous knowledge can be collective, intergenerational, relational, and governed by obligations that do not expire merely because a statutory term ends.
This does not mean copyright is irrelevant. Mukurtu can support copyright and Creative Commons licenses. It means that copyright should not be our only vocabulary for deciding what responsible access looks like.
Christen asks us to historicize the public domain. Cultural materials did not always arrive in museums, archives, or datasets through consensual exchange. They may have been collected during colonial rule, removed from communities, or documented without communities controlling subsequent circulation.
A legal declaration that an item is now in the public domain does not erase that history. Legal availability and ethical permission are not identical.
Traditional Knowledge Labels provide additional information about community expectations for attribution, seasonal use, gender restrictions, culturally sensitive material, outreach, and other forms of responsibility. They do not replace copyright law. They add a vocabulary that copyright and standard licenses often lack.
Student annotations to raise:

Katie H. (katieh9, Section B) highlighted Christen’s argument that Western nations could construct the public domain by drawing on Indigenous resources without acknowledgment or redress. Open annotation
Aurora J. (Auroraj3, Section B) described this as a case where a lack of restriction can itself become oppressive. That phrasing gives us a useful way to question whether unrestricted circulation always disperses power. Open annotation

title: Openness & Organization
text:
Who Is Melanie Walsh?





Assistant Professor, University of Washington Information School
Co-leads the Post45 Data Collective
Works on cultural data, books, libraries, and public readership

What changes when cultural data is closed?


Melanie Walsh is an Assistant Professor in the University of Washington Information School and an Adjunct Assistant Professor of English. Her projects include the Post45 Data Collective, Responsible Datasets in Context, AI for Humanists, and What’s Seattle Reading?
Her work joins literary study with data curation and computational methods. In this essay, she asks a deceptively simple question: where is the data that would let us study contemporary books, publishing, and reading?

title: Openness & Organization
section: Where Is All the Book Data?
text:
Where Is All the Book Data?




Walsh begins with questions that sound answerable: Which books sold during the pandemic? What did people borrow? Which authors get published and promoted? Yet the data needed to answer these questions is fragmented, expensive, proprietary, incomplete, or unavailable to researchers.
The New York Times bestseller list gives rankings but not the underlying sales totals. BookScan supplies much of the industry’s sales intelligence, but access is restricted and costly. The data can shape acquisitions, advances, marketing campaigns, subsidiary rights, and the selection of comparable titles.

title: Openness & Organization
section: What Is BookScan? What are some of the problems with BookScan?
text:
What Is BookScan? What are some of the problems with BookScan?
![] (https://www.publishersmarketplace.com/bookscan/images/VisualizeData-580.png)

BookScan is a commercial source for book-sales data used throughout publishing. Walsh reports that an unfavorable sales history can cause an editor to pass on a book and can affect an author’s advance, marketing, book tour, and rights.
The striking issue is asymmetry. Authors and scholars may be governed by these numbers without being able to inspect the underlying data, understand its omissions, or challenge its use.
Walsh cites a 2009 estimate that publishing-house licenses cost between $350,000 and $750,000 per year. Academics were explicitly excluded from licensing when she inquired. This is not simply data that happens to be missing. It is valuable infrastructure whose access is organized around industry power.
Student annotations to raise:

Jack G. (jgoby2, Section A) asked why academics are banned from BookScan and wondered whether the restriction could be related to book banning. I should distinguish content censorship from commercial control over market data, while asking what both prevent outsiders from seeing. Open annotation
Erin C. (echon5, Section B) asked who actually has access and what incentives the owner has for keeping the data closed. Open annotation

A dataset can govern people who cannot inspect it.

Acquisitions
Advances
Marketing
Translation and subsidiary rights
“Comparable” titles

96% of the most frequently used comparable titles were written by white authors.
Laura McGrath found that 96 percent of the most frequently used comp titles were written by white authors. Since publishers use promising past sales to decide which books look commercially viable, historical inequalities can become evidence for repeating those inequalities.
This is a feedback loop: past publication and promotion produce sales data; the sales data defines what appears marketable; those judgments shape future publication and promotion.
Walsh calls BookScan a conservative force in the industry. The data is also incomplete. It claims broad coverage of physical and leading ebook sales, but it misses direct-to-consumer sales, events, some specialty retailers, and library sales. Powerful data does not need to be complete to structure decisions.
Katie H. (katieh9, Section B) connected this feedback loop to the striking similarity of contemporary book covers. Her observation lets me ask how a dataset of past sales might shape not only which books are acquired but also how books are packaged and made visually legible as comparable products. Open annotation

title: Openness & Organization
text:
What is Post45 Data?


Could Open Data Become Counterdata? Walsh proposes open cultural data as a way to study and challenge the culture industries. The Post45 Data Collective publishes datasets so researchers can receive credit for the labor of collecting and cleaning them and so others can combine them.
Walsh discusses Richard Jean So and collaborators’ dataset of more than 8,000 widely read books from major publishers. Their labor-intensive demographic research found that 95 percent of identified authors published across the studied period were white. Aggregate data made a systemic pattern visible.
Walsh calls this kind of work counterdata: data created or combined to contest the stories told by powerful institutions and proprietary systems.
This is a direct continuation of Data Feminism. D’Ignazio and Klein showed that missing data is often produced by power: institutions collect what serves science, surveillance, or selling while other needs remain uncounted. They also introduced counterdata created by activists and communities to make structural violence visible. Walsh asks whether open cultural data can play a similar role in publishing by making aggregate exclusion inspectable rather than anecdotal.
Student annotations to raise:

Gavin W. (gavinwang, Section A) emphasized that public datasets become more powerful when they are interoperable and can be connected. Open annotation
Hong Ju J. (hongjuj2, Section A) described open counterdata as a response to closed corporate data. I can use these two comments together to ask when combining datasets redistributes analytical power and when linkage might create new risks. Open annotation

title: Openness & Organization
section: What Does Library Data Reveal and Risk?
text:
What Does Library Data Reveal and Risk?


The Seattle Public Library releases monthly title-level checkout totals extending back to 2005, separated by formats such as print, ebook, and audiobook. Individual patron information is removed and de-identified.
The history is unusual. Before 2017, the library itself was not retaining ordinary circulation histories, in keeping with strong library privacy traditions. Yet George Legrady’s installation Making Visible the Invisible had been receiving and visualizing checkout activity since 2005, preserving title-level historical data.
This example makes the tension concrete. Circulation data can reveal cultural patterns, but reading histories can also expose political beliefs, health concerns, sexuality, religion, and other intimate interests. Aggregation and de-identification are choices about what research value to retain and what risk to reduce.
Mazen A. (malee22, Section A) was surprised that an artwork preserved circulation information the library itself was not retaining. This is a useful prompt about preservation by accident: when does a visualization become an archive, and who anticipated that its underlying data would later support research? Open annotation

title: Openness & Organization
section: Why Did Data Privacy Become a Legal Right?
text:
Why Did Data Privacy Become a Legal Right?




If data is useful, does that mean it should be collected and released?


Purpose limitation
Data minimization
Storage limitation
Security and accountability




Privacy law developed alongside new institutional capacities to collect, combine, and automate records about people. After World War II, European privacy protections were shaped partly by the recognition that state registries and identification systems could be used for surveillance, persecution, and discrimination. Article 8 of the 1950 European Convention on Human Rights recognized a right to respect for private and family life.
As governments and businesses computerized records during the 1960s and 1970s, privacy became a data-processing problem as well as a domestic one. Several European countries adopted national data-protection laws. The Council of Europe’s Convention 108, opened for signature in 1981, became the first legally binding international instrument devoted specifically to personal data protection.
The European Union’s 1995 Data Protection Directive attempted to harmonize national rules as digital networks and cross-border commerce expanded. A directive required member states to implement shared goals through their own national laws, which still produced variation across Europe.
The General Data Protection Regulation was adopted in 2016 and became enforceable on May 25, 2018. Unlike the earlier directive, the regulation applies directly across EU member states. It also responds to an internet economy built around platforms, behavioral tracking, large databases, and international data transfers. Its territorial reach can include organizations outside Europe when they offer goods or services to, or monitor the behavior of, people in the EU.
The GDPR does not say that personal data can never be processed. It requires a lawful basis and makes organizations responsible for how they process it. Its core principles include lawfulness, fairness, and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimization; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; and accountability.
Data minimization is especially useful for our projects. The question is not only whether a field might be interesting. It is whether we need to collect it for the stated purpose. Purpose limitation similarly asks whether data gathered for one reason should later be repurposed for another.
People also receive rights involving notice, access, correction, erasure in specified circumstances, restriction, portability, objection, and certain automated decisions. The so-called “right to be forgotten” is therefore not an unlimited power to erase any information from history. It is one qualified right within a larger regulatory system, balanced against legal obligations, freedom of expression, archiving, research, and public interest.
This history helps distinguish the Seattle Public Library from BookScan. Refusing to retain individual borrowing histories is not merely a failure to collect potentially useful data. Libraries have treated reading privacy as part of intellectual freedom: people should be able to seek information without creating a durable record that could later expose or chill their inquiry.
This connects to Manovich’s category of digital traces from our definitions and disciplines class. Browsing, searching, reviewing, borrowing, and clicking can all become behavioral data even when someone never set out to create a cultural record. It also returns to the location-data example in Data Feminism: a dataset can omit names and email addresses while still making people’s movements and intimate activities identifiable. The history of data protection is partly the history of recognizing that institutions gain new power when traces can be stored, linked, and analyzed at scale.
Is De-Identified Data Anonymous?
Removed names \(\neq\) removed identities







Pseudonymized
Anonymized




Identifiers replaced or separated
No longer reasonably linkable to a person


Reidentification remains possible
Intended to prevent reidentification


Still personal data under GDPR
Outside GDPR if genuinely anonymous



The history of data privacy also explains why removing names is not enough. In earlier paper systems, taking a name off a record could make linkage difficult. Computational systems make it much easier to combine quasi-identifiers such as ZIP code, age, gender, location histories, dates, occupations, or unusual behavior.
Researchers demonstrated this problem repeatedly as large datasets became available. In the 1990s, computer scientist Latanya Sweeney famously showed that combinations of ZIP code, birth date, and sex could uniquely identify a large portion of the U.S. population. She linked supposedly anonymous health records to public voter-registration data and identified the medical record of Massachusetts governor William Weld. The lesson was not that useful research data can never be shared. It was that identifiability depends on what other data exists and what computational linkages are possible.
Under European data-protection guidance, pseudonymization reduces direct linkability by replacing or separating identifiers, but someone may still be reidentified using additional information. Pseudonymized records therefore remain personal data and remain covered by the GDPR.
Anonymization aims to make records no longer identifiable by means reasonably likely to be used. If data is genuinely anonymous, it falls outside the GDPR. Achieving that threshold can be difficult, especially with small populations, rare characteristics, precise locations, longitudinal histories, or publicly available companion datasets.
Aggregation can reduce risk by publishing totals rather than row-level histories. Other approaches include suppressing rare values, broadening categories, limiting precision, restricting access, or releasing synthetic data. Each technique trades analytical detail for protection, and none should be described as anonymous without examining realistic reidentification risks.
For the Seattle circulation data, monthly title-level totals preserve evidence about collective reading while avoiding patron-level histories. But even aggregate data needs review: very small counts, distinctive communities, or linked datasets can sometimes reveal more than designers intended.

title: Openness & Organization
text:
What is Fair Use?


In Authors Guild v. HathiTrust, university libraries created a repository containing millions of digitized books. HathiTrust used the copies for full-text search, access for patrons with certified print disabilities, and certain replacement uses.
The Second Circuit held in 2014 that full-text search was a “quintessentially transformative” fair use. Search results did not provide the book itself; they enabled a different function. The court also held that providing accessible copies to print-disabled patrons was fair use.
The whole books had to be copied for the system to work, but the amount copied was assessed in relation to the new purpose. This is an important distinction between making a computational copy and distributing a substitute copy to the public.
We introduced HathiTrust earlier through the history of mass digitization. Google began scanning research-library books at enormous scale in 2004, applying the logic of web search to print collections. Participating libraries received digital copies that helped form HathiTrust’s repository. At that point, I asked students to distinguish digitization, preservation, discoverability, and full public access. This case supplies the legal history behind those different interface states.
The earlier example of The Crisis is useful here. A digitized representation can be preserved, OCRed, cataloged, and computationally searchable even when copyright determines whether a user sees complete page images, a snippet, or only a bibliographic record.

title: Openness & Organization
text:
How has fair use evolved?


This case needs careful phrasing. It is Bartz v. Anthropic, not Authors Guild v. Anthropic. The Authors Guild supported authors and provided guidance, but the named plaintiffs included Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber, and Kirk Wallace Johnson.
In June 2025, the district court distinguished two acts. It held that training language models on lawfully acquired books was transformative fair use. It did not excuse Anthropic’s acquisition and retention of millions of pirated books in a central library.
The parties reached a $1.5 billion settlement concerning pirated books. The court granted final approval on July 20, 2026. The settlement resolves specified past claims; it does not settle every legal question about generative AI, outputs, or future uses.
The distinction is crucial for today’s theme: a potentially lawful analytical purpose does not erase the provenance of the source material.









HathiTrust
Anthropic




Institution
Library consortium
Commercial AI company


Source
Library collections
Purchased and pirated books


Purpose
Search and accessibility
Model training and a research library


Public output
Search results or authorized access
Generative model outputs


Central question
Transformative use
Transformative use and provenance



Both projects copied books at enormous scale, so “they copied everything” does not resolve the legal or ethical question.
HathiTrust’s design limited what ordinary users could retrieve and supported search and accessibility. Anthropic developed commercial models and also assembled a central library that included pirated copies. The district court treated model training and acquisition as analytically distinct.
This comparison gives us four questions for any mass cultural dataset: What was copied? How was it acquired? What is the new purpose? What can users retrieve or regenerate?

title: Openness & Organization
text:
Which Term Answers Which Question?







Term
Core Question




Copyright
Who controls specified uses of creative expression?


Fair use
When may copyrighted material be used without permission?


Public domain
Is the work free of copyright restrictions?


License
What uses has a rights holder authorized?


Privacy
Is information flowing appropriately, and could people be harmed?


Access
Who can obtain, interpret, or use the material in practice?




I want to separate these terms before moving to the court cases.
Copyright does not protect facts as such, though a particular selection or expression may be protected. Fair use is a case-specific limitation on copyright, not a blanket exception for anything educational. Courts consider purpose and character, the nature of the work, the amount used, and market effects.
Public domain describes copyright status, not ethical neutrality. A license communicates permission from a rights holder. Privacy asks about people, context, expectations, and harm. Access includes practical conditions such as cost, format, disability access, technical skill, and documentation.

title: Openness & Organization
text:
What Makes the Governors Dataset “Open”?


Now I want to apply the readings to A Historical Dataset of U.S. Governors. We should identify what is actually open: Can we download the data? Is there a license? Can we find the sources? Is the methodology documented? Can we understand how categories were constructed?
The dataset concerns public figures and historical records, so its privacy risks differ from patron-level library circulation or community cultural heritage. That does not make it neutral. We should still ask which offices, dates, identities, affiliations, and sources were selected and standardized.
We should also examine the essay as part of the dataset. Context and documentation are not decorations around data; they shape whether reuse is informed and responsible.
This connects directly to Rawson and Muñoz’s work on the NYPL menu data. They found that an open download was not automatically transparent or reusable: the data still embodied crowdsourcing workflows, transcription variation, cataloging decisions, and the scalable needs of an institution. Their response was not simply to “clean” the records but to document and curate differences in relation to research questions.
Aurora J. (Auroraj3, Section B) asked what happens when the publicly available biographies used as source material change over time. This is the provenance question I want students to notice: downloading a current webpage does not automatically preserve the evidence on which an earlier record was based. Open annotation
What Does the Dataset Organize?

People into records
Political careers into fields
Historical change into consistent categories
Sources into evidence
Uncertainty into documented decisions—or silence

Organization is an argument. Turning governors into rows requires decisions about what counts as a governor, how to handle territorial governments, acting governors, party changes, interrupted terms, changing state boundaries, identity categories, and conflicting sources.
This returns us to ontology. The schema defines what kinds of entities and relationships the dataset can express. Openness allows us to inspect and challenge those decisions only if the documentation preserves them.
I want to ask students where they can see interpretive labor and where they still encounter uncertainty. What would be difficult to infer from the final table alone?
This is also where our earlier work on MARC, library metadata, and authority control returns. Shared fields and standards make records interoperable, but they also stabilize particular categories. Data Feminism asked who has the power to classify; Rawson and Muñoz asked how communities might build alternative authorities; the Governors dataset lets us inspect how those questions appear in an apparently straightforward historical table.
Student annotations to raise:

Aurora J. (Auroraj3, Section B) questioned the dataset’s method of identifying known women and assigning every remaining governor to the male category. She also asked what counts as college attendance and how geographic edge cases such as Washington, D.C., fit the rules. Gender annotation; education annotation
Jack G. (jgoby2, Section A) highlighted the records in which governors’ birth dates came after their terms began. This is a useful distinction between correcting a demonstrable error and treating a culturally complicated category as if it merely needed cleaning. Open annotation

title: Openness & Organization
text:
What is web scraping?


Publicly reachable does not automatically mean:

Public domain
Licensed for reuse
Free of personal information
Welcome at any scale
Ethically detached from its context

Web scraping intensified as more cultural activity moved online and browsers, search engines, archives, and later machine-learning companies automated collection at large scales.
Scraping is a method for requesting and extracting web content. It is not itself a legal or ethical permission. A scraper may encounter copyright, privacy, contractual terms, technical access controls, database rights in some jurisdictions, and obligations to communities represented in the material.
The fact that a browser can display a page answers only a technical access question. It does not tell us whether mass collection, redistribution, commercial use, or model training is permitted or responsible.
This returns to Manovich’s optimism about using APIs, crawling, and scraping to map a cultural universe too large for any person to browse. At the time, we noted his brief warning about user privacy. Christen now gives that warning a deeper history: scale can detach cultural materials from the people, protocols, and contexts that governed their circulation. The relevant question is not only whether our code can retrieve a page but what social relationship our collection method creates.

title: Openness & Organization
section: What Kind of Permission Are We Checking?
text:
What Kind of Permission Are We Checking?







Signal
What It Can Tell Us




robots.txt
Which paths compliant crawlers are asked to access or avoid


HTTP status
Whether the server will fulfill this request


Terms and licenses
Which forms of access or reuse are authorized


Privacy and community protocols
What collection or circulation may cause harm




I want to keep these layers separate because they are easy to collapse into the single question, “Can I scrape this?”
The Robots Exclusion Protocol emerged in 1994 as webmasters and crawler developers tried to prevent automated systems from overwhelming sites. A site places a plain-text file at the root address, such as https://tolkiengateway.net/robots.txt. Rules organized under User-agent identify crawlers and use directives such as Disallow and Allow to describe paths. The protocol was formalized as an Internet standard in RFC 9309 in 2022.
robots.txt is a request to compliant crawlers, not an authentication system or technical barrier. It does not grant a copyright license, waive terms of service, provide consent from people represented in the data, or settle whether collection is ethical. Conversely, a license may authorize reuse of content without promising that a server will permit thousands of automated requests.
This connects directly to our web-scraping lesson. Tolkien Gateway’s robots.txt does not impose a blanket ban on our small scholarly scraper, but it asks automated visitors to behave responsibly. We therefore identify ourselves with an honest User-Agent, add a delay between requests, and stop if the server refuses or rate-limits us.
The HTTP response is another layer. A 200 tells us that this particular request succeeded. A 403 tells us that the server understood and refused it. Even if a robots.txt rule appears to permit a path, Cloudflare or another access-control system may still block automated requests. That is the difference between a site’s stated crawling policy and its enforced technical boundary. Using a browser emulator or evasion package to defeat the block does not create permission; for this course, a block means we choose another source or an authorized API.
Terms and licenses answer related but distinct questions. Terms of service may govern the relationship between a user and a platform. A Creative Commons license grants specified copyright permissions for covered content. Neither necessarily grants permission to collect personal information at scale, burden a server, or detach culturally governed material from its community context.
Christen helps extend the checklist beyond legal ownership. A scrape may comply with robots.txt, receive a 200, and collect openly licensed files while still violating community protocols or exposing sensitive knowledge. Before collecting, I want students to check the site’s crawling guidance, technical response, terms or license, privacy risks, and community expectations rather than treating any one signal as the final answer.

title: Openness & Organization
section: Who Gets to Decide What Becomes Open?
text:
Who Gets to Decide What Becomes Open?


I want to begin by resisting the idea that openness is automatically good or that restriction is automatically bad. Today’s readings give us two different reasons to question those assumptions.
Christen asks what happens when calls for universal openness ignore colonial histories and living communities’ authority over knowledge. Walsh asks what happens when corporations keep consequential cultural data closed and use it to make decisions about whose books get published.
The recurring questions for today are:

Who has the authority to make information open?
Who benefits from access, and who bears the risk?
When does restriction concentrate power?
When can restriction instead be a form of care, sovereignty, or accountability?

What Is Christen’s Core Argument?
We need more than open/closed, free/proprietary, and public/private.
When does restriction enforce power?
When does restriction return authority?
Christen is not defending corporate DRM, nor is she arguing that all information should be closed. She asks us to distinguish a corporation controlling consumers from a marginalized community defining protocols for its own cultural heritage.
Her core argument is that openness must be situated historically and socially. Universal openness can reproduce exclusion when it ignores how communities lost control over their materials in the first place.
Mukurtu “turns control on its head” by giving access decisions to communities and users. The question is not control versus no control. It is who controls what, through which relationships, and toward what ends.
Student annotations to raise:

Mazen A. (malee22, Section A) asked whether objections to Mukurtu are genuinely objections to restricting information or objections to communities and collectives controlling access. Open annotation
Allison Q. (allisonqiu, Section B) wrote that public availability can take away a community’s ability to determine how its knowledge is shared and interpreted. Open annotation

title: Openness & Organization
text:
Is “Open” One Thing?


Accessible
Publicly visible
Openly licensed
In the public domain
Reusable
Ethically shareable


These terms often get collapsed, but they describe different conditions.
Something can be publicly visible online and still be copyrighted. A dataset can be downloadable but lack a license that permits reuse. A work can be in the legal public domain while still containing culturally sensitive knowledge. A repository can be technically accessible while remaining unusable because of inaccessible design, missing documentation, or paywalls.
Privacy is yet another question: it concerns people, information flows, expectations, and possible harms. Copyright concerns rights in creative expression. Neither one alone tells us whether sharing is ethical.
This returns us to several earlier classes. Project Gutenberg showed us that public-domain status can make cultural materials easier to download and compute with. Our discussion of Aaron Swartz and JSTOR showed that technically obtaining a file, receiving access through an institution, and having permission to redistribute it are different things. Lenna showed that persistent public circulation can continue even when the person represented asks a community to stop. Today I want to put names to those distinctions rather than treating all of them as a single question of openness.
Do Christen and Walsh Disagree?


Christen asks:
When does openness reproduce extraction?

Walsh asks:
When does closed data preserve institutional power?

What would responsible access require in each case?
I do not think these readings cancel each other out. They identify different locations of power.
Christen examines cultural materials whose circulation was often taken away from Indigenous communities. Returning decision-making authority may require differentiated access.
Walsh examines data held by corporations that use secrecy to govern authors, publishing, and cultural visibility. Opening that data could redistribute the capacity to scrutinize the industry.
Together they suggest that “open” is not the first question. We should first ask who currently has power, how the data was acquired, who is represented, who faces harm, and who can make or contest decisions.

title: Openness & Organization
section: What Should “Open” Require From Our Projects?
text:
What Should “Open” Require From Our Projects?


Provenance — Where did the material come from?
Authority — Who can decide how it circulates?
Purpose — What use does the project enable?
Risk — Who could be harmed by release or reuse?
Access — Who can actually use it?
Documentation — What choices and limits remain visible?


This is the project connection. I do not want students to assume they must release every field publicly or choose a standard open license without reflection.
For each dataset, they should document sources and acquisition; identify relevant rights holders and represented communities; explain the purpose of collection; consider privacy, cultural sensitivity, and downstream misuse; choose an access model and license where appropriate; and record uncertainty and limitations.
Different parts of one project can have different access conditions. Documentation may be public while sensitive records are restricted. Aggregate results may be open while row-level data is withheld. The responsible choice should follow the material and relationships, not an automatic rule.

title: Creating & Curating
section: Against Cleaning by Rawson and Muñoz
text:
Against Cleaning by Rawson and Muñoz





Dr. Katie Rawson






Dr. Trevor Muñoz




Katie leads the library at the Annenberg School of Communication. She provides research support for the field of Communication to students, faculty, and the wider community. She offers one-on-one and group research instruction and works to make the Annenberg Library a welcoming space for individual and collaborative learning.
Before coming to the Annenberg School, she was Director of Learning Innovation at Penn Libraries. Previously, she had been Managing Editor of Southern Spaces, Humanities Librarian for English at Emory University, and the Coordinator for Digital Research at the University of Pennsylvania Libraries.
Katie has a PhD from the Graduate Institute of Liberal Arts at Emory University. She researches and teaches on academic collaboration, data curation in the humanities, computational text analysis, and food history and culture.
Trevor Muñoz is the Director of the Maryland Institute for Technology in the Humanities (MITH). He provides management and strategic direction for MITH’s portfolio of digital humanities research, community building, and public programming. His own current research is centered in a community-university collaboration dedicated to preserving and sharing the heritage of the historic African American community of Lakeland in Prince George’s County, Maryland, through community members’ own voices. His work has focused on humanities approaches to data curation [1] [2], the strategic opportunities and challenges of doing digital humanities work within the institutional and cultural structures of academic research libraries [3] [4], and on the design and sustainability of interdisciplinary research collaborations. Muñoz is a member of the founding team of the African American History and Culture and Digital Humanities (AADHum) Initiative and has served, since 2017, as a Co-Principal Investigator for the major grant from The Andrew W. Mellon Foundation that supports AADHum. With Jennifer Guiliano, he serves as Co-Director of the Humanities Intensive Learning + Teaching (HILT) Institute. Muñoz previously served as MITH’s Associate Director and also as Assistant Dean for Digital Humanities Research in the University of Maryland Libraries. Muñoz holds an MA in Digital Humanities from the Department of Digital Humanities at King’s College London and an MS in Library and Information Science from the School of Information Sciences at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign.

title: Creating & Curating
text:
What is data cleaning?

What are some methods of data cleaning that you have heard of or tried?

“ractitioners, critics, and popularizers of new methods of data-driven research treat the concept of “data cleaning” as integral to such work without remarking on the oddly domestic image the term makes—as though a corn straw broom were to be incorporated, Rube Goldberg–like, into the design of the Large Hadron Collider. In reality, data cleaning is a consequential step in the research process that we often make opaque by the way we talk about it. The phrase “data cleaning” is a stand-in for longer and more precise descriptions of what people are doing in the initial phases of data-intensive research. If you work with data or pay attention to discussions among practitioners who do, you have probably heard or read somewhere that 80 percent of that work is “cleaning” (cf. Wickham).” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 279)
“Many times the specifics of data cleaning are not described anywhere at all, but instead reside in the general professional practices, materials, personal histories, and tools of the researchers. That we employ obscuring language like “data cleaning” should be a strong invitation to scrutinize, perhaps reimagine, and almost certainly rename this part of our practice.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 279)
“The persistence of an element that is “out of focus” in discussions of dataintensive research does not invalidate the findings of such research, nor is it meant to cast researchers using these methods under suspicion. Rather, the collective acceptance of a connotative term, “cleaning,” suggests two assumptions: first, that researchers in many domains consider the consequences of whatever is done during this little-discussed (80 percent) part of the process as sufficiently limited or bounded so as not to threaten the value of any findings; and second, relatedly, that there is little to be gained from a more precise description of those elements of the research process that currently fall under the rubric of cleaning.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 279)

title: Creating & Curating
text:
Why “Against Cleaning”?

Does their argument remind you of any previous readings?

title: Creating & Curating
section: Why is data cleaning counter to how humanists think about data?
text:
Why is data cleaning counter to how humanists think about data?



“Yet the humanities cannot import paradigms and practices wholesale from other fields, whether from “technoscience” or the nearer “social” sciences, without risking the foreclosure of specific and valuable humanistic modes of producing knowledge. If we are interested in working with data, and we accept that there is something in our work with data that is like what other fields might call “data cleaning,” we have no choice but to try to articulate both what it is and what it means in terms of how humanists make knowledge.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 280)
“In other data-intensive fields in which researchers have long been explicit about their framing orders, the limits of results are often understood and articulated using specialized discourses. For example, in climate science, researchers confine their claims to the data they can work with and report results with margins of error. While humanities researchers do have discourses for limiting claims (acknowledging the choice of an archive or a particular intellectual tradition), the move into data-intensive research asks humanists to modify such discourses or develop new ones suitable for these projects.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 281)



What is the problem of reductiveness in data cleaning? How does it relate to the humanist tradition of studying difference?
“Admittedly, this may only be an issue of the present moment, one experienced as a tax on those humanities researchers who wish to adopt new methods by asking them to overexplain their work processes. Once such methods are more widely practiced, the data-intensive humanities researcher may also be able to toss off the shorthand of “data cleaning.” For now, however, there is significant value in being arrested by the obfuscation of this phrase. By taking first a descriptive approach (precisely saying what we mean by data cleaning) and, second, speculating on alternative approaches, we intervene in an unresolved conversation about data and reductiveness in the humanities.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 280)
“When humanities scholars recoil at data-driven research, they are often responding to the reductiveness inherent in this form of scholarship. This reductiveness can feel intellectually impoverished to scholars who have spent their careers working through particular kinds of historical and cultural complexity. The modern humanities have invested mental and moral energy into, and reaped insights from, studying difference. Bethany Nowviskie summarizes this tradition in this volume’s Chapter 37, “Capacity through Care”: “The finest contribution of the past several decades of humanities research has been to broaden, contextualize, and challenge canonical collections and privileged views. Scholars do this by elevating instances of neglected or alternate lived experience—singular human conditions, often revealed to reflect the mainstream.”” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 280)
“From within this worldview, data cleaning becomes maligned because it is understood as a step that inscribes a normative order by wiping away what is different. The term “cleaning” implies that a dataset begins as “messy.” “Messy” suggests an underlying order: it supposes things already have a rightful place, but they are not in it—like socks on the bedroom floor rather than in the bureau or the hamper.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 280)
“In other data-intensive fields in which researchers have long been explicit about their framing orders, the limits of results are often understood and articulated using specialized discourses. For example, in climate science, researchers confine their claims to the data they can work with and report results with margins of error.1 While humanities researchers do have discourses for limiting claims (acknowledging the choice of an archive or a particular intellectual tradition), the move into data-intensive research asks humanists to modify such discourses or develop new ones suitable for these projects.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 281)

title: Creating & Curating
section: What is the Curating Menus Project?
text:
What is the Curating Menus Project?


Why do the authors call it a naive tool?
“To contribute to the development of new discourses and the practice of critically attuned data work, we scrutinize cleaning through a reflection on our own work with Curating Menus. Curating Menus is a research project that aims to curate and analyze the open data from New York Public Library’s What’s on the Menu? We set off to answer questions like the following: Can we see the effect of wartime food rationing in what appeared on menus during World War I? Or, can we track the changing boundaries of what constituted a “dish” over time? To do this, we thought we would need to “clean” the “messy” data. What became evident was that cleaning up or correcting values was a misleading—and even unproductive—way to think about how to make the data more useful for our own questions and for other scholars studying food. Under the rubric of cleaning, we began with a technical solution to what we had imagined was a technical problem.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 281)

title: Creating & Curating
section: What is the What’s on the Menu Project?
text:
What is the What’s on the Menu Project?


“The NYPL data is a linked network graph of unique URLs for dishes and menus. The Curating Menus dataset is an organized hierarchy of concepts from the domain of food. We made a set of labels that we believe would facilitate humanities researchers’ understanding of the scope, diversity, and value of the NYPL’s dataset. The two datasets are connected by links from concept labels in our dataset to dishes in the NYPL dataset. Our interaction with the NYPL dataset thus became a process of evaluating which variants in the names of dishes revealed new information, which we should in turn account for in our own data, and which variants were simply accidents of transcription or typesetting. The process freed us to attend to difference and detail, rather than attempting to clean it away. Without cleaning, we could be sensitive to questions about time, place, and subject. This kind of attention is imperative if humanities researchers are to find the menu data valuable for their scholarship.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 283)

title: Creating & Curating
text:
How was the data created?


What is crowdsourcing? What are some other examples of crowdsourcing? https://www.zooniverse.org/projects
The “What’s on the Menu?” site was a historical milestone for NYPL and represents the first NYPL-built API. The site was a crowdsourced project to transcribe dishes and prices from the Library’s collection of digitized menus to create a searchable index and set of visualization tools that show changes in cuisine and prices over time. More than 17,000 of 45,000 menus were digitized for the project. A crowdsourced geocoding component was also added in order to map various restaurant locations across New York City. Throughout the course of the project, 1,335,570 dishes were transcribed from 17,562 menus. Users have consistently requested API keys throughout the life of the project to explore the data and build their own projects.
“Paul Beaudoin from the NYPL Labs team discusses some of the logic behind their approach to these kind of projects in a blog post announcing Scribe, an opensource software platform released in 2015, but derived from the library’s experience with crowdsourced transcription projects.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 286)
“Beaudoin describes how the Scribe platform is based on “simplification [that] allows us to reduce complex document transcription to a series of smaller decisions that can be tackled individually . . . the atomicity of tasks makes projects less daunting for volunteers to begin and easier to continue.” F” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 286)
“The NYPL Labs team is explicit about its commitments to designing for scalability. We know from work in the domain of scholarly editing that what comprises “transcription” is not self-evident.6 It could be modeled and implemented in software in a number of ways. The menus project uses optical character recognition (OCR) software to generate bounding boxes that determine what human volunteers will transcribe. In this, we can see the precision nesting of scales at work. OCR software is designed to scalably produce machine-readable, machine-processable digital text from images of printed material. In the case of the menus, the software can detect regions of text within the digital images; however, due to the variation in typefaces, the aging of inks and paper, and other nonscalable elements, the output of the OCR algorithm is not a legible set of words.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 286)
“It constructs the act of transcription in such a way that it matches the scalable process of digitization and ways of understanding the content of a menu that privilege scalable data.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 287)
“In addition, the project was designed so that people did not have to create accounts or sign in to submit transcriptions. Creators and managers of such projects are working to make more data and to allow more people to participate in making data. This entails creating systems that treat volunteers as interchangeable in the service of allowing more work to get done more quickly. However, what is construed as a scalable workforce is, in fact, made up of people who have different levels of understanding or adherence to the guidelines and different perceptions or interpretations of the materials. When we understand this workforce as a collection of individuals, we can see how any crowd as large as the one that has worked on the menus project will contain such diversity. The analytic apparatus of Tsing’s nonscalability theory makes all these design choices visible and allows us to see the transcription task, as framed within What’s on the Menu?, as another moment of articulation between scalable and nonscalable elements.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 287)

What was the problem with their initial approach to cleaning the data? How did they change their approach? Who has heard of or used open refine before? https://openrefine.org/ What is the problem of normalizing and crowdsourcing? “Variation in the strings of text transcribed from menus was obscuring our ability to do things as simple as count how many dishes were in the dataset. Working with Lydia Zvygintseva, we attempted to reduce the number of variations using OpenRefine, an open-source software tool designed for these types of tasks. When the scale of the problem overwhelmed the capabilities of that tool, we discovered that it was possible to run the clustering algorithms popularized by OpenRefine using custom Python scripts (Muñoz). The output of one of these scripts was a list of variant values such as the following” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 281)
“We had not yet recognized that the data model around which the dataset was organized was not the data model we needed to answer our research questions. At the time, the main challenge seemed to be processing enough values quickly enough to “get on with it.” At that point in the research process, the Python scripts we were using were small, purpose-built command line programs. After some deliberation, we decided to build a simple web application to provide the task-specific user interfaces we would need to tackle the challenge of NYPL’s menu data.2 The piece of software we built does, in some ways, the opposite of what one might expect” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 282)
“A cluster of values like the one for “Potatoes Au Gratin” is presented to the user, and he or she must make a decision about how to turn that cluster of variants into a single value. Our tool sorts the variants by the number of times they appear across the dataset. So the decision may be to simply save the most commonly occurring value as the normalized form: “potatoes au gratin.” Or it might be to modify that value based on a set of rules we have defined.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 282)
“The tool surfaces near-matches, but it does not automate the work of collapsing them into normalized values. Instead, it focuses the user’s attention and labor on exactly that activity. In other words, in our initial version of computer-assisted data curation, we still had to touch each data point. This caused us to doubt that we could use this method with a whole dataset the size of the one from What’s on the Menu?; however, it was intellectually productive.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 282)
“In the process of normalizing values, we found ourselves faced with questions about the foods themselves. Choosing the “correct” string was not a self-contained problem, but an issue that required returning to our research questions and investigating the foods themselves. Since the research questions we were asking required us to maintain information about brands and places, we often had to look up items to see which was the correct spelling of the brand or place name.3” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 283)

title: Creating & Curating
section: How did they build their data model? How did their data model transform?
text:
How did they build their data model? How did their data model transform?


“We realized that the changes we were making were not “corrections” that would “clean up” the original dataset, but rather formed an additional information set with its own data model. What we thought were data points were, in fact, a synthesis or mash-up of different kinds of information within a half-finished or half-articulated data model. This data model was sufficient for the original aim of the project—supporting an application that facilitated crowdsourced transcription—but it is insufficient for scholarly inquiry. To ask research questions, we needed to create our own dataset, which would work in context with the NYPL dataset.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 283)
“The NYPL data is a linked network graph of unique URLs for dishes and menus. The Curating Menus dataset is an organized hierarchy of concepts from the domain of food. We made a set of labels that we believe would facilitate humanities researchers’ understanding of the scope, diversity, and value of the NYPL’s dataset. The two datasets are connected by links from concept labels in our dataset to dishes in the NYPL dataset. Our interaction with the NYPL dataset thus became a process of evaluating which variants in the names of dishes revealed new information, which we should in turn account for in our own data, and which variants were simply accidents of transcription or typesetting. The process freed us to attend to difference and detail, rather than attempting to clean it away. Without cleaning, we could be sensitive to questions about time, place, and subject. This kind of attention is imperative if humanities researchers are to find the menu data valuable for their scholarship.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 283)
“We know that the response to this friction is not to retreat from working at scale. Instead we have to find ways of working while being aware that precision nesting hides diversity and that there are consequences to diversity being hidden.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 287)
“Our answer to this challenge is an index. We are suggesting that indexing is a more precise replacement for some of the work that travels under the name of “cleaning.” An index is an information structure designed to serve as a system of pointers between two bodies of information, one of which is organized to provide access to concepts in the other. The list of terms and associated page numbers from the back of a book is one familiar example. An array of other terms that people use alongside “cleaning” (wrangling, munging, normalizing, casting) name other important parts of working with data, but indexing best captures the crucial interplay of scalability and diversity that we are trying to trace in this chapter. We began to think of the work we were doing as building something like a backof-the-book index for the What’s on the Menu? data. We aimed to create additional data structures around and atop the existing data, generating links between a set of names or categories we created and the larger and more heterogeneous set of data from NYPL. Ultimately, we decided to build two interconnected indexes: one focused on historical food concepts and one on the organizations connected to the menus (businesses, community organizations, fraternal societies, etc.).” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 288)
“If we had felt no unease continuing the lineage of precision nesting that links the scales of digitization and crowdsourced transcription, we could have proceeded with a completely algorithmic approach: “cleaning” our data using scripts, linguistic rules, and even machine learning. These methods yield results by predictively circumscribing variants in language so as to aggregate and enable analysis at another level of abstraction. We can see the usefulness of these algorithmic approaches, but we also know that they would hide diversity in the menus. However, to understand the implications of these diversity-hiding methods, we needed to create a grounded approach to making a data model for our index.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 288)
“Today, when we look at a list of variations on “Potatoes au Gratin” or some other group of transcriptions, we focus on the task of choosing a label that will be a node in our dataset and that will serve as a pointer to all the other transcribed values in the NYPL dataset. We are building the set of labels from the set of data, rather than beginning by writing some large, hierarchical domain model. We want to represent the concept of two eggs and bacon, not caring if it was written “bacon and two eggs” or “2 Eggs and Bacon.” To get from transcription to concept, we began with a set of simple rules: spell out numbers and use lowercase letters. Actually engaging with the menu transcriptions quickly raised other questions. For example, on the question of place names, we decided to apply capitalization rules (in accord with style guides like The Chicago Manual of Style) that say that you capitalize when the reference to place is literal, but not when the reference makes a generic association:” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 288)
“In building our index, we are conscientiously creating scalability. We know that scalability is a process of articulations between different scales; however, Tsing suggests—and we believe—that those articulations are often hidden. Conversely, indexes are tools of scalability that make these articulations explicit.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 289)
