title: Creating & Curating
section: How did A History of Menus is a Menu of History work with the same data?
text:
How did A History of Menus is a Menu of History work with the same data?

What did you learn about the history of restaurants from this data?

Restaurant dining in America began in the 1830s. These were not the old taverns serving alcohol and hearty grub, but as spaces for culinary pleasure. By the late 1800s, they firmly catered to America’s new world elite, who sought to emulate what they believed was the height of culture: French aristocracy.
Restaurant dining was one way the post-Civil War elite distinguished themselves from the masses. French was an aspect of that gatekeeping—luxury was another.
The American aristocratic restaurant of the late-1800s didn’t just serve food that paired complex cooking technique with luxury ingredients, it also publicly flaunted that decadence.
The public nature of this luxury was useful to differentiate the status and power of the elite: what they ate, how much of it, and with what customs and trappings.
Feasting in public also became easier than hosting at home. As industrialization offered more kinds of employment to the lower classes, elite households started to lose domestic staff. Restaurants offered another space for the elite to be seen, hosting events of all kinds, such as community celebrations—like this one for a Scottish expat society—memorials, and club meetings.
Into the early 20th century, industrialization produced a working middle class who desired more than old taverns and dives.
At the same time, the technological innovation transforming the labor market also made it cheaper to produce, transport, and preserve food.
Menus at the turn of the 20th century are beginning to show major departures from the menus of just a few decades earlier. Nevermind public displays of wealth—there was now a whole new public to serve.
The elite European menu took hours to experience. The middle-class restaurateur understood that workers wanted a good deal and a complete meal in a matter of minutes. A new wave of shoppers could also be convinced to stop for a meal among their errands.
That works a lot better when everything is one one plate.
In the early 1900s, the largest period of immigration in American history brought a host of new food cultures to American cities. The emerging middle class in those cities saw this culinary diversity as a source of national pride and immigrant entrepreneurship as a symbol of American accomplishment.
Italian and German restaurants were early challengers to French dominance in dining, but middle class diners found that there were Chinese, Russian, and Syrian restaurateurs serving local immigrant populations who would be happy to take their business, too.
While ethnic food didn’t fix racism in America, dining in America did diversify across age and gender in this era. Aristocratic French restaurants had once been the province purely of men; later, lunch counters and other new eateries segregated the sexes. But as the century progressed, restaurants both shifted to mixed gender dining rooms and began to cater to entire families.

title: Creating & Curating
section: How does the interactive map differ from the menu history article?
text:
How does the interactive map differ from the menu history article?


Depicted are 5,000 menus from the New York Public Library’s Buttolph Collection, pulled from an archive of over 25,000 menus and dated from 1880-1920. Most of the menus were painstakingly assembled by one woman.
From 1900 to 1925, Frank Buttolph dedicated herself to collecting menus, tirelessly visiting restaurants, soliciting menus in newspaper ads, and contacting menu printers. She said, “[My] work has been the only thing I had to live for. It was my heart, my soul, my life.”
For example, pictured is one such menu she personally archived: The Plaza in 1897, a high-end NYC restaurant, where the canvas-back duck runs $120 in today’s dollars. Note how different the menu looks versus today: the number of items, dessert options, and French words.
Yet, the industrial revolution created a new upper-class generation who aspired to different ideals, and restaurants were one way to signal their riches. That is, the restaurant began as a status symbol.
Yet Buttolph’s archive was pigeonholed as the “feminine instinct for accumulation,” rather than the serious work of an archivist. She insisted that she wasn’t a 20th century foodie; she argued that, 100 years into the future, the menus would be valuable to historians, but she admitted she wasn’t sure how.
What a prediction! Take, for example, that the archive is a window into early 19th-century elite society, particularly that of wealthy white men, and it is not difficult to find racist caricatures of Black Americans and Indigenous peoples and sexist tropes in menu designs. Women often had their own menus, called “Ladies Ordinary,” as they were not allowed to dine alone in the same room as men.

title: Creating & Curating
section: How does scale relate to Deep Fried Data?
text:
How does scale relate to Deep Fried Data?


In our case, the deep-fryer is a toolbox of statistical techniques. The names keep changing—it used to be unsupervised learning, now it’s called big data or deep learning or AI. Next year it will be called something else. But the core ideas don’t change. You train a computer on lots of data, and it learns to recognize structure.
These techniques are effective, but the fact that the same generic approach works across a wide range of domains should make you suspicious about how much insight it’s adding.
And in any deep frying situation, a good question to ask is: what is this stuff being fried in?
For this reason I’ve referred to machine learning as money laundering for bias. It’s easy to put anything you want in training data.
For example, if you go to Google translate and paste in an Arabic-language article about terrorism or the war in Syria, you get something that reads like it was written by a native speaker of English. If you type in a kid’s letter from camp, or an extract from a novel, the English text reads like it was written by the Frankenstein monster.
Besides these issues of bias, there’s also an opportunity cost in committing to computational tools. What irks me about the love affair with algorithms is that they remove a lot of the potential for surprise and serendipity that you get by working with people.
If you go searching for patterns in the data, you’ll find patterns in the data. Whoop-de-doo. But anything fresh and distinctive in your digital collections will not make it through the deep frier.
We’ve seen entire fields disappear down the numerical rabbit hole before. Economics came first, sociology and political science are still trying to get out, bioinformatics is down there somewhere and hasn’t been heard from in a while.
Before you spend a lot of time peeling and julienning your data, consider—is this really the best way to go?

title: Creating & Curating
section: How does bias relate to data cleaning?
text:
How does bias relate to data cleaning?


“For example, if you go to Google translate and paste in an Arabic-language article about terrorism or the war in Syria, you get something that reads like it was written by a native speaker of English. If you type in a kid’s letter from camp, or an extract from a novel, the English text reads like it was written by the Frankenstein monster. This isn’t because Google’s algorithm is a gung-ho war machine, but reflects the corpus of data it was trained on. I’m sure other languages would show their own irregularities. Prejudice isn’t always a problem. Some uses of machine learning are inherently benign. In an earlier talk, we heard about identifying poetry in newspapers based on formatting, an excellent use of image recognition. OCR is another area where there are no concerns.” (Cegłowski, 2016, p. 2)
“I’d be very wary of using “sentiment analysis” or anything to do with social networks without careful experimental design. I find it helpful to think of algorithms as a dim-witted but extremely industrious graduate student, whom you don’t fully trust. You want a concordance made? An index? You want them to go through ten million photos and find every picture of a horse? Perfect. You want them to draw conclusions on gender based on word use patterns? Or infer social relationships from census data? Now you need some adult supervision in the room.” (Cegłowski, 2016, p. 2)
“Besides these issues of bias, there’s also an opportunity cost in committing to computational tools. What irks me about the love affair with algorithms is that they remove a lot of the potential for surprise and serendipity that you get by working with people. If you go searching for patterns in the data, you’ll find patterns in the data. Whoop-dedoo. But anything fresh and distinctive in your digital collections will not make it through the deep frier. We’ve seen entire fields disappear down the numerical rabbit hole before. Economics came first, sociology and political science are still trying to get out, bioinformatics is down there somewhere and hasn’t been heard from in a while. Before you spend a lot of time peeling and julienning your data, consider—is this really the best way to go? Computers eliminate drudgery. But the excitement is the human potential. Today, for the first time, we can make things available to anyone on the planet who has an internet connection. I don’t think we’ve internalized the enormity of that step.” (Cegłowski, 2016, p. 3)

title: Creating & Curating
section: What are alternatives to the language of cleaning?
text:
What are alternatives to the language of cleaning?


“Nonscalability theory encourages us to grapple with this dynamic at each point of articulation in the process of making scalable objects. The collection of these menus was also scalable. The system set up for their accession and processing treated the menus not only as interchangeable objects but also like the many other paper materials that entered the collections of the NYPL in the twentieth century. Perhaps the clearest evidence of this is in their cataloging. The catalog cards fit each menu into the same frame—with fields for the dining establishment, the date of creation and date of accession, and the sponsor of the meal, if available.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 285)
“Cataloging is a way of suppressing or ignoring the great differences in the menus, choosing one type of data to attend to. The cards index the collection so that the institution has a record of its holdings and a user can find a particular object. The menus, with their scalable and nonscalable features, become scalable library inventory through this process” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 285)
“Cataloging’s aim is to find a way to make items at least interchangeable enough not to break the system. The practice is rife with examples of catalogers navigating encounters with difference. Catalogers practice nonscalability theory constantly” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 285)
“Digitization is also a process designed for scalability. As long as an object can fit into the focal area of an imaging device, its size, texture, and other material features are reduced to a digital image file. The zooming enabled by high-resolution digital images is one of Tsing’s prime examples of design and engineering for scalability. In the distribution of digitized images, the properties of the digital surrogate that are suited to scalability are perpetuated, while the properties of the original that are nonscalable (the feel of the paper, its heft or daintiness) are lost.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 286)

title: Creating & Curating
text:
What is Non-Scalability Theory?







“Anna Tsing offered us a valuable theoretical framework through which to approach these issues. In “On Nonscalability: The Living World Is Not Amenable to Precision-Nested Scales,” Tsing critiques scalability as an overarching paradigm for organizing systems (whether world trade, scientific research, or colonial economies). By scalability, Tsing means the quality that allows things to be traded out for each other in a totalizing system without regard to the unique or individual qualities of those things—like many stalks of sugarcane (which are biological clones of one another) or, subsequently, workers in a factory.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 283)
“While scalable design creates only one relationship between elements of a system (what Tsing calls “precision nesting”), nonscalable phenomena are enmeshed in multiple relationships, outside or in tension with the nesting frame.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 284)
“Currently, the imagination of the cultural heritage world has been captured by crowdsourced information production on the one hand and large-scale institutional aggregation on the other: the What’s on the Menu? project exemplifies both of these trends. Our difficulties working with the open data from this project suggest that it is a vital moment to consider the virtues of nonscalability theory in relation to digital scholarship. Engineering crowdsourced cultural heritage projects usually involves making object transcription, identification, and the development of metadata scalable.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 284)
“The images of menus and the metadata about them are also being republished through projects like the Digital Public Library of America (DPLA), another example of how things get shaped and parsed for purposes of scaling up to ever wider distribution. Tsing reminds us, “At best, scalable projects are articulations between scalable and nonscalable elements, in which nonscalable effects can be hidden” (515). She argues that the question is not whether we do or do not engage in scalable or nonscalable processes. To explore the articulations between scalable and nonscalable, Tsing tells the story of the contemporary matsutake industry, which encompasses both foraging” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 284)
“Following Tsing, we came to see points of articulation that had previously been invisible to us as would-be consumers of scaled data. Beginning from the creation of the original, physical menus and tracing the development of the crowd-created data, we identify and account for “nonscalable elements”—and consequently, edge further and further from the terminology of “cleaning.”” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 284)

title: Creating & Curating
text:
Scale & Menus



A menu describes what a restaurant serves—but a menu also describes who is being served. They reflect the class, gender, political, technological, and environmental shifts of history. The thousands of menus in this collection document a period of fundamental transformation – and the birth of the society and the restaurant we know today. (The Pudding, 2026)



“Making menus is a scalable process. Although menus are sometimes handwritten or elaborately printed on ribbon-sewn silk, the format of a menu is designed to be scalable. Menus are an efficient typographical vehicle for communicating a set of offerings for often low-margin dining enterprises. Part of the way that we know that menus are scalable is how alike they appear. “Eggs Benedict” or “caviar,” with their accompanying prices, may fit interchangeably into the “slots” of the menu’s layout.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 285)



How does scalability relate to datafying menus?
“Making menus is a scalable process. Although menus are sometimes handwritten or elaborately printed on ribbon-sewn silk, the format of a menu is designed to be scalable. Menus are an efficient typographical vehicle for communicating a set of offerings for often low-margin dining enterprises. Part of the way that we know that menus are scalable is how alike they appear. “Eggs Benedict” or “caviar,” with their accompanying prices, may fit interchangeably into the “slots” of the menu’s layout. Within the menus themselves, we also see evidence of the nexus of printing scalability, dish scalability, and cost in, for example, the use of ellipses to express different options:” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 285)
“These strong genre conventions and the mass production of the menus as physical objects allow us to see and treat them as scaled and scalable.4 However, the menus also express nonscalable elements—historical contingencies and encounters across difference. Some of these nonscalable elements are revealed by the kind of questions we find ourselves asking about the experience of ordering from these menus. How were they understood as part of the interactions among purveyors, customers, and diners? How did diners navigate elements like the pervasive use of French in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries? How did they interpret the particular style and content of cover images or quotations? Evidence for these questions manifests in the menus as objects,” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 285)

title: Creating & Curating
section: What about community based approaches? What are authorities or taxonomies?
text:
What about community based approaches? What are authorities or taxonomies?


“In building our index, we are conscientiously creating scalability. We know that scalability is a process of articulations between different scales; however, Tsing suggests—and we believe—that those articulations are often hidden. Conversely, indexes are tools of scalability that make these articulations explicit.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 289)
“One of the mechanisms that librarians and archivists have used to build and maintain large, distributed information systems is a set of practices referred to as authority control. In brief, these practices involve creating defined and agreedon taxonomies, as well as guidelines for the application of such arrangements of terms. The Library of Congress Subject Headings represent one instance of authority control. Maintaining such a system is labor intensive and has been used only for supporting core library activities like managing collections and supporting patrons in finding materials. Libraries and archives are trying to take advantage of technological developments in linked data—merging their centuries-old authority control practices with the affordances of the World Wide Web. However, what relatively few have seized on are new opportunities to apply the practices of authority control outside the original core needs of collection organization and wayfinding.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 289)
“There is a need for projects that take “authority work” as an invitation to encourage creativity, an invitation for making and building. In such a model, multiple regimes of authorities might be built up from critically aware and engaged intellectual communities to meet their own specific needs while also participating in larger technological and information systems.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 289)
“humanities scholars point out that the structure and content of a specific archive or collection represent and even re-create certain cultural logics. For example, the systems of describing collections, such as the widely used Library of Congress Subject Headings, reify concepts about persons or cultures that should be interrogated more closely or perhaps discredited and dismantled altogether. For the most part, librarians, archivists, and information scientists acknowledge these flaws and perhaps even work to remedy them in the course of maintaining systems that preserve whatever partial archives do exist or helping patrons find information they need. We are looking for new forms of collective action that can be expressed through the professional work of humanities scholars and librarians. This is not simply a call for the production of more data—attempting to subvert the work of categorization and classification through the production of ever more local, finely wrought distinctions, details, and qualifications.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 290) How do we balance reductivity with preserving diversity? “Our aim is to develop ways of working that validate local experiences of data without removing them from a more global network of information exchange.7 These practices, as we imagine them, resonate with Bethany Nowviskie’s interpretation of the Afrofuturist philosophy of Sun Ra (as expressed by Shabaka Hutchings), which claims, “Communities that have agency are able to form their own philosophical structures”(” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 290)
“Discussions of cleaning data fail to capture this need. The cleaning paradigm assumes an underlying, “correct” order. However tidy values may look when grouped into rows or columns or neatly delimited records, this tidiness privileges the structure of a container, rather than the data inside it. This is the same diversity-hiding trick that nonscalability theory encourages us to recognize.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 290)
“But it is not enough to recognize how cleaning suppresses diversity; we must also envision alternate ways of working. The first thing we must do with our datasets, rather than normalizing them, is to find the communities within which our data matters. With those communities in mind and even in dialogue with them, we must ask these questions: What are the concepts that structure this data?” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 290)

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
text:
The World Wide Web

From Wikipedia:

“The World Wide Web (WWW), commonly known as the Web, is an information system where documents and other web resources are identified by Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), which may be interlinked by hypertext, and are accessible over the Internet. The resources of the WWW are transferred via the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and may be accessed by users by a software application called a web browser and are published by a software application called a web server.”



While this is technically accurate, there’s a lot of important history and concepts packed into this definition. Let’s break it down piece by piece to understand how the web actually works and where it came from.
Key concepts to understand: - URLs: how we identify and locate resources - Hypertext: linked documents - HTTP: the protocol for transferring data - Web browsers: applications that display web pages - Web servers: applications that host web pages

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
text:
Histories of the Web: Memex
The core idea of hypertext and the web is about linking information across machines.
We’ve seen this previously with Vannevar Bush’s Memex (1940s), which envisioned using microfilm to link information


The web didn’t emerge from nowhere. There were important antecedents and influences.
Vannevar Bush wrote an influential essay called “As We May Think” that imagined a device called the Memex using microfilm to store and link information. This was visionary thinking about interconnected information.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
text:
Histories of the Web: Xanadu







Project Xanadu Schematic





Ted Nelson’s Project Xanadu (1960s-70s) - create a system to link any information to any other. You can read more at [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Xanadu] Ted Nelson developed Project Xanadu, which tried to create a system where you could link any piece of information to any other piece. It was very influential but never fully realized. He also coined in 1963 hypertext and hypermedia.

The computer world is not just technicality and razzle-dazzle. It is a continual war over software politics and paradigms. With ideas which are still radical, WE FIGHT ON. We hope for vindication, the last laugh, and recognition as an additional standard– electronic documents with visible connections.
We propose a new kind of writing– PARALLEL PAGES, VISIBLY CONNECTED.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
section: Histories of the Web: Mouse & NLS
text:
Histories of the Web: Mouse & NLS







Douglas Engelbart and his team at the Stanford Research Institute (SRI) developed the NLS (oN-Line System) in the 1960s. NLS was a revolutionary computer system that introduced many concepts we take for granted today, including the mouse, windowing systems, and hypertext.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
text:
Histories of the Web: ARPANET







The ARPANET was the first network to implement the TCP/IP protocol suite, which is the foundation of the modern internet. It was developed by the U.S. Department of Defense’s Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) in the 1969. The TCP/IP was invented in the 1970s by Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn. The ARPANET was a precursor to the internet, and it connected various research institutions and universities, allowing them to share information and resources.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
text:
Histories of the Web: USENET


Created in 1979 by graduate students at Duke and UNC Distributed messages through decentralized, topic-based newsgroups Used Unix-to-Unix Copy Protocol (UUCP) over telephone connections Predated the World Wide Web by more than a decade
Rather than visiting a centralized website, users subscribed to distributed newsgroups such as sci.math or soc.history. Many practices we associate with social media appeared here: threaded discussion, community moderation, FAQs, pseudonyms, spam, and flame wars. But Usenet was decentralized. Messages circulated among participating servers rather than living on one company’s platform.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
section: Histories of the Web: Humanist Listserv
text:
Histories of the Web: Humanist Listserv


Founded by Willard McCarty on May 7, 1987 An email discussion group for humanities computing Functioned as a moderated, international electronic seminar Built an intellectual community before academic websites
HUMANIST began when email was still relatively uncommon among humanists. It connected scholars interested in computing and the humanities across institutions and disciplines. It was more than an announcement list. McCarty described it as a seminar, and its editorial moderation helped establish norms for intellectual exchange. By 1999 it had approximately 1,100 subscriptions.

section: Histories of the Web: World Wide Web
text:
Histories of the Web: World Wide Web







Tim Berners-Lee’s initial vision for the web




But it was really Tim Berners-Lee working at CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research) in the 1980s and 1990s who developed the World Wide Web as we know it. This diagram shows Berners-Lee’s initial vision for the web. You can actually explore it via an emulator at https://worldwideweb.cern.ch/browser/, which allows you to “party like it’s 1989” and see the first web browser in action.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
section: What did Berners Lee Invent Exactly?
text:
What did Berners Lee Invent Exactly?
Berners-Lee developed three key components:


URI




HTTP




HTML


The three components he created were revolutionary:

URI/URL - Berners-Lee saw this as the web’s most fundamental innovation. URIs enable hypertext links to direct browsers to specific resources. By giving every resource a unique identifier, you could create a truly interconnected system.
HTTP - This is the protocol (set of rules) for how computers communicate when transferring web content. It’s a simple request-response system: browser requests something, server responds with data.
HTML - This became the “fabric” or “connective tissue” of the web. With HTML as a universal language, anyone could create web pages that anyone else could view, regardless of their computer or software.

Berners-Lee created HTML as part of a larger system for sharing linked documents across computers at CERN.
This is why the “H” in HTML matters: hypertext. HTML gave people a way to write documents that could link to other documents. URLs gave those documents addresses. HTTP gave browsers and servers a way to request and send those documents. The browser made the whole system usable.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
text:
What is a URL?

A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is a web address—a string of characters that provides a way to access a specific resource on the web.
URLs are made up of different components:



URL Anatomy



A URL is a type of URI and is commonly called a web address. Berners-Lee envisioned URIs as a way to identify anything on the web. A URL goes further by providing a way to access a specific resource. URLs are made up of different components, which you can see in this diagram:
This diagram is from the Mozilla Web Docs, which provide a great overview of the topic https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Howto/Web_mechanics/What_is_a_URL. You’ve already encountered URLs when we created an a tag in our HTML page.
From the Hypothesis annotations:

“Are there any differences between the two to make note of?”
— Fianna Sullivan (FiannaS), Section A


“It is fascinating that the URI is considered the web’s most fundamental innovation. This highlights that the core architecture of online information retrieval wasn’t built around search engines, but rather on a standardized system of direct, linkable addresses.”
— Min Kim (mink4), Section A

I should pause here and ask the class how they understand the relationship among a URI, a URL, and a web address.
A URI, or Uniform Resource Identifier, identifies a resource. A URL, or Uniform Resource Locator, is a type of URI that tells us how and where to access that resource. The distinction is identification versus location. Every URL is a URI, but not every URI is a URL.
In everyday web use, people often use URL, URI, link, and web address loosely. For this course, the key point is that URL is the more specific term. Berners-Lee’s broader idea was that resources needed stable identifiers so documents could connect directly to one another.
1990–1994: identifiers came first. Berners-Lee’s early web architecture needed a universal way to identify resources across different protocols. His 1994 RFC called these Universal Resource Identifiers. “Universal” later became Uniform. The point was broader than location: anything on the web needed a standardized identifier. RFC 1630’s history in RFC 2396
1994: URL became the practical term. RFC 1738 standardized Uniform Resource Locators, including familiar schemes such as http:, ftp:, and file:. A URL described how a resource could be accessed and where it was located. RFC 1738
The 1990s distinction: standards writers envisioned URI as the broad category, with two major kinds: - URL: locate or retrieve something. - URN: give something a persistent name, such as urn:isbn:…, regardless of its current location.
1998: URI became the umbrella standard. RFC 2396 merged the previously separate URL specifications into one generic URI syntax. This produced the familiar explanation that URLs are a subset of URIs. RFC 2396
2005: the distinction became less rigid. RFC 3986 retained URI as the standards term but explained that “locator” and “name” describe how an identifier is used, not necessarily separate syntactic categories. A URI can function as a name, a locator, or both. RFC 3986
Modern browser practice favors “URL.” The WHATWG URL Standard explicitly standardizes on URL, arguing that maintaining separate URL, URI, and IRI terminology creates confusion and does not reflect how browser parsing actually works. WHATWG URL Standard

What types of hyperlinks exist?


Internal links




External links




Incoming links




Anchors or page fragments

More on hyperlinks: Mozilla: Types of Links

In the example above, we created an external link because we linked to a webpage outside our own website.
Mozilla’s categories are about the relationship between websites and webpages. Anchors or page fragments are a little different: they link to a specific section within a webpage, like the sidebar navigation on our course site.
But URLs are more than just links; they are the way we access webpages. Mozilla describes URLs as akin to postal addresses, an analogy I find helpful. Just as you need an address to send a letter, you need a URL to send a request to a webpage. Before delving into the anatomy of URLs, understanding domain names and the web’s functionality is beneficial.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
text:
How does the web work?
What is this model?

How the internet works

Client = computer that requests data
Server = computer that hosts and sends data


While we often talk about the “cloud,” the concept of the web was originally based on the idea of a “web” of interconnected computers.
A computer can act as a client, a server, or both depending on the software it is running and its role in a particular interaction. This core idea of a client requesting and a server responding remains central to how the web functions.
The data sent from servers to clients usually consists of HTML documents, but it can also include images, videos, audio, or virtually any type of data.
Here’s a simplified diagram showing this relationship.
From the Hypothesis annotations:

“The cloud is a network for remote computers to offer extra storage and computing power for other devices across the internet.”
— Drew Bowen (drewbowen), Section A

This makes a useful connection to the cloud. I want to ask what becomes less visible when we use the metaphor of a cloud.
The cloud still consists of physical computers in data centers. When our browser requests a webpage, it acts as a client. The computer responding to that request acts as a server. Client and server describe roles, not permanent kinds of computers. A computer can play either role in a different interaction, and one machine can run both client and server software.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
section: How do Clients and Servers Communicate?
text:
How do Clients and Servers Communicate?

Client-Server communication
This simplified diagram shows the basic back-and-forth: 1. Client sends a request 2. Server receives the request 3. Server sends back a response 4. Client receives the response
This happens billions of times per second across the internet.
Although our current internet is vastly more complex, this core idea of a client requesting data and a server hosting and sending data remains central to how the web functions.
Much of the data sent from servers to clients consists of HTML documents, but it can also include images, videos, audio, or virtually any type of data.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
text:
What is HTTP?
What is the difference between http:// and https://?




URL Protocol



HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is how clients and servers communicate.
You’ll notice URLs start with http:// or https://—this indicates the protocol being used.
Tim Berners-Lee developed HTTP as the standard way to transmit data across the web. It’s a simple request-response protocol.
The scheme or protocol tells the browser how to communicate with the server.
The first part of a URL is the scheme/protocol. This tells the browser what set of rules to use when communicating with the server.
Common schemes: - http:// - unsecured connection - https:// - secured connection (the ‘s’ stands for “secure”) - ftp:// - file transfer protocol - file:// - local file on your computer
Most modern websites use https:// because it encrypts the data being transmitted, which is important for security and privacy.
Does anyone know of other protocols that are used in URLs? (e.g., ftp://, file://, etc.)

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
section: How can you see an HTTP response?
text:
How can you see an HTTP response?


When you enter a URL in your browser:

Browser sends an HTTP request to a server
Server validates the request
Server sends back an HTTP response with status codes

When you type “google.com” into your browser, you’re actually:

Sending an HTTP request to Google’s server
The server checks if the request is valid
If valid, the server sends back the HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and other files that make up the Google homepage

The key innovation of HTTP is that it’s stateless—each request is independent. This makes it simple and efficient.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
section: What is an HTTP status code?
text:
What is an HTTP status code?


Most important:

200 OK = request successful
404 Not Found = resource doesn’t exist When a server responds to an HTTP request, it sends back a status code that indicates what happened.

Status codes are grouped by number range:

1xx = informational
2xx = success (200 is the most common)
3xx = redirection
4xx = client errors (404 is very common—“page not found”)
5xx = server errors

When you’ve seen an error message saying a page doesn’t exist, you were seeing a 404 error. This is a status code sent back by the HTTP protocol when the server couldn’t find the requested resource.
One famous 404 page is this one:

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
text:
What does 404 indicate?

Has anyone seen this before?
Many websites have fun with their 404 pages since users will see them when they try to access a page that doesn’t exist. This is an opportunity to be creative while still communicating that something went wrong.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
section: What is the difference between Websites, Browsers, and Search Engines?
text:
What is the difference between Websites, Browsers, and Search Engines?


It’s important to understand these distinctions:
A website is a collection of related web pages. For example, our course website is one website, but it contains many different pages. A website is identified by its domain name and is published on one or more web servers.
A web browser is software you run on your computer. You can use it to open HTML files stored on your computer (using the file:// protocol) or to access websites hosted on servers (using http:// or https://).
A search engine is a service that crawls the web, indexes content, and lets you search for things. Search engines use automated programs called “bots” or “spiders” that follow URLs to discover and index content.
All three use the HTTP protocol, but they serve different purposes.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
text:
Histories of the Web: Mosaic


Released by NCSA at UIUC in 1993 Developed by a team including Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina Displayed images directly alongside text Made browsing easier for people outside specialist computing communities
Mosaic was not the first web browser. Tim Berners-Lee had already built a browser and editor, and several other browsers existed before Mosaic. Its importance came from accessibility and presentation. Mosaic was easier to install and use, and it displayed images directly within webpages rather than opening them separately. Those design decisions helped transform the Web from a system primarily used by researchers and technical specialists into a popular visual medium. There is also a direct UIUC connection: Mosaic was developed at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications. Andreessen later co-founded Netscape, connecting Mosaic’s university origins to the rapid commercialization of the Web.

URL Authority/Domain Name

section: What is Sandra Bullock typing in this clip?
text:
What is Sandra Bullock typing in this clip?
https://youtu.be/M1K-B8QVLyo?t=242




IPv4 Address



Originally, you accessed websites using IP addresses (series of numbers identifying a computer): Before domain names existed, you had to remember IP addresses to access computers. An IP address looks like 192.168.1.1 or similar.
For example, the 1995 classic, thriller movie The Net, starring Sandra Bullock, there’s a scene where she searches using IP addresses. You can watch a clip here:
IP addresses are still used today under the hood, but they’re not user-friendly. Imagine having to remember your bank’s website as 104.21.32.105 instead of bank.com!

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
text:
What is DNS?


The [Domain Name System (DNS)]is like a “phone book” or “address book” that translates IP addresses into human-readable domain names.
Every time you enter a URL in your browser:

Browser queries DNS server: “What IP address is associated with google.com?”
DNS returns the IP address
Browser connects to that IP address using HTTP

DNS is a critical piece of internet infrastructure. It’s a distributed system of computers (DNS servers) that maintains a database mapping domain names to IP addresses.
When you type “google.com” into your browser, the browser doesn’t actually know where Google’s servers are. It sends a query to a DNS server asking “What’s the IP address for google.com?” The DNS server responds with the IP address, and then the browser can make its HTTP request to that address.
This system is what makes the web human-friendly. Without DNS, we’d have to remember hundreds of IP addresses.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
section: What is the difference between top and second-level domains?
text:
What is the difference between top and second-level domains?

Domain Name Structure
Two main components:

Top-Level Domain (TLD) = .com, .org, .edu (coordinated through ICANN)
Second-Level Domain (SLD) = google in google.com (registered by individuals/organizations)

Domain names have a hierarchical structure, read right-to-left.
Top-Level Domains (TLDs): - Originally meant to indicate the type of organization (.com for commercial, .org for organization, .edu for education) - Now also include country codes (.uk for United Kingdom, .ca for Canada) - Coordinated through ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers), with different registries operating individual TLDs - There’s actually a long history and fraught politics around TLDs since they’re often tied to nation states
Interesting note: While there’s a .us for the United States, most US websites use .com or .gov (for government). This reflects how commercially-driven the early web was.
Second-Level Domains (SLDs): - The part to the left of the TLD - mozilla in mozilla.org - Registered through domain name registrars like GoDaddy - Important: you don’t own a domain in perpetuity—you lease it and must renew it
This rental model leads to two interesting phenomena: 1. You have to keep paying to keep your domain 2. Domain name speculation—people buy domains hoping to sell them for profit
For more on TLDs, see this article about dead TLDs: https://astrid.tech/2022/04/05/1/dead-tlds/
For more on internet governance and the politics of domains, read books like Milton Mueller’s Networks and States or Laura DeNardis’ The Global War for Internet Governance.
There’s also Ingrid Burrington’s fascinating piece on visiting a Domain-Names Conference: https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2017/02/domain-names-dot-horse/516438/

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
section: Who Connects Us to the Internet?
text:
Who Connects Us to the Internet?

How did internet access become a commercial service?

An Internet Service Provider, or ISP, connects another network or individual device to the Internet. An ISP provides access to the Internet rather than specifically to the Web. Once connected, users can reach web servers alongside email, file transfer, streaming media, and other Internet services.
The basic technical services include a connection to the provider’s network, an IP address, routes that carry packets toward other networks, and often a DNS resolver that translates domain names into IP addresses. ISPs therefore occupy a different layer from browsers, websites, search engines, hosting companies, and domain registrars, even when one corporation offers several of those services.
Commercial internet access emerged from an infrastructure originally concentrated in government, military, and academic institutions. ARPANET provided an early experimental network. Beginning in 1986, the National Science Foundation’s NSFNET connected universities and supercomputing centers and became a major backbone for the growing U.S. Internet. Its acceptable-use rules initially limited commercial activity on the federally supported backbone.
During the late 1980s and early 1990s, the NSF encouraged regional networks to serve commercial customers while private long-distance networks such as PSI, UUNET, and ANS CO+RE expanded. On April 30, 1995, the NSF decommissioned the NSFNET backbone after commercial providers had developed enough capacity to carry the traffic. This is one important institutional moment in the privatization of Internet infrastructure. It did not mean that governments or universities disappeared from the network, but private firms increasingly controlled the routes through which ordinary users connected.
For many households, early commercial access meant a modem calling a local provider over the telephone network. Services such as AOL and CompuServe began as proprietary online services and increasingly offered gateways to the broader Internet. Independent local ISPs also sold dial-up accounts. Telephone and cable companies later provided DSL and cable broadband, followed by fiber and cellular access.
That transition also changed how people understood themselves online. Earlier university and government users generally received network access through an institution. Commercial services turned connectivity into a consumer product: customers paid by the hour or through monthly subscriptions, installed software from promotional disks, and called a local access number. Companies such as AOL and CompuServe initially offered comparatively enclosed environments with their own forums, news, email, and curated portals. Their eventual gateways to the wider Internet marked a shift from joining a proprietary online service to purchasing access to an open network of independently operated services.
It is therefore useful to treat the commercialization or privatization of the Internet as a gradual institutional transition rather than a single event. Public funding, university research, military investment, telephone infrastructure, private backbone companies, and household subscription services overlapped. The 1995 retirement of the NSFNET backbone is an important marker, but the commercial Internet was assembled from public research and infrastructure rather than created independently by private companies.
The word provider can conceal several kinds of businesses. An access ISP supplies the “last mile” between a customer and the network. Larger transit or backbone providers carry traffic over long distances. Networks also connect directly through peering agreements and Internet exchange points rather than paying another provider to carry all their traffic. The Internet works through this interconnection of independently operated networks rather than through one central network owner.
ISPs nevertheless hold considerable power. They can observe connection metadata, block or throttle traffic, comply with state censorship and surveillance requirements, and determine where service is affordable or available. Debates over net neutrality concern whether providers should treat lawful traffic equally or privilege particular services. Uneven broadband access also means that the physical location and income of users continue to shape participation in digital culture.
This is distinct from ICANN’s role. ISPs operate access and routing infrastructure. ICANN coordinates shared identifiers such as domain names and supports the system through which networks find unique destinations. ICANN does not operate or regulate Internet service providers.
Sources: National Science Foundation, “Birth of the Commercial Internet”; Internet Society, “A Brief History of the Internet”.

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
section: Histories of the Web: Submarine Cables
text:
Histories of the Web: Submarine Cables

What infrastructure carries culture as data across oceans?

The language of cyberspace and cloud computing can make network communication seem immaterial. In practice, the global Internet depends on cables, landing stations, data centers, routers, electrical power, and workers who build and maintain them. Satellites matter for some locations and uses, but submarine fiber-optic cables carry the vast majority of intercontinental Internet traffic.
The history of these cables predates digital computing. Submarine telegraph cables began connecting nearby coastlines in the mid-nineteenth century. The first transatlantic cable entered service in 1858 and allowed Queen Victoria and President James Buchanan to exchange messages, but it failed after only a few weeks. A durable transatlantic connection was completed in 1866. These projects compressed communication between Europe and North America from the time required for an ocean voyage to minutes, while depending on enormous investments of capital, engineering, ships, labor, and imperial cooperation.
The early global cable network developed alongside colonial and commercial power. Routes connected imperial centers to colonies, ports, military installations, commodity markets, and financial institutions. Cable ownership and landing rights shaped which places became communication hubs and whose messages moved quickly. The Internet inherited parts of this geography rather than beginning with an empty or evenly connected world.
By the late nineteenth century, Britain controlled much of the world’s submarine telegraph network. Its cables linked London to colonial administrations, military outposts, shipping routes, and markets, allowing information valuable to governance, finance, and journalism to circulate quickly through imperial centers. Rival states developed their own routes partly because dependence on another empire’s cables created strategic vulnerability. Communication infrastructure was never simply a neutral channel: its geography reflected political power and helped reproduce it.
Contemporary cable routes do not perfectly replicate nineteenth-century networks, but they often follow inherited patterns of coastal access, commercial importance, and geopolitical influence. Major financial and population centers attract redundant high-capacity connections, while islands and less profitable regions may depend on only one or two links. The history helps explain why global connectivity remains geographically uneven even as the technologies change.
Submarine telephone systems later carried voice communication. TAT-1, inaugurated in 1956, was the first transatlantic telephone cable. TAT-8 entered service in 1988 as the first transatlantic fiber-optic cable. Fiber sends information as pulses of light and provides far greater capacity than earlier copper systems. Repeaters placed along the seabed amplify the signal, while landing stations connect the submarine system to terrestrial networks.
Submarine cables do not connect individual laptops directly. They form long-distance links within the larger Internet. A request may travel from a home through an access ISP, across regional and backbone networks, through a cable landing station, beneath an ocean, and then through other networks before reaching a server. Routing protocols select paths through this network of networks, and the return path may differ from the outgoing one.
Historically, telecommunications companies and international consortia financed most major cables. Large technology and cloud companies now finance or own substantial portions of new cable capacity because their services move enormous quantities of data among data centers. Ownership of the physical route therefore affects competition, surveillance, national security, and control over digital infrastructure.
Cables concentrate global communication in particular corridors and landing points. Anchors, fishing activity, undersea earthquakes, equipment failures, and deliberate attacks can damage them. Specialized repair ships locate the break, raise the cable from the seabed, splice it, and return it to the ocean. Redundant routes usually keep a single break from disconnecting heavily connected regions, but places served by only one or two cables remain especially vulnerable.
This infrastructure also depends on labor that tends to disappear from popular accounts of the Internet: surveyors who select routes, factory workers who manufacture cable, crews who load and lay it, technicians who operate landing stations, marine engineers who diagnose faults, and repair crews who work at sea. Nicole Starosielski describes cable systems as environments made through ongoing relationships among technology, geography, regulation, and human maintenance. The cable is not installed once and then forgotten; global communication has to be continually maintained.
The map is useful because it makes network geography visible, but it should not be mistaken for a neutral or permanent picture. Routes change, mapmakers simplify their positions, and planned cables may appear alongside active systems. Even so, it reveals that the circulation of digital culture depends on privately financed infrastructure, territorial landing rights, maintenance labor, and unequal geographic connections.
Sources: Submarine Cable Map; APNIC, “The Future of Undersea Internet Cables”; History of the Atlantic Cable and Submarine Telegraphy; Nicole Starosielski, The Undersea Network (2015); Simone M. Müller, Wiring the World (2016).

title: Introduction to the Web & Servers
text:
Who Coordinates Domain Names?

Who should have authority over a global naming system?

ICANN stands for the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers. It does not govern everything that happens online. Its narrower but enormously important role is coordinating the internet’s system of unique identifiers, including the top level of the Domain Name System.
This work predates ICANN. Beginning in the 1970s, computer scientist Jon Postel kept track of identifiers used by ARPANET and the growing internet. That work developed into the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, or IANA. For years, these functions remained closely connected to research institutions and contracts with the United States government.
ICANN was established in 1998 as a California nonprofit. The U.S. government intended to move DNS policy and technical coordination into a private organization that could include international participation. That origin matters because the internet was becoming global while important parts of its naming infrastructure still reflected its history in the United States.
In 2016, the U.S. Department of Commerce allowed its IANA functions contract to expire. Stewardship formally transitioned to what ICANN calls the global multistakeholder community. This did not transfer control of the entire internet to ICANN. It changed the oversight arrangement for coordinating unique names, numbers, and protocol parameters.
So what is the relationship between ICANN and IANA today? ICANN is the broader nonprofit organization and governance structure. IANA is the name for a set of technical coordination functions. These functions include maintaining the DNS root zone, coordinating global IP address allocation, and recording protocol parameters that allow internet systems to work together.
Since the 2016 transition, an ICANN affiliate called Public Technical Identifiers, or PTI, has performed the IANA functions on ICANN’s behalf. ICANN is PTI’s sole member and contracts with PTI to perform this technical work. In simplified terms, the ICANN community develops policies and provides oversight, while PTI carries out the day-to-day IANA operations. People still commonly say that “IANA” performs this work, even though PTI is the legal organization operating the functions.
It is useful to distinguish these layers: ICANN is an organization, IANA describes functions, and PTI is the ICANN affiliate that performs those functions. None of them controls the content that travels across the internet. Their role is to keep its shared identifiers unique and interoperable.
The term multistakeholder means that ICANN’s policy processes involve technical organizations, businesses, governments, civil society groups, and individual internet users. This differs from placing the DNS directly under one national government or an intergovernmental body such as the United Nations. But participation is uneven. It takes time, money, technical knowledge, language access, and institutional support to participate consistently, so we should still ask whose interests carry the most influence.
International governance is visible in country code top level domains such as .uk, .ca, and .ng. Countries and territories have their own domain authorities, but those domains still need to function within one interoperable global root. Governments also participate in ICANN through its Governmental Advisory Committee, although ICANN is not itself a government organization.
Internationalized Domain Names add another layer. Early DNS standards centered the Latin alphabet and ASCII. ICANN’s internationalization work has helped make domains available in writing systems including Arabic, Chinese, Cyrillic, and Devanagari. This makes the politics of infrastructure especially visible: even the characters allowed in a web address shape who can name, represent, and find culture online.
Sources: ICANN History Project; IANA Stewardship Transition; Post-Transition IANA.

title: Styling the Cultural Web
section: What type of Markup Language is this?
text:
What type of Markup Language is this?


Another important markup language is TEI. It has a long history in Computing in the Humanities. TEI is used to encode texts in a way that makes them machine-readable. You can read more about it at https://tei-c.org/what-is-tei/.
Today we are used to having OCR and other tools that can help us digitize texts, and then programming languages like Python and R that let us manipulate text into data (a topic we’ll cover later in the semester). But in the early days of the web, this was not the case, which made it difficult for machines to know what was in a text. This is where TEI comes in, as it allows us to encode texts in a way that makes them useable to machines. For example, TEI often involves marking what a date is, or what a person’s name is, or what a place is. This allows us to search and analyze texts in ways that would be impossible without TEI.
TEI and HTML both were created in the same historical moment, the early days of the web. HTML was created by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991, while TEI was created in 1987.
The Old Bailey Online project (started in 1999) is one of the older Digital Humanities projects that’s still in operation. They’ve been digitizing the records of the Old Bailey, the central criminal court of England and Wales. They use TEI/XML to encode the text of the records, which allows them to be searched and analyzed in sophisticated ways.
What’s unique about the Old Bailey is that they manually marked up all the text using a “double rekeying” strategy—having each text transcribed twice and then automatically compared to identify errors. They did this because OCR software in the 1990s wasn’t good enough for eighteenth-century print, especially from microfilm.
This incredibly laborious process resulted in 99.9% accurate transcriptions. The authors note that “XML markup would not have worked with the kind of error-ridden text produced by OCR methodologies, so applying complex markup was dependent on adopting rekeying.”
Not only did this facilitate accurate searching, but it meant that the text could be reused in subsequent digital projects. This example shows us that rigorous markup and encoding requires significant human effort, but that effort creates very high-quality data.

title: Styling the Cultural Web
text:
What does HTML stand for?







Click for Definition



HTML is not a programming language—it’s a markup language used to:

Tell your browser how to structure web pages
Create documents that are rendered in your browser
Make content appear or act a certain way

While TEI is still in use today, by far the most popular of all markup languages is HTML, which stands for HyperText Markup Language. HTML is the language of the web and is used to create web pages. This might be surprising to learn but when you go to a website, it is just showing you a document (just like our .txt or .md files). The difference is that this document is written and marked-up in HTML and is rendered by your browser.
This is an important distinction. HTML is purely about structure and presentation. It doesn’t perform logic or calculations. Unlike Markdown, which uses simple symbols, HTML uses more formal “tags” that describe the semantic meaning and structure of content.
So while in Google Docs you might use the GUI to format text, or in Markdown we use # symbols, in HTML we use a series of tags. Tags have a name, a series of key/value pairs called attributes, and some textual content.
When you visit a website, you’re viewing an HTML document rendered by your browser.

Creating an HTML file is really simple—it’s just a text file with the .html extension. You can create it with the command line or a text editor. Once you create the file with some HTML tags in it, you can open it in any web browser.
I can then save this file and open it in a browser. To do this, I can either right click on the file and select open with and then select my browser, or simply go to my preferred browser and select Open File. We’ll talk more about web browsers in the next lesson, but some popular ones include Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge.
We should see our text in the browser, just like we did with our Markdown file. So everything is working so far!

title: Styling the Cultural Web
text:
How is HTML structured?
What tags could we add to make our content more organized?

What happens if we add <p> and </p> tags around our text?

This is a key realization—when you add HTML tags to your content and view it in the browser, you don’t see the tags themselves. The browser interprets the tags as instructions for how to display the content, but doesn’t show the tags to the user.
So even though you added <p> and </p> tags, the browser just displays “My first page!” without showing the tags. This can be confusing at first—did the tags actually do anything? Are they there?

text:
How can we inspect the HTML of a webpage?




Inspect Page



This is one of the most important skills for web development. When you right-click and select “Inspect,” your browser opens a panel showing you the actual HTML source code of the page you’re viewing.
This works on any website—not just your own pages. You can inspect any website to see how it was built, what HTML structure it uses, what CSS is applied, etc. This is how you learn web development.
Different browsers have slightly different names: - Chrome/Edge: “Inspect” or “Inspect Element” - Firefox: “Inspect Element” - Safari: “Inspect Element”
You can read more about Chrome Developer Tools here: https://developers.google.com/web/tools/chrome-devtools/console/ And Firefox Developer Tools here: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Tools/Page_Inspector/How_to/Open_the_Inspector

title: Styling the Cultural Web
text:
What is an HTML attribute?

HTML elements can have attributes—extra information about the element.

This diagram is also from the Mozilla docs and you can read more about how HTML elements can also have attributes here.

Attributes appear in the opening tag and provide additional information about how the element should behave or what it contains. They follow a specific syntax: the attribute name, followed by an equals sign, then the value wrapped in quotes.
Some guidelines for attributes: - There should be a space between the element name and the first attribute - Multiple attributes should be separated by spaces - The attribute name is followed by an equal sign - The attribute value is wrapped in opening and closing quote marks

title: Styling the Cultural Web
text:
What is an href attribute?
Bonus what sorts of tags do we use href with?

The href attribute is used with anchor (<a>) tags to specify the URL of the page the link goes to. The value of the href attribute is the URL you want to link to. For example, <a href="https://www.example.com">Click here</a> creates a link that says “Click here” and takes you to “https://www.example.com” when clicked.

title: Styling the Cultural Web
text:
Reviewing Common HTML Tags

How could I add a header to my page?
What about a list of items? How can we nest lists?
What about a link to another page?


These are some of the most common tags you’ll encounter. There are many more tags available, but these cover the basic structural elements of most web pages.

Headings go from h1 (most important) to h6 (least important)
Paragraphs are blocks of text
Divs are generic containers that you can style
Anchors create links to other pages
Lists can be ordered (numbered) or unordered (bulleted)

You can find a full list at W3Schools: https://www.w3schools.com/tags/ref_byfunc.asp

title: Styling the Cultural Web
section: What are some of the limitations of HTML?
text:
What are some of the limitations of HTML?

But HTML also has some limitations. Take a look at this helpful overview of HTML’s shortcomings by Alison Parrish (bold added for emphasis)

HTML documents are intended to add markup to text to add information that allows browsers to display the text in different ways—e.g., HTML markup might tell the browser to make the font of the text a particular size, or to position it in a particular place on the screen.


Because the primary purpose of HTML is to change the appearance of text, HTML markup usually does not tell us anything useful about what the text means, or what kind of data it contains. When you look at a web page in the browser, it might appear to contain a list of newspaper articles, or a table with birth rates, or a series of names with associated biographies, or whatever. But that’s information that we get, as humans, from reading the page. There’s (usually) no easy way to extract this information with a computer program.

This is a critical limitation. HTML can tell you that something is a heading or a paragraph, but it can’t tell you that it’s a product price or a person’s name (unless you add special attributes). When you look at a web page in the browser, it might appear to contain a list of newspaper articles, or a table with birth rates, or a series of names with biographies. But that’s information we get as humans from reading the page. There’s usually no easy way for a computer program to automatically extract that meaning.
This is why TEI was developed—to add semantic meaning to markup. And it’s also why modern HTML encourages using semantic tags like <article>, <nav>, and <footer> to give more meaning to the structure.
HTML is Forgiving (But Messy)

HTML is also notoriously messy—web browsers are very forgiving of syntax errors and other irregularities in HTML (like mismatched or unclosed tags). For this reason, we need special libraries to parse HTML into data structures that our Python programs can use, libraries that can make a “good guess” about what the structure of an HTML document is, even when that structure is written incorrectly or inconsistently.

Browsers are deliberately forgiving of HTML errors because the early web was chaotic, and they wanted to make the web work for everyone. This is good for user experience but bad for data extraction.
If you forget to close a tag, the browser will usually figure out what you meant and render it anyway. This means invalid HTML can still display, which is why we need special parsing libraries when we want to programmatically analyze HTML.

title: Styling the Cultural Web
text:
Learn More About HTML
Understanding these limitations is important as we start to work with HTML and other web technologies. For more detailed information, I recommend reading through this introduction from Mozilla on HTML.

title: Styling the Cultural Web
Styling the Cultural Web
text:
What is the DOM?

Document Object Model
html
├── head
│   └── title
└── body
    ├── h1
    ├── p
    └── ul
        ├── li
        └── li

The DOM is how programming languages understand and manipulate the structure of a web page. It’s a tree structure where each HTML element is a node. JavaScript can traverse this tree, find specific elements, modify them, add new ones, or remove them.
Think of a webpage as a tree with many branches. Each branch and leaf could be a piece of text, a picture, or a button. JavaScript can work with this tree to change what appears on the page.
This is incredibly powerful. It means you can create dynamic, responsive pages that change based on user input or data from servers, all without reloading the page.

title: Styling the Cultural Web
section: The Three Pillars of the Web
text:
The Three Pillars of the Web



Technology
Purpose




HTML
Structure - what things are


CSS
Presentation - how things look


JavaScript
Behavior - what things do




HTML alone creates a functional webpage, but it’s not very beautiful or interactive. To create modern websites, we need three technologies working together.
HTML provides the semantic structure and content. CSS controls how everything looks. JavaScript makes things interactive.
The combination of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript is what makes the modern web possible. Yes, it can be complex, but this complexity is necessary to create the rich, interactive experiences we expect from websites today.
For example, think about Gmail or Google Maps. These are incredibly interactive applications running in your browser. They’re possible because of the combination of these three technologies.
Also note that these technologies can make websites slow to load (large JavaScript files can take a long time) and difficult to maintain. This is an ongoing challenge for web developers.
Looking at projects like whatisdigitalhumanities, you can even see the effort required by exploring the commit history on GitHub—showing many contributions over time as people continuously update, fix, and improve the site.

text:
Recap: The Command Line
We’ve learned how to:
