title: Ecosystems & Environments
section: What is the syntax of a class?
text:
What is the syntax of a class?

# Define a class
class Blank:
    pass  # Pass means "Move along, please. Nothing to see here."

# Create an instance of the class and invoke it
Blank()

To define a class, we use the keyword class followed by the class name and a colon. All the logic of the class is indented, just like with functions, loops, and conditionals. We instantiate the class using its name and parentheses.
In this case, since the class has no actual logic in it, just the keyword pass, which is a reserved keyword in Python and that tells Python to do nothing. So when we call the class, nothing actually happens. For any class, when you invoke it, it executes the __init__ method, which is another built in method from Python (this one is called a constructor method). Thus, since our example above didn’t define any logic for the built-in __init__ method, nothing happened.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
section: How could we create a class for our movies?
text:
How could we create a class for our movies?

class Movie:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.movie_name = name

a_movie = Movie("The Matrix")
a_movie.movie_name

The __init__ method runs when you create an instance. self represents that instance, which is why it is conventionally the first parameter of an instance method. You can read more about class scope here.

__init__() runs when an instance is created
self refers to that particular instance
Attributes store data
Methods define behavior

self is the first argument to any method in a class. It refers to the specific instance you’ve created. When you set self.movie_name = name, you’re creating an attribute on that instance.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
section: How do we add methods to a class?
text:
How do we add methods to a class?
Methods are functions inside a class. They operate on the instance’s data.

def add_directors(self, directors):
    """Adds directors to the movie"""
    if isinstance(directors, list) is False:
        directors = [directors]
    self.directors.extend(directors)

Instance methods conventionally take self as the first parameter. This allows them to access and modify the instance’s attributes. Notice the docstring, which documents what the method does.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
section: How can we add more attributes to a class?
text:
How can we add more attributes to a class?

class Movie:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.movie_name = name
        self.directors = []
        self.release_year = None
        self.age = 0
        self.sequels = []
Initialize attributes as empty or None to structure your data.

By initializing attributes in __init__, you define the shape of your class. This makes it clear what data the class will hold.
Attributes: Data stored in the class (like self.movie_name)
Methods: Functions that operate on that data (like add_directors())
This separation of data and behavior is the core of object-oriented programming. It makes code more organized and reusable.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Adding More Functionality
So what’s going in this code block?
class Movie:
    """Contains methods for data about a movie

    Methods:
    --------
    add_directors
    add_release_year
    calculate_age
    """
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.movie_name = name
        self.directors = []
        self.release_year = None
        self.age = 0
        self.sequels = []
        self.prequels = []


    def add_directors(self, directors):
        """Adds a list of directors of the movie

        Method argument:
        -----------------
        directors(list) -- A list of people who director the movie
        """
        if isinstance(directors, list) is False:
            directors = [directors]

        self.directors.extend(directors)


    def add_release_year(self, year):
        """Adds the release year of the movie

        Method argument:
        -----------------
        year(integer or string) -- A year the movie was released
        """

        self.release_year = int(year)

    def add_sequels(self, sequels):
        """Adds a list of sequels to the movie

        Method argument:
        -----------------
        sequels(list) -- A list of sequels to the movie
        """
        if isinstance(sequels, list) is False:
            sequels = [sequels]

        self.sequels.extend(sequels)

    def add_prequels(self, prequels):
        """Adds a list of prequels to the movie

        Method argument:
        -----------------
        prequels(list) -- A list of prequels to the movie
        """
        if isinstance(prequels, list) is False:
            prequels = [prequels]

        self.prequels.extend(prequels)


    def calculate_movie_age(self):
        """Calculates the age of the movie
        """
        from datetime import date
        self.age = date.today().year - self.release_year

a_movie = Movie("The Matrix I")
a_movie.add_directors(["Lana Wachowski", "Lilly Wachowski"])
a_movie.add_release_year(1999)
a_movie.add_sequels(["The Matrix II", "The Matrix III", "The Matrix IV"])
a_movie.calculate_movie_age()
print(a_movie.age)
print(a_movie.add_directors.__doc__) # To view the docstring for the method

First we’re taking our Movie class and expanding it so that it can contain more information about each movie. We still only initially create the class with one argument - the movie’s name. But we’ve also added additional attributes to the __init__ function. First, we have directors, which holds a list; then release year, which is an integer; age, which is also an integer; sequels, which is a list; and prequels, which is also a list.
Do you notice that the syntax here looks like a dictionary? That’s because we can use a similar pattern to dictionaries for creating our attributes.
While this function is somewhat similar to our Movie class, we’ve also added a number of functions, which we call methods to the class.
The first method add_directors takes two arguments, self and directors. Just like in the __init__ method, self represents the class instance and directors is a list of directors. In the __init__ method, we define the directors attribute on self as an empty list. Then in our add_directors method we extend this initial empty list, adding the new directors to the list.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Adding More Methods
What if we wanted to add a method for printing out an entire movie’s information? What is this code doing and how can we call this method?
def get_movie_info(self):
    """Prints out the movie's information
    """
    for key, value in self.__dict__.items():
        print(f"{key}: {value}")

What if we wanted to add a method for printing out an entire movie’s information? We could try looping through the class object and print out each attribute. Or we could use the built-in __dict__ functionality that prints out the values for a class. We can then call this method on our a_movie object. This is a very simple example of a class, but it’s a good start. We can use classes to store complex data structures and then use methods to manipulate that data. We can also use classes to create reusable code that can be used in multiple scripts.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Adding More Classes
What if we wanted to store prequels and sequels as instances of our Movie Class? What is this code doing exactly?
class Movie:
    """Contains methods for data about a movie

    Methods:
    --------
    add_directors
    add_release_year
    calculate_age
    """
    def __init__(self, name, release_year=None):
        self.movie_name = name
        self.directors = []
        self.release_year = release_year
        self.age = 0
        self.sequels = []
        self.prequels = []

    def add_directors(self, directors):
        """Adds a list of directors of the movie

        Method argument:
        -----------------
        directors(list) -- A list of people who director the movie
        """
        if isinstance(directors, list) is False:
            directors = [directors]

        self.directors.extend(directors)

    def add_release_year(self, year):
        """Adds the release year of the movie

        Method argument:
        -----------------
        year(integer or string) -- A year the movie was released
        """

        self.release_year = int(year)

    def calculate_movie_age(self):
        """Calculates the age of the movie
        """
        from datetime import date
        self.age = date.today().year - self.release_year

    def add_sequel(self, sequel, release_year):
        """Adds a sequel to the movie

        Method argument:
        -----------------
        sequel(string) -- The name of the sequel
        release_year(integer) -- The release year of the sequel
        """
        sequel_movie = Movie(sequel, release_year)
        self.sequels.append(sequel_movie)

    def add_prequel(self, prequel, release_year):
        """Adds a prequel to the movie

        Method argument:
        -----------------
        prequel(string) -- The name of the prequel
        release_year(integer) -- The release year of the prequel
        """
        prequel_movie = Movie(prequel, release_year)
        self.prequels.append(prequel_movie)

    def get_movie_info(self):
        """Prints out the movie's information
        """
        for key, value in self.__dict__.items():
            if key in ['sequels', 'prequels']:
                print(f"{key}: {[movie.movie_name for movie in value]}")
            else:
                print(f"{key}: {value}")

    def calculate_movie_order(self):
        """Calculates the order of movies based on release year
        """
        all_movies = [self] + self.sequels + self.prequels
        all_movies.sort(key=lambda movie: movie.release_year)
        return [movie.movie_name for movie in all_movies]

a_movie = Movie("The Matrix I")
a_movie.add_directors(["Lana Wachowski", "Lilly Wachowski"])
a_movie.add_release_year(1999)
a_movie.calculate_movie_age()
a_movie.add_sequel("The Matrix II", 2003)
a_movie.add_sequel("The Matrix III", 2003)
a_movie.add_sequel("The Matrix IV", 2021)
a_movie.add_prequel("The Matrix 0", 1998)
a_movie.get_movie_info()
print(a_movie.calculate_movie_order())

This is a more complex version of our Movie class. We’ve added two new methods, add_sequel and add_prequel, which create additional Movie instances. We also added calculate_movie_order, which uses a short lambda function to sort the movies by their release year.
This type of programming is called object-oriented programming and it’s a very powerful way to organize your code. It’s also a very common way to organize code in Python, and you’ll see it often, even if you don’t write it yourself.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
section: How do we add inline comments?
text:
How do we add inline comments?

movie = dict()  # Could also write {}
Use # to comment a single line.

Inline comments are useful for explaining why you did something, not necessarily what the code does (the code itself should be clear about that).

title: Ecosystems & Environments
section: How do we add block comments?
text:
How do we add block comments?

def add_directors(self, directors):
    """Adds directors to the movie

    Arguments:
    directors (list) -- List of director names
    """
    # implementation here


Docstrings are triple-quoted strings at the start of functions/classes.
print(a_movie.add_directors.__doc__) # To view the docstring for the method

You’ll notice that earlier we were able to print out the block comment for the add_directors method. This is because the block comment is actually a special type of comment called a docstring that is used to document a function or a class. The docstring is the first thing that appears in a function or class and is enclosed in triple quotes. It’s a good idea to add a docstring to every function and class you write, as it helps other people understand your code and also helps you remember what your code does.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Documentation


In addition to comments, the other main resource for understanding how to use a class or function is the documentation. The documentation is a set of instructions that explains how to use a class or function.
This documentation explains how to define a class, how to create an instance of a class, and how to use methods in a class. It also explains how to use inheritance, which is a way to create a new class that inherits the attributes and methods of an existing class.
Learning to read documentation is a critical skill, so would highly recommend taking a look at the documentation when it is available.




Python Documentation




Good documentation helps others (and future you) understand the code. It’s an investment that pays off when you revisit code months later.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
section: What is the Python Standard Library?
text:
What is the Python Standard Library?



Python Standard Library


The Python Standard Library contains modules built into Python.

pathlib is a great example. Instead of working with file paths as strings, you can use Path objects that are smarter and cross-platform.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
pathlib
Let’s scroll down to the pathlib module.

PathlibNow click on the link to the pathlib module.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
pathlib Methods

Pathlib MethodsFirst take a look at the current pathlib source code. Notice how it is organized, and try to find the definition of class Path (hint: use Control+F or Command+F).
Let’s take a look at the methods in the class Path https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#methods. How would we would print out the current working directory using pathlib?

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Importing Libraries
Let’s try importing pathlib into our script.
import pathlib

pathlib.Path()

Or import a specific class:
from pathlib import Path

We can easily bring classes into other code using the import keyword (another reserved word!), which does some magic to allow us to use classes defined in other files. This is how we can use parts of the Python Standard Library that aren’t directly built into the base language. It’s also how we use modules written by other programmers from the larger Python community. We can even use import to import our own classes.
The syntax for importing is import followed by the name of the module. In this case, we’re importing the pathlib module. Once we’ve imported the module, we can use the classes and functions defined in the module. There’s two ways to do this. We can either use the . operator to access the class or function:
Or we can use the from keyword to import a specific class or function from the module. Both options give us access to the same Path class, but they create different names in our script. With import pathlib, we write pathlib.Path(). With from pathlib import Path, we write the more concise Path().

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Aliasing Imports
import pathlib as pl

Now you can use pl.Path() instead of pathlib.Path().

With import statements, you can also alias the module or class you’re importing. This is often used to make the code more readable or to avoid conflicts with other classes or functions that have the same name.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Using pathlib
So now that we’ve explored ways to import pathlib, let’s try using this module. We’ll start by using pathlib to print out the current working directory.
from pathlib import Path

current_directory = Path.cwd()
print(current_directory)

Path.cwd() shows the directory where Python is currently looking. This is useful when a relative file path fails because it lets us compare Python’s location with the file’s actual location. We will introduce .read_text() separately once we have created a Path for a real file.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
File Input and Output
But pathlib is useful not just for printing out working directories, it can also let us load in files.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Reading in Data
Let’s try it out with Pathlib by passing in one of the datasets from the Responsible Datasets in Context Project that we have been reviewing each week. You can use any of the datasets, but I’m selecting the one by Os Keyes and Melanie Walsh. “U.S. National Park Visit Data (1979-2023) – Responsible Datasets in Context.” Responsible Datasets in Context, June 1, 2024. https://www.responsible-datasets-in-context.com/posts/np-data/.
Once you’ve downloaded the data, you should have a file called US-National-Parks_RecreationVisits_1979-2023.csv. Now let’s try using pathlib to read in the data.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Reading Files
from pathlib import Path

file = Path('US-National-Parks_RecreationVisits_1979-2023.csv')
print(file, type(file))
Now if this code worked, it should show you the path of your spreadsheet and then the type of the object, either <class 'pathlib.PosixPath'> or <class 'pathlib.WindowsPath'>. Calling Path() creates the appropriate concrete path class for the current operating system. PosixPath and WindowsPath are subclasses of Path, so they share the same general interface while handling operating-system-specific path conventions.

Depending on where your file is located, you might need to change the path. pathlib lets us construct the path in a way that works across macOS, Linux, and Windows:
file = Path.home() / "Downloads" / "US-National-Parks_RecreationVisits_1979-2023.csv"
The / operator joins the path components using the correct separator for the operating system. Computers need the exact path, so if you are unsure where Python is looking, use Path.cwd() to print the current working directory.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Reading Files
We can also look at the methods built into the Path class. One in particular is useful for us: read_text(), which reads the contents of a file and returns them as a string. Read more about it in the Path.read_text() documentation and test it out in your script.
from pathlib import Path

file = Path('US-National-Parks_RecreationVisits_1979-2023.csv')
print(file, type(file))

print(file.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
What does this do?

When you save your script and rerun the code, you should see the contents of the CSV file in your terminal. If you save the result of read_text() to a variable and check its type, you will see that it is a string. Specifying encoding="utf-8" also makes our assumption about the text encoding explicit and produces more consistent behavior across operating systems.
The CSV is still structured as rows and columns, but read_text() does not interpret that structure; it gives us the file’s raw text. We can manipulate that string without entering the data by hand, but later we will use tools designed to parse structured data.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
The open Built-in Function
So far we’ve been using pathlib to work with files, but Python also provides the built-in open() function for reading and writing files.
For example, we could use the open() built-in function in Python.

The open function is a built-in function that lets you read and write files. It’s very flexible and is commonly used in Python code.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
File Input - Basic Approach
To open a file for reading (input), we just do:
input_file = open("US-National-Parks_RecreationVisits_1979-2023.csv", "r", encoding="utf-8")
text = input_file.read()
print(text)
input_file.close()
Here, we use the open() function to open a file in mode "r" (read). open() returns a file object that provides methods for reading and writing.

In this case, the read method reads in data from the input_file file object and stores it as a string in text. We can also pass a Path object to the open function.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Using Path Objects with open
We could even just pass in our Path object to the open function:
file = Path('US-National-Parks_RecreationVisits_1979-2023.csv')
input_file = open(file, "r", encoding="utf-8")
text = input_file.read()
print(text)
input_file.close()
At the end, we close the file so that its operating-system resources are released. Closing a file also ensures that buffered output has been written when we are writing rather than reading.

We should not rely on Python eventually closing the file for us. Forgetting to close files can exhaust available file handles, lock a file on some systems, or leave buffered writes unfinished. The with statement on the next slide handles this reliably.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
The with Statement
Often, you’ll see file handling used with the with keyword:
with open("US-National-Parks_RecreationVisits_1979-2023.csv", "r", encoding="utf-8") as input_file:
    print(input_file.read())
This performs the same reading operation, but the file is automatically closed at the end of the block, even if an error occurs.

The with statement is a context manager that ensures the file is closed automatically. This is the preferred way to handle files in Python.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
File Output

File output is very similar. We just use mode w, which overwrites the file specified. We can also use x (which only works for new files) or a (which appends data at the end of the file).








Character
Mode
Description




r
Read (default)
Open an existing file for reading


w
Write
Open for writing, truncating an existing file or creating a new one


a
Append
Open for writing at the end, creating the file if needed


r+
Read and write
Open an existing file for both reading and writing


x
Exclusive creation
Create a new file and fail if it already exists

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Writing to a File Example
To understand file output, let’s try working with a file that doesn’t exist:
with open("new_text.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as output_file:
    for i in range(100):
        output_file.write(str(i**2) + "\n")
Once you run it, you should see a new file in your directory called new_text.txt, containing a list of numbers.

We created those numbers using the built-in range() function and the file object’s write() method. The with block ensures that all buffered output is written and the file is closed.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Type Conversion with write()
Here’s something tricky: i and i**2 are integers, but a text file’s write() method expects a string. If we try output_file.write(i**2), we’ll get: TypeError: write() argument must be str, not int
To get around this, we can convert from int to string using str():
"4"+str(4)  # produces "44"
int("4")+4  # returns 8
The newline character "\n" inserts a line break. Without it, all the numbers would be on the same line.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Example: Save Movie Info
Here’s a function to save the movie’s information to a file:
def save_movie_info(self, file_name):
    """Saves the movie's information to a file

    Method argument:
    -----------------
    file_name(string) -- The name of the file to save the movie's information to
    """
    with open(file_name, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(f"Movie Name: {self.movie_name}\n")
        f.write(f"Directors: {', '.join(self.directors)}\n")
        f.write(f"Release Year: {self.release_year}\n")
        f.write(f"Age: {self.age}\n")
        f.write(f"Sequels: {', '.join([sequel.movie_name for sequel in self.sequels])}\n")
        f.write(f"Prequels: {', '.join([prequel.movie_name for prequel in self.prequels])}\n")

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Using Save Movie Info
Now you can call this function on your a_movie object:
a_movie = Movie("The Matrix I")
a_movie.add_directors(["Lana Wachowski", "Lilly Wachowski"])
a_movie.add_release_year(1999)
a_movie.add_sequel("The Matrix II", 2003)
a_movie.add_sequel("The Matrix III", 2003)
a_movie.add_sequel("The Matrix IV", 2021)
a_movie.add_prequel("The Matrix 0", 1998)
a_movie.calculate_movie_age()
a_movie.save_movie_info("movie_info.txt")

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Example: Read Movie Info
Here’s a function to read in a file and set the movie’s information:
def read_movie_info(self, file_name):
    """Reads in a file and sets the movie's information based on the file

    Method argument:
    -----------------
    file_name(string) -- The name of the file to read the movie's information from
    """
    with open(file_name, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        lines = f.readlines()
        self.movie_name = lines[0].split(": ")[1].strip()
        self.directors = lines[1].split(": ")[1].strip().split(", ")
        self.release_year = int(lines[2].split(": ")[1].strip())
        self.age = int(lines[3].split(": ")[1].strip())
        self.sequels = [Movie(sequel.strip()) for sequel in lines[4].split(": ")[1].strip().split(", ")]
        self.prequels = [Movie(prequel.strip()) for prequel in lines[5].split(": ")[1].strip().split(", ")]

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Using Read Movie Info
Now you can call this function on your a_movie object:
a_movie = Movie("The Matrix I")
a_movie.read_movie_info("movie_info.txt")
a_movie.get_movie_info()

These examples show how to integrate file I/O with your class methods to persist and restore object data.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
section: What is a Virtual Environment? Why do we need one?
text:
What is a Virtual Environment? Why do we need one?


Virtual environments solve the “dependency hell” problem—where different projects need different versions of the same library.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Why Virtual Environments Matter

From the Python documentation:

“Python applications will often use packages and modules that don’t come as part of the standard library. Applications will sometimes need a specific version of a library, because the application may require that a particular bug has been fixed or the application may be written using an obsolete version of the library’s interface.


This means it may not be possible for one Python installation to meet the requirements of every application. If application A needs version 1.0 of a particular module but application B needs version 2.0, then the requirements are in conflict and installing either version 1.0 or 2.0 will leave one application unable to run.


The solution for this problem is to create a virtual environment, a self-contained directory tree that contains a Python installation for a particular version of Python, plus a number of additional packages.”

You can read more here about virtual environments.


We’ve learned to use libraries that come pre-installed with Python, but now we need to install additional libraries. Before we do, we need to create a virtual environment.
A virtual environment is a self-contained directory that contains a Python installation plus additional packages, isolated from the global Python installation.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
What About pip?
pip is Python’s package installer. A virtual environment created with venv normally includes it automatically, so we do not need to install packages globally before creating .venv.

install pip

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Check pip After Activation
After .venv is created and activated, check the environment’s copy of pip with:
python -m pip --version
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
If Python reports that pip is unavailable, follow the official pip installation instructions or ask an instructor for help.

Using python -m pip ensures that we are checking or updating pip for the same Python interpreter selected by the active environment. We will run these commands after activation rather than modifying the system Python installation.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
venv
Now we’ll use the built-in Python virtual environment, called venv, which you can read more about here https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html. One thing to note is that there are LOTS of different ways to setup your virtual environment (which lots of people have very strong feelings about). I like this answer from Stack Overflow for giving an overview of the differing options https://stackoverflow.com/a/65854168/7437781.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Creating Virtual Environments
Now that we have a sense of what a virtual environment is, let’s create a project-local environment named .venv. We’ll start in VS Code and then look at the equivalent terminal commands.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
section: Creating Virtual Environments in VS Code
text:
Creating Virtual Environments in VS Code







Note


This information has been adapted from the VS Code documentation for Python environments.



In VS Code, first open your is310-coding-assignments project folder and then open the Command Palette:

Mac: ⇧⌘P
Windows: Ctrl+Shift+P

You can also access the Command Palette by clicking on the View menu and selecting Command Palette.
Once it is open, type Python: Create Environment and select it from the menu. Choose Venv, which uses Python’s built-in virtual-environment tool.



Create Environment Dropdown




venv is built into Python. VS Code now also exposes environment creation through the Python sidebar’s Environment Managers view, but Python: Create Environment remains a clear route through the same process. Make sure a project folder is open before creating the environment so .venv is created in the correct location.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Selecting Python Version
Once you select Venv, you’ll be prompted to select the Python interpreter used to create the environment. Choose a currently supported Python 3 interpreter. If multiple versions are installed, select the recent version you have been using for this course.

Create Environment Name

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Locating Your Virtual Environment
Once VS Code creates the environment, you should see a .venv folder inside the project folder. If you try this without opening a folder first, VS Code will ask you to open a workspace.

Created Environment

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Keep the .venv Name and Location
Do not rename or move .venv after creating it. Virtual environments contain paths to their original location. If you need a different name or location, delete the environment and create a new one there.
We will consistently use .venv for this repository. The leading period also helps identify it as project configuration rather than coursework, and later we will add .venv/ to .gitignore so it is not committed to GitHub.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Activating Your Virtual Environment





Virtual Environment Activated



VS Code should select the newly created .venv automatically. The interpreter list organizes environments by type and location, helping us distinguish the project environment from globally installed Python interpreters.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Activated Venv in VS Code

Virtual Environment ActivatedOnce you select the virtual environment, its Python interpreter should appear in the VS Code status bar. This selection tells VS Code which Python to use when running code, debugging, and providing language features.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Not Activated? Select Interpreter!
If .venv is not selected, open the Command Palette, choose Python: Select Interpreter, and select the interpreter inside .venv. You can also select the Python version shown in the status bar to switch interpreters.

Select Python Interpreter

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Final Check
After selecting .venv, close any terminal that was already open and create a new VS Code terminal. You should see (.venv) at the beginning of the prompt, indicating that the environment is active.

Activate Virtual Environment

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Creating Virtual Environments in Terminal (Optional)
VS Code provides a convenient interface for creating virtual environments, and I recommend that method for this course. The following slides show the equivalent terminal workflow because you may see me use it in class and because it makes the underlying commands visible.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Start in the Project Folder
To create the environment in the terminal, first navigate to your is310-coding-assignments project directory. We will create .venv directly inside that project, matching the VS Code convention.
cd path/to/is310-coding-assignments

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Creating Virtual Environments in Terminal
On macOS or Linux:
python3 -m venv .venv
On Windows PowerShell:
python -m venv .venv
If Windows does not recognize python, try py -m venv .venv.

The command asks the selected Python interpreter to run its built-in venv module and create an environment in .venv. It may appear to do nothing, but a new .venv directory should appear in the project. Students should create only one environment for this course repository. Unrelated projects should have their own environments so their dependencies do not conflict.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Activating Virtual Environments
On macOS, Linux, or WSL:
source .venv/bin/activate
On Windows Command Prompt:
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat
On Windows PowerShell:
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
If you are getting errors in PowerShell, you may need to change your execution policy. You can do this by running the following command:
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope Process

Activation adjusts the terminal’s path so that python and installed packages come from .venv rather than the system-wide Python. The command differs because macOS/Linux shells, Command Prompt, and PowerShell use different activation scripts. After activation, the prompt should begin with (.venv).
The PowerShell execution-policy command uses -Scope Process, so the change applies only to the current PowerShell session. Students should only activate scripts they understand and trust.
To verify the exact Python executable now in use, run python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)". Its path should point inside the project’s .venv directory.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Deactivating Virtual Environments
To deactivate your virtual environment in the terminal:
deactivate
Your virtual environment will no longer be in the terminal prompt.
This removes (.venv) from the terminal prompt. In VS Code, closing the active terminal and opening a new one after selecting a different interpreter also starts a new shell context.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Adding to .gitignore
Virtual environments are specific to your computer. Don’t commit them to git.
Add this to your .gitignore:
.venv/
Or if you accidentally committed it:
git rm -r --cached .venv
Then add .gitignore, commit the change, and run git status to confirm that .venv is no longer tracked.

Since we are using git to track our work, we don’t want to include our virtual environment in our repository. This is because the virtual environment is specific to your computer and the libraries you have installed. If someone else were to clone your repository, they wouldn’t have the same virtual environment as you. This is why we add the virtual environment to our .gitignore file. This file tells git to ignore certain files or directories when tracking changes. You can add the following line to your .gitignore file to ignore your virtual environment:
Now when we run git status, we should not see the environment among the tracked changes. Only run git rm if .venv was already staged or committed; --cached removes it from Git’s index without deleting the local environment.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
section: Installing Libraries with pip in venv
text:
Installing Libraries with pip in venv
Now that we have our virtual environment created and activated in VS Code, we can start to try installing external Python libraries.
Today, we will try installing the Python package Rich by running the following command:
python -m pip --version
python -m pip install rich
Remember: Always do this with your virtual environment activated!

Using python -m pip ties pip to the same active Python interpreter. This is more reliable than calling pip or pip3 directly when several Python installations exist. Before installing, verify that (.venv) appears in the prompt.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Testing the Installation
To verify the installation worked:
python -m pip show rich
Or check all installed libraries:
python -m pip list
Either command should show whether Rich is installed and which version is present.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Recording Package Requirements
Do not commit or share .venv. Record the packages needed to recreate it:
python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
Someone who clones the repository can create and activate their own environment, then install the same versions:
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

The environment contains machine-specific executables and paths, while requirements.txt is a small, portable text record of installed packages and versions. Students should review the file before committing it and regenerate it whenever they intentionally add or update dependencies.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
site-packages
You can also look in your virtual environment directory and see if there is a site-packages directory. This is where all the libraries you install with pip are stored. You can see that the Rich library is installed in the site-packages directory.

Rich Installed

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
The Rich Library


Rich is a Python library created by Will McGugan to add formatted text, tables, progress indicators, and other visual elements to terminal applications. Its source code and development history are available in the Rich GitHub repository.




Rich History

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Rich Features





Rich Features



We can start to get a sense of what the library can do by looking at the features listed on the GitHub repository but we can also read the documentation for the library to get a better sense of what it can do https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/introduction.html.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Rich Documentation

This documentation is very detailed, but we can start with the Quickstart guidelines https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/introduction.html#quick-start to get a sense of how to use the library.
From the guidelines we can see how to import the library into our Python script. In your is310-coding-assignments directory, create a new folder called python-libraries and create a new file called rich_example.py. In this file, add the following code:
from rich import print

print("Hello, [bold magenta]World[/bold magenta]!", ":vampire:")

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Rich Outputs

Run it:
python rich_example.py
# Or, from the repository root:
python python-libraries/rich_example.py
You should see the following output in your terminal:
Hello, World! 🧛



Rich Example


Notice that the word world is in bold and magenta and that there is a vampire emoji at the end of the sentence. This is the power of the Rich library.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Rich Tables


Rich has powerful classes like Console and Table for formatting:
from rich.console import Console
from rich.table import Table

console = Console()

table = Table(title="Star Wars Movies")
table.add_column("Released", style="cyan", no_wrap=True)
table.add_column("Title", style="magenta")
table.add_column("Box Office", justify="right")
table.add_row("Dec 20, 2019", "Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker", "$952,110,690")
table.add_row("May 25, 2018", "Solo: A Star Wars Story", "$393,151,347")
table.add_row("Dec 15, 2017", "Star Wars Ep. VIII: The Last Jedi", "$1,332,539,889")
table.add_row("Dec 16, 2016", "Rogue One: A Star Wars Story", "$1,332,439,889")

console.print(table)

And you should see the following output in your terminal:



Rich Table




As you can likely tell, both Console and Table are classes built into the Rich library that allow us to format our text in different ways. We can see that we are able to add a title to our table, add columns, and add rows to our table. We can also see that we are able to format our text in different ways, such as changing the color of the text, justifying the text, and wrapping the text.

We can also click the small green source button to see the source code for the class https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/_modules/rich/console.html#Console.

title: Ecosystems & Environments
text:
Full Assignment
Command Line Data Curation

title: Scrape On & Off
text:
What Is Web Scraping?


What changes when we treat a webpage as data rather than as a page to read?

I want to begin by asking students to reconstruct the definition rather than giving it to them. Web scraping is the programmatic retrieval and extraction of information from webpages. It usually combines two actions: requesting a resource from a server and parsing the returned HTML so that selected elements can become structured records.
This builds directly on our earlier HTML and web lessons. We are not encountering a new kind of information. We are using code to work with the same headings, paragraphs, lists, links, attributes, and nested elements that students used to build webpages.
The shift is interpretive as well as technical. A person can look at a page and understand its layout. A scraper needs explicit instructions about what counts as a record, where the relevant information lives, and which parts of the interface should be ignored.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: Why Might We Scrape the Web?
text:
Why Might We Scrape the Web?


What purposes besides research might web scraping serve?

Scraping can support research, aggregation, migration, accessibility, monitoring, and preservation. I want students to remember that scraping is not only a commercial data-extraction technique.
SUCHO, Saving Ukrainian Cultural Heritage Online, formed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Volunteers used crawling, scraping, and web-archiving tools to preserve threatened Ukrainian cultural heritage websites. This connects back to our discussions of the Internet Archive and mass digitization: automated collection can preserve vulnerable culture, but deciding what to collect still requires people, priorities, infrastructure, and care.
A crawler discovers pages by following links. A scraper extracts selected material from those pages. A web-archiving workflow may use both, but these terms describe different tasks.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: If a Page Is Public, Can We Scrape It?
text:
If a Page Is Public, Can We Scrape It?


What does public access permit, and what does it not settle?

Public visibility is not automatic permission to collect, republish, or analyze material however we want. We need to distinguish technical accessibility from legal permission and ethical responsibility.
The hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn litigation is useful because it shows why “is scraping legal?” is too broad a question. hiQ was a workforce-analytics company that scraped information from public LinkedIn profiles to produce products intended to identify employees who might leave and map employees’ skills. LinkedIn sent hiQ a cease-and-desist letter and used technical measures to block it. hiQ then asked a federal court to stop LinkedIn from blocking its access while the lawsuit proceeded.
The narrow question before the Ninth Circuit was whether hiQ was likely violating the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, or CFAA, by accessing profile information that any member of the public could view without logging in. The court treated the CFAA primarily as an anti-intrusion law and concluded that publicly accessible pages were not analogous to a computer system protected by an authorization gate. In 2019 it upheld a preliminary injunction in hiQ’s favor. The Supreme Court later vacated that judgment and asked the Ninth Circuit to reconsider it after Van Buren v. United States clarified the CFAA. In 2022, the Ninth Circuit again concluded that hiQ had raised a serious claim that scraping the public profiles did not constitute access “without authorization” under that particular CFAA provision. The 2022 Ninth Circuit opinion and the Supreme Court docket show that procedural history.
This was a ruling about a preliminary injunction and one part of one federal statute, not a declaration that public data may always be scraped or reused. Back in the district court, LinkedIn also pursued claims involving its User Agreement and state law. The court concluded that the agreement prohibited scraping and found that hiQ had breached it in several respects, although factual disputes remained around some defenses. The parties ultimately resolved the litigation through a consent judgment in December 2022. That judgment included $500,000 against hiQ, deletion requirements, and a permanent injunction restricting its future use of LinkedIn. The consent judgment and permanent injunction is a useful counterpoint to summaries claiming that hiQ simply established that web scraping is legal.
The larger lesson is that technical access and legal permission are different layers. A scraper might avoid CFAA liability under one theory and still face questions involving contracts, copyright, privacy, trespass, misappropriation, or state and international law. It also matters whether pages require authentication, whether the scraper circumvents technical barriers, what the platform’s terms prohibit, what data is collected, and how that data is reused.
Ethically, I want to ask who created the material, what audience they expected, whether the data concerns identifiable or vulnerable people, what harms might follow from aggregation, and whether quotations remain searchable even after usernames are removed.
This connects directly to Tuesday’s discussion. Openness is not a single condition. Being able to view information does not mean it is public domain, openly licensed, ethically reusable, or appropriate to redistribute as a dataset. What Does the GDPR Change?
Personal data does not become unrestricted research material merely because it is publicly visible.


What is the lawful basis for collecting it?
Were people told how their data would be used?
Are we collecting only what the project needs?
How long will we retain it, and with whom will we share it?

The European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation took effect in 2018. It regulates the processing of personal data, including collecting, storing, analyzing, and sharing it. The regulation does not simply declare all web scraping legal or illegal, and it does not ban scraping names and email addresses as a single categorical rule.
Instead, a project processing personal data needs a lawful basis and must follow principles including transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, security, and accountability. Special categories of sensitive data receive additional protection.
Public availability does not remove these obligations. A person’s decision to post information for one audience is not necessarily consent for researchers or companies to aggregate it into a reusable dataset.
The GDPR applies within a particular legal jurisdiction, but its questions are useful beyond Europe: Why are we collecting this? Do people understand the new use? Are we collecting more than necessary? What risks emerge when separate traces are combined?
This lesson is an introduction to responsible research practice, not legal advice. For current guidance, see the European Data Protection Board’s discussion of anonymisation, pseudonymisation, and web scraping.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: Is Legal the Same as Ethical?
text:
Is Legal the Same as Ethical?


Whose expectations and possible harms should shape our collection choices?

Melanie Walsh emphasizes that legal access or institutional approval does not automatically make a data-collection practice ethical. Internet data can expose people to unwanted scrutiny or harm when it is aggregated, quoted, or redistributed beyond its original setting.
Anonymization creates its own tension. Removing a username may protect someone, but a verbatim quotation can remain searchable. Removing attribution can also deny an internet user recognition as a creator. There is no single solution that works for every platform, community, and research question.
Walsh describes developing a project-specific framework based on context, publicness, likely consequences, and the people involved. In some work, she seeks permission before quoting users. In her textbook, she uses a threshold of publicness, such as verified accounts or highly visible posts.
IRB stands for Institutional Review Board. Universities use IRBs to review research involving human subjects. Whether a web-data project requires formal review depends on the data, interaction, risks, and institutional rules. Researchers should not decide that question solely from whether a page can be opened without logging in.
For our assignments, the important habit is to ask not only whether we can automate collection, but whether we should collect, retain, quote, and publish each field.

title: Scrape On & Off
text:
What Does robots.txt Tell Us?


Is robots.txt permission, a prohibition, or something else?

robots.txt communicates operational instructions to automated crawlers. Rules can identify user agents and mark paths as allowed or disallowed. Some sites also request a crawl delay.
It is not a copyright license, contract, privacy policy, or complete ethical framework. Following it does not settle every question, and ignoring it is a clear warning that our automation conflicts with the site’s stated preferences.
Tolkien Gateway’s file is unusually conversational. It asks responsible visitors not to scrape too fast and blocks several named commercial crawlers. That does not grant unrestricted permission, but it gives us useful operational guidance for a small educational project: identify ourselves, slow down, and stop when the server refuses a request.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: What Are the Two Main Jobs in Our Scraper?
text:
What Are the Two Main Jobs in Our Scraper?


requests
How do we retrieve the page?


BeautifulSoup
How do we search its HTML?



requests handles HTTP. requests.get() returns a Response object. We inspect response.status_code and pass response.text, the returned HTML string, to Beautiful Soup.
Beautiful Soup parses the string into an object that represents the document tree. That lets us search by tags and attributes rather than manipulate one enormous string.
The installation and import names differ:
python -m pip install requests beautifulsoup4 rich
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
This is a useful reminder that the name published on PyPI does not always match the name imported into Python.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: Why Return to Our Virtual Environment?
text:
Why Return to Our Virtual Environment?




Where will Python install our new packages?

How can we tell which environment is active?



Before installing anything, students should open the coding-assignment repository in VS Code and select or activate its virtual environment. The environment gives this project its own Python executable and package directory, keeping its dependencies separate from other projects and the system Python.
The terminal prompt should normally begin with (.venv) after activation. Students can also verify the interpreter and installer with:
python --version
python -m pip --version
On macOS, Linux, or WSL, the terminal activation command is:
source .venv/bin/activate
On Windows PowerShell:
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
If VS Code has selected the environment but an already-open terminal does not show (.venv), close that terminal and open a new one.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: Where Should We Install the Packages?
text:
Where Should We Install the Packages?
python -m pip install requests beautifulsoup4 rich

Which Python receives these packages? How can we check?

Before running this command, students should activate the virtual environment for their coding-assignment repository. The environment keeps this project’s dependencies separate from global Python and unrelated projects.
Using python -m pip asks the same interpreter invoked as python to run its pip module. This is clearer than relying on a standalone pip command that might point to another Python installation.
Useful checks include:
python --version
python -m pip --version
python -m pip list
On Windows PowerShell, the installation command is the same after activation. The activation command differs:
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install requests beautifulsoup4 rich

title: Scrape On & Off
text:
What Is a Software Library?


How is using a library different from writing every part of a scraper ourselves?

A software library is a collection of reusable code organized around one or more purposes. It lets our program use logic written and maintained elsewhere rather than requiring us to implement every operation ourselves.
The term is broad rather than a formal unit in Python. We can speak of Python libraries, JavaScript libraries, or operating-system libraries. Python’s Standard Library ships with Python and includes modules such as pathlib, csv, and time. Third-party libraries such as Requests, Beautiful Soup, and Rich are distributed separately and need to be installed.
Beautiful Soup provides classes and methods for parsing and searching HTML or XML. We still decide what to find, what to record, and what the results mean. The library assists with the operation; it does not supply the research question.

title: Scrape On & Off
text:
What Is a Python Package?



Python Package Index homepage



Why do people sometimes use “package” and “library” interchangeably?

A package is a more specific Python concept: code organized so it can be installed and imported. Packages are the units distributed through repositories such as the Python Package Index, or PyPI.
A library may consist of one package, so ordinary conversation often blurs the terms. For this lesson, the practical distinction is:

A library describes reusable functionality and purpose.
A package describes how Python code is organized and distributed.

When we use pip, we install a package into the active Python environment. When we write an import statement, we make code from an installed package available to our script.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: How can we import Beautiful Soup?
text:
How can we import Beautiful Soup?





import beautifulsoup4

Installation name or import name?



The name installed from PyPI is beautifulsoup4, but the Python package imported by code is named bs4. These names often match, but they do not have to.
This is why the documentation matters. Rather than guessing from the pip install command, we should look at the package’s quick-start instructions.
The usual import is:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
This imports the BeautifulSoup class directly from the bs4 package. We could instead write:
import bs4
soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup(html_doc, "html.parser")
I would avoid from bs4 import * because it hides which names came from the package and can create collisions.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: What Does Beautiful Soup Need From Us?
text:
What Does Beautiful Soup Need From Us?

soup = BeautifulSoup(html_doc, "html.parser")

What are the two arguments?

The first argument is the markup to parse. In our introductory example, html_doc is a multiline Python string containing HTML. Later, it will be response.text from a web request.
The second argument identifies the parser. A parser reads markup and constructs the tree that Beautiful Soup lets us navigate. We use Python’s built-in html.parser, so students do not need to install another dependency.
Other choices include lxml and html5lib. They differ in speed, dependencies, and how they repair malformed HTML. Parser choice can sometimes change the resulting tree, particularly with broken markup. For our pages, html.parser keeps the setup simple and works adequately.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: How Does Beautiful Soup First See HTML?

title: Scrape On & Off
section: How Can We Extract the Links?
text:
How Can We Extract the Links?
links = soup.find_all("a")

for link in links:
    print(link.get("href"))
    print(link.get_text())

What is each loop iteration holding?

find_all("a") searches the parsed document and returns all matching anchor tags. The result behaves like a list, so each iteration assigns one Beautiful Soup Tag object to link.
link.get("href") retrieves the value of the HTML attribute. link.get_text() retrieves the text nested inside the tag. For the first link, those values are http://example.com/elsie and Elsie.
I can ask students what would change if we wrote:
links = soup.find_all("a", class_="sister")
The trailing underscore in class_ avoids a conflict with Python’s reserved word class.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: What Kind of Object Did We Find?
text:
What Kind of Object Did We Find?
first_link = soup.find("a")

print(type(first_link))
print(first_link.name)
print(first_link.attrs)
print(first_link.get_text())

How does a Tag connect HTML attributes, nested text, and Python methods?

Beautiful Soup describes four main object types: BeautifulSoup, Tag, NavigableString, and Comment. Students only need to focus on the first two today.
The BeautifulSoup object represents the parsed document as a whole. A Tag represents one HTML element. The tag’s .name is a, .attrs contains attributes such as href and class, and .get_text() returns its nested textual content.
This connects to our recent Python discussion of classes and objects. Beautiful Soup is not returning raw dictionaries. It returns objects with stored data and methods for navigating or extracting from the document.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: How Do We Move Through the Tree?
text:
How Do We Move Through the Tree?
paragraphs = soup.find_all("p")

for paragraph in paragraphs:
    print(paragraph.get_text(" ", strip=True))
    print(paragraph.parent.name)

What do “parent,” “child,” and “descendant” mean in HTML?

HTML is a tree because elements can contain other elements. A direct container is the parent; elements immediately inside it are children; everything nested beneath it is a descendant.
Beautiful Soup methods often search descendants. Properties such as .parent let us move upward. Methods such as .find_next() move through document order.
The point is not to memorize every navigation operation. Students should know that the structure exists, inspect the HTML, and consult the documentation for the operation that fits the page.
This prepares the transition to Project Gutenberg: rather than search a small sample string, we will inspect a real page and decide which part of its tree contains our intended records.

title: Scrape On & Off
text:
What Do These Methods Return?
soup.find("h2")
soup.find_all("h2")
element.find_next("ol")
element.get_text(" ", strip=True)
link.get("href")

Which returns one element, many elements, text, or an attribute?

Ask students to match each method to its result:

.find() returns the first matching tag or None.
.find_all() returns a list-like collection of every matching tag.
.find_next() searches forward in document order.
.get_text() extracts visible text from a tag and its descendants.
.get("href") retrieves an attribute value from a tag.

The optional separator in get_text(" ", strip=True) places spaces between text nodes and removes leading and trailing whitespace. It does not guarantee that every piece of interface text has been excluded.

title: Scrape On & Off
text:
Why Does HTML Structure Matter?


Which element represents one item? Which element contains the list?

Before writing a selector, I should open the page and use Inspect. The visible layout is produced by nested HTML elements. We need to identify the repeated element that corresponds to our unit of analysis and a stable parent that distinguishes it from unrelated content.
On Project Gutenberg’s Top 100 page, the headings name different lists, an ordered list contains the entries, and each li represents one listed item. Searching the entire document for every li retrieves unrelated interface elements too. The code becomes more meaningful when it follows the page’s local structure.
This is also why scrapers are brittle. A design change can alter the HTML structure without changing the page’s visible purpose.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: What Happens If We Search Too Broadly?
text:
What Happens If We Search Too Broadly?


titles = soup.find_all("li")
What will this collect besides book titles?

This is an important debugging and interpretation question. The code is syntactically correct, but the result does not match the research intention because the search covers the whole document.
I can ask students how they would narrow the search. One approach is to find the relevant heading or id, navigate to the following ordered list, and only then find its list items:
top_books = soup.find(id="books-last1")
book_items = top_books.find_next("ol").find_all("li")
Selectors operationalize our concept of the dataset. A selector can run without errors while collecting the wrong things. How Does a Webpage Become a Dataset?

Identify a question
Inspect the page
Select repeated records
Extract fields
Structure dictionaries
Save CSV or JSON

The technical pipeline begins with an intellectual decision. We need a question and a unit of analysis before choosing selectors.
For every repeated item, we can create a dictionary:
records.append({
    "list_name": list_name,
    "title": item.get_text(" ", strip=True),
    "link": item.find("a").get("href"),
})
The keys become fields in the dataset. Their names and values encode our interpretation of the page. A list of dictionaries is useful because every dictionary represents one row-like record with the same expected fields.
Saving the output is not the end. We should inspect the CSV, verify sample records against the pages, and document where and when the data came from.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: What Does a Server Tell Us?
text:
What Does a Server Tell Us?




What do these status codes suggest?

200
403
404
429
500



I can ask students to interpret each code before reviewing it:

200 OK: the server fulfilled the request.
403 Forbidden: the server understood but refused it.
404 Not Found: the requested resource was not found.
429 Too Many Requests: we have been rate-limited and should stop or slow down.
500 Internal Server Error: the server encountered an error.

A 200 only tells us that the server returned something. We should inspect the response because bot-protection pages can sometimes return HTML that is not the content we expected. A successful request also does not answer whether reuse is responsible.
This is why the homework begins with a status-code check before students commit to a site.

title: Scrape On & Off
text:
What Is Happening Here?
response = requests.get(url)
soup = BeautifulSoup(response.text, "html.parser")

What are the types of response, response.text, and soup?

For the demo, I can run:
print(type(response))
print(type(response.text))
print(type(soup))
response is a Requests Response object. response.text is a Python string. soup is a Beautiful Soup object representing the parsed document.
The parser name tells Beautiful Soup how to interpret the markup. We use Python’s built-in html.parser, which is adequate for this lesson and does not require another dependency.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: What Is Wrong With This Link?
text:
What Is Wrong With This Link?
/ebooks/84

Why might requests.get() fail if we use it by itself?


https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/84

/ebooks/84 is a relative URL. A browser resolves it using the current site’s origin. A Python script needs us to provide that context.
For this site we can combine the base address and path:
book_url = "https://www.gutenberg.org" + relative_link
This connects to the web lesson’s distinction between internal and external links. It also demonstrates why inspecting actual values matters before sending hundreds of requests.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: What Changes When We Look At More Complex Sites?
text:
What Changes When We Look At More Complex Sites?

How is scraping one index page different from building records from many detail pages?

Project Gutenberg lets us practice extracting repeated items from one page. Tolkien Gateway introduces a two-level workflow:

Scrape category pages to discover character names and URLs.
Visit each character page to calculate measurements.

This scales the number of requests and therefore the responsibility. It also creates provenance we should preserve: the category page tells us why a character entered the dataset, while the detail page supplies the measurements.
The category is not merely a convenient technical container. It is an editorial classification created by the wiki community.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: When Should We Not Keep Scraping?
text:
When Should We Not Keep Scraping?

What should we do when a site returns 403, 429, or a bot-protection page?

Stop and reassess. Students should not use evasion tools simply because the ordinary request was blocked.
Possible alternatives include:

Look for an official API.
Look for a downloadable export or dataset.
Use a permitted archived copy.
Contact the site or community.
Choose a different source.
Reduce the scope and request rate if the server explicitly permits access.

Fandom.com is a useful example. Cloudflare now blocks simple automated requests to many Fandom-hosted wikis. Some communities have also left Fandom because of advertising and platform control, moving to independent infrastructure such as wiki.gg or Miraheze. Platform ownership shapes both the culture documented and researchers’ access to it.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: What Should a Responsible Request Include?
text:
What Should a Responsible Request Include?
HEADERS = {
    "User-Agent": "is310-course-scraper/1.0 "
    "(student project; netid@illinois.edu)"
}

response = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=30)
time.sleep(1)

Why identify ourselves and deliberately make the script slower?

The User-Agent identifies the client making the request. Browsers send one automatically. Our script supplies an honest description and contact address instead of pretending to be another browser or crawler.
The timeout prevents the script from waiting indefinitely. time.sleep() spaces out requests so that our loop does not hit the server as rapidly as the computer can operate. The delay is part of the research method, not decoration.
I should emphasize that trying to bypass a block with another library is not the goal. If a site refuses automated access, students should find an API, downloadable dataset, archived copy, or different source.

title: Scrape On & Off
text:
What Question Are We Asking?


How does Tolkien Gateway distribute attention between literary and adaptation-created characters?

The website is too large for a meaningful instruction to “scrape Tolkien Gateway.” We need a bounded comparison and an account of what could count as evidence.
We compare two categories maintained by Tolkien Gateway editors:

Characters in The Lord of the Rings
The Rings of Power television-series characters

These are not equivalent populations. They differ in age, source material, number of editors, cultural history, and category rules. The comparison is exploratory rather than a definitive measurement of fandom.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: Where Do Our Records Come From?
text:
Where Do Our Records Come From?






What has the wiki already decided for us?

The two category pages supply character links, but they also supply classifications. We record source_url so future users can see which category produced each record, and we derive character_type as literary or adaptation from that source.
Ask students what might be missing or contested. Characters can appear across books and adaptations. Category membership may be incomplete or governed by local editorial rules. Some adaptation-created characters may be composites or transformations of literary figures. Our simple type field compresses those complexities.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: How Do We Find Every Character?
text:
How Do We Find Every Character?

characters_section = category_page.find(id="mw-pages")
character_items = characters_section.find_all("li")

The lesson deliberately breaks the search into readable stages instead of one dense CSS selector. First find the page section, then find each list item, then find the link inside the item.
During the demo, I can open developer tools and ask students to identify id="mw-pages". Then we can connect that HTML attribute to the .find(id="mw-pages") call.
The function returns a list of dictionaries containing the character name, category-derived type, source URL, and full character URL. This is the first stage of the dataset, before any measurements are added.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: What Part of a Character Page Should Count?
text:
What Part of a Character Page Should Count?


What would happen if we counted the entire webpage?

The full page includes navigation, sidebars, footer text, scripts, interface labels, and other material that is not the character article. We narrow the analysis to:
content = soup.select_one("#mw-content-text .mw-parser-output")
This still does not produce pure article prose. The selected element may contain captions, tables, references, and templates. The selector is a documented research decision, not a magical extraction of the page’s true content.

title: Scrape On & Off
text:
What Might Count as Attention?



Measurement
Possible interpretation




Words
Length of documentation


Characters
Another measure of text extent


All internal links
Every connection made in the article


Unique internal links
Breadth of distinct wiki destinations




Which of these is fandom attention, and which is only a proxy?

All four are proxies. A longer page could reflect popularity, abundant source material, a long publication history, sustained editorial labor, controversy, or formatting conventions. Links can reflect navigational style as much as cultural attention.
The distinction between word count and character count gives us two imperfect views of length. split() treats whitespace-separated pieces as words; it is not linguistic tokenization. Character count includes spaces and punctuation.
The point is not that proxies are invalid. The point is that we must name what we calculated and avoid silently substituting it for the larger concept we care about.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: Why Count All and Unique Links?
text:
Why Count All and Unique Links?
Elrond, Elrond, Elrond, Galadriel, Galadriel

All links: 5
Unique links: 2


What different kind of page might each measure reward?

The total captures every qualifying occurrence. The unique count captures the range of distinct destinations.
The script first creates a regular list of all qualifying internal links. It then builds another list and adds a URL only if it is not already present. This uses data structures students already know:
unique_internal_links = []
for href in internal_links:
    if href not in unique_internal_links:
        unique_internal_links.append(href)
Neither result is automatically better. Comparing them can reveal whether a page repeatedly returns to a few topics or connects outward to many pages.

title: Scrape On & Off
section: How Do We Define an Internal Link?
text:
How Do We Define an Internal Link?
for link in content.find_all("a", href=True):
    href = link["href"]
    if href.startswith("/wiki/") and "#" not in href:
        links.append(href)

What does this include that we may not actually want?

This deliberately simple rule keeps relative links to wiki pages and excludes fragment links to sections of the current page.
It may still include categories, files, templates, help pages, dates, people, and other destinations that are not equivalent. That imperfection is productive for discussion. We can improve the code later, but each additional exclusion also encodes another judgment about which relationships count.
The script can be reproducible and still measure something broader than intended. Reproducibility makes the decision visible; it does not make the decision neutral.

What can a link to the television series tell us about a literary character?
