title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: What Changes When We Look At More Complex Sites? How does a Wiki differ from Project Gutenberg?
text:
What Changes When We Look At More Complex Sites? How does a Wiki differ from Project Gutenberg?


Project Gutenberg lets us practice extracting repeated items from one page. Tolkien Gateway introduces a two-level workflow:

Scrape category pages to discover character names and URLs.
Visit each character page to calculate measurements.

This scales the number of requests and therefore the responsibility. It also creates provenance we should preserve: the category page tells us why a character entered the dataset, while the detail page supplies the measurements.
The category is not merely a convenient technical container. It is an editorial classification created by the wiki community.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
Where Did Wikis Come From?



Ward Cunningham


What changes when readers can also edit the webpage?

Ward Cunningham launched WikiWikiWeb in 1995 as part of the Portland Pattern Repository, a site where software developers could collaboratively document and discuss programming patterns. He wanted a web space that visitors could revise quickly rather than a collection maintained by one webmaster.
The word wiki comes from the Hawaiian word for quick. Cunningham encountered the name through Honolulu’s Wiki Wiki Shuttle and used it to emphasize rapid editing.
A wiki combines several ideas that matter for this course: pages can be edited through the browser, links connect pages into an evolving knowledge structure, and revision histories preserve evidence of change. The content and the system for organizing it develop together.
This history helps us see Tolkien Gateway as more than a website containing facts. It is a collaboratively maintained knowledge system whose categories, links, page names, and revisions reflect community decisions.
Historical context: WikiWikiWeb’s account of its history and this history of Cunningham’s first wiki.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: How Did Wikipedia Change the Scale of Wikis?
text:
How Did Wikipedia Change the Scale of Wikis?



Wikipedia homepage on March 3, 2001



Wikipedia launched in January 2001 as an experiment connected to Nupedia, an earlier free encyclopedia with a slower expert-review process. The early Wikipedia screenshot emphasizes participation: visitors are invited to edit pages, create links, and help the encyclopedia grow.
The first Wikipedia ran on UseModWiki, open-source software written in Perl that stored pages as text files. The site quickly accumulated more pages, revisions, contributors, and readers than that software had been designed to manage.
Wikipedia contributors responded by developing database-backed software in PHP and MySQL. Wikipedia adopted it in 2002, and the software received the name MediaWiki in 2003. The change supported Wikipedia-specific structures including namespaces, talk pages, contribution histories, and watchlists.
This is useful preparation for the API section later today. MediaWiki’s Action API exposes selected parts of the same database-backed page, category, revision, and link structure.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: How Did Wikis Become Cultural Infrastructures?
text:
How Did Wikis Become Cultural Infrastructures?



Wookieepedia and Wikipedia


What kinds of cultural knowledge do fan communities organize differently?

Wikipedia demonstrated that large groups could build an extensive reference work through wiki software and community governance. Fan communities adapted the model to document fictional worlds, media franchises, games, and other forms of popular culture in much greater detail than a general encyclopedia usually would.
Wookieepedia began in 2005, the same year as Tolkien Gateway. These communities did more than write summaries. They developed taxonomies, naming conventions, distinctions between canon and adaptation, templates, policies, and standards of evidence.
Those organizational choices become part of our data. A category page decides which characters appear in our starting population. A redirect decides where a character’s evidence is stored. Internal links encode relationships editors considered worth making explicit.
That gives us the transition to the scraper: if wiki communities organize cultural knowledge through pages, categories, and links, what can we learn by measuring those structures? What might our measurements miss about disagreement, revision, or community governance?
Tolkien gateway
Community Portal

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: How Do We Know if We Can Access a Site?
text:
How Do We Know if We Can Access a Site?




Tolkien Gateway robots.txt


What should we do when a site returns 403, 429, or a bot-protection page?

Stop and reassess. Students should not use evasion tools simply because the ordinary request was blocked.
Possible alternatives include:

Look for an official API.
Look for a downloadable export or dataset.
Use a permitted archived copy.
Contact the site or community.
Choose a different source.
Reduce the scope and request rate if the server explicitly permits access.

Fandom.com is a useful example. Cloudflare now blocks simple automated requests to many Fandom-hosted wikis. Some communities have also left Fandom because of advertising and platform control, moving to independent infrastructure such as wiki.gg or Miraheze. Platform ownership shapes both the culture documented and researchers’ access to it.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
What are request headers?
Why do we capitalize the headers variable? Why identify ourselves and deliberately make the script slower?
HEADERS = {
    "User-Agent": "is310-course-scraper/1.0 "
    "(student project; netid@illinois.edu)"
}

response = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=30)
time.sleep(1)

The User-Agent identifies the client making the request. Browsers send one automatically. Our script supplies an honest description and contact address instead of pretending to be another browser or crawler.
The timeout prevents the script from waiting indefinitely. time.sleep() spaces out requests so that our loop does not hit the server as rapidly as the computer can operate. The delay is part of the research method, not decoration.
I should emphasize that trying to bypass a block with another library is not the goal. If a site refuses automated access, students should find an API, downloadable dataset, archived copy, or different source.
For the live demo, create tolkien_gateway_scraper.py and begin with the complete setup from the lesson:
import csv
import time

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
from rich.console import Console
from rich.table import Table


BASE_URL = "https://tolkiengateway.net"
LITERARY_CATEGORY_URL = f"{BASE_URL}/wiki/Category:Characters_in_The_Lord_of_the_Rings"
ADAPTATION_CATEGORY_URL = f"{BASE_URL}/wiki/Category:The_Rings_of_Power_(TV_series)_characters"
RINGS_OF_POWER_PATH = "/wiki/The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Rings_of_Power"
HEADERS = {
    "User-Agent": "is310-course-scraper/1.0 (student project; netid@illinois.edu)"
}
REQUEST_DELAY = 1.0
RESULTS_OUTPUT = "tolkien_gateway_characters.csv"

console = Console()
Then add the one function responsible for downloading and parsing any page:
def fetch_soup(url):
    if not url:
        console.print("[yellow]No URL was found for this page.[/yellow]")
        return None

    response = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=30)
    time.sleep(REQUEST_DELAY)

    if response.status_code != 200:
        console.print(f"[red]Could not download {url}: HTTP {response.status_code}[/red]")
        return None

    return BeautifulSoup(response.text, "html.parser")
I can first test this function with fetch_soup(LITERARY_CATEGORY_URL) before building the rest of the pipeline.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
What Questions Could We Ask?


In the lesson I focus on: How does Tolkien Gateway distribute attention between literary and adaptation-created characters? But what other questions could we ask?
The website is too large for a meaningful instruction to “scrape Tolkien Gateway.” We need a bounded comparison and an account of what could count as evidence.
We compare two categories maintained by Tolkien Gateway editors:

Characters in The Lord of the Rings
The Rings of Power television-series characters

These are not equivalent populations. They differ in age, source material, number of editors, cultural history, and category rules. The comparison is exploratory rather than a definitive measurement of fandom.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: How does the website structure what we can count?
text:
How does the website structure what we can count?






What has the wiki already decided for us?

The two category pages supply character links, but they also supply classifications. We record source_url so future users can see which category produced each record, and we derive character_type as literary or adaptation from that source.
Ask students what might be missing or contested. Characters can appear across books and adaptations. Category membership may be incomplete or governed by local editorial rules. Some adaptation-created characters may be composites or transformations of literary figures. Our simple type field compresses those complexities.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: How Might We Find Every Character?
text:
How Might We Find Every Character?

characters_section = category_page.find(id="mw-pages")
character_items = characters_section.find_all("li")

The lesson deliberately breaks the search into readable stages instead of one dense CSS selector. First find the page section, then find each list item, then find the link inside the item.
During the demo, I can open developer tools and ask students to identify id="mw-pages". Then we can connect that HTML attribute to the .find(id="mw-pages") call.
The function returns a list of dictionaries containing the character name, category-derived type, source URL, and full character URL. This is the first stage of the dataset, before any measurements are added.
Live-demo code:
def scrape_characters(category_page, source_url):
    characters = []
    if category_page is None:
        return characters

    characters_section = category_page.find(id="mw-pages")
    if characters_section is None:
        return characters

    if source_url == LITERARY_CATEGORY_URL:
        character_type = "literary"
    else:
        character_type = "adaptation"

    character_items = characters_section.find_all("li")
    for item in character_items:
        link = item.find("a", href=True)
        if link is None:
            continue

        characters.append({
            "character": link.get_text(" ", strip=True),
            "character_type": character_type,
            "source_url": source_url,
            "character_url": f"{BASE_URL}{link['href']}",
        })

    return characters
After adding it, test the discovery stage before visiting every detail page:
literary_page = fetch_soup(LITERARY_CATEGORY_URL)
literary_characters = scrape_characters(literary_page, LITERARY_CATEGORY_URL)
console.print(literary_characters[:3])

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: What Part of a Character Page Should Count?
text:
What Part of a Character Page Should Count?

What would happen if we counted the entire webpage?

The full page includes navigation, sidebars, footer text, scripts, interface labels, and other material that is not the character article. We narrow the analysis to:
content = soup.select_one("#mw-content-text .mw-parser-output")
This still does not produce pure article prose. The selected element may contain captions, tables, references, and templates. The selector is a documented research decision, not a magical extraction of the page’s true content.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
What Might Count as Attention?



Measurement
Possible interpretation




Words
Length of documentation


Characters
Another measure of text extent


All internal links
Every connection made in the article


Unique internal links
Breadth of distinct wiki destinations



Which of these is fandom attention, and which is only a proxy? Why is attention culturally interesting?

All four are proxies. A longer page could reflect popularity, abundant source material, a long publication history, sustained editorial labor, controversy, or formatting conventions. Links can reflect navigational style as much as cultural attention.
The distinction between word count and character count gives us two imperfect views of length. split() treats whitespace-separated pieces as words; it is not linguistic tokenization. Character count includes spaces and punctuation.
The point is not that proxies are invalid. The point is that we must name what we calculated and avoid silently substituting it for the larger concept we care about.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: Why Count All and Unique Links?
text:
Why Count All and Unique Links?
Elrond, Elrond, Elrond, Galadriel, Galadriel
All links: 5
Unique links: 2
What different kind of page might each measure reward?

The total captures every qualifying occurrence. The unique count captures the range of distinct destinations.
The script first creates a regular list of all qualifying internal links. It then builds another list and adds a URL only if it is not already present. This uses data structures students already know:
unique_internal_links = []
for href in internal_links:
    if href not in unique_internal_links:
        unique_internal_links.append(href)
Neither result is automatically better. Comparing them can reveal whether a page repeatedly returns to a few topics or connects outward to many pages.
The complete helper from the lesson is:
def get_internal_links(content):
    if content is None:
        return []

    links = []
    for link in content.find_all("a", href=True):
        href = link["href"]
        if href.startswith("/wiki/") and "#" not in href:
            links.append(href)

    return links
What does this include that we may not actually want?
This deliberately simple rule keeps relative links to wiki pages and excludes fragment links to sections of the current page.
It may still include categories, files, templates, help pages, dates, people, and other destinations that are not equivalent. That imperfection is productive for discussion. We can improve the code later, but each additional exclusion also encodes another judgment about which relationships count.
The script can be reproducible and still measure something broader than intended. Reproducibility makes the decision visible; it does not make the decision neutral.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
Who Appears in Both Worlds?

What can a link to the television series tell us about a literary character?

For literary characters only, the script checks whether the internal-link list contains the exact path for The Rings of Power. It stores the result as True or False in rings_of_power_link.
This creates a simple overlap field without trying to match character names across the two categories. However, False does not prove that a character is absent from the show. It may mean the wiki page does not contain the expected link, the editors use a different page structure, or our extraction missed it.
This is a useful example of how a Boolean field can look more certain than the evidence that produced it.
This is the complete detail-page analysis function to live code next:
def analyze_character(character):
    soup = fetch_soup(character["character_url"])
    record = character.copy()
    record["word_count"] = 0
    record["character_count"] = 0
    record["internal_link_count"] = 0
    record["unique_internal_link_count"] = 0
    record["rings_of_power_link"] = False

    if soup is None:
        return record

    content = soup.select_one("#mw-content-text .mw-parser-output")
    if content is None:
        return record

    article_text = content.get_text(" ", strip=True)
    internal_links = get_internal_links(content)
    unique_internal_links = []
    for href in internal_links:
        if href not in unique_internal_links:
            unique_internal_links.append(href)

    record["word_count"] = len(article_text.split())
    record["character_count"] = len(article_text)
    record["internal_link_count"] = len(internal_links)
    record["unique_internal_link_count"] = len(unique_internal_links)
    if record["character_type"] == "literary":
        record["rings_of_power_link"] = RINGS_OF_POWER_PATH in internal_links

    return record
Test one record before starting the full loop:
console.print(analyze_character(literary_characters[0]))

text:
Why Break the Scraper Into Functions?

scrape_characters()

main()
What single responsibility does each function have?

Once the analysis works for one record, add the output functions:
def save_csv(records, output_path):
    if not records:
        console.print(f"[yellow]No records to save to {output_path}[/yellow]")
        return

    with open(output_path, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=records[0].keys())
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(records)


def print_results_table(records):
    table = Table(title="Literary and Adaptation Character Pages")
    table.add_column("Character", style="cyan")
    table.add_column("Type", style="green")
    table.add_column("Literary Character in Rings of Power", style="magenta")
    table.add_column("Words", justify="right")
    table.add_column("Characters", justify="right")
    table.add_column("All Links", justify="right")
    table.add_column("Unique Links", justify="right")

    for record in sorted(records, key=lambda record: record["word_count"], reverse=True):
        table.add_row(
            record["character"],
            record["character_type"],
            str(record["rings_of_power_link"]),
            str(record["word_count"]),
            str(record["character_count"]),
            str(record["internal_link_count"]),
            str(record["unique_internal_link_count"]),
        )

    console.print(table)
The terminal table sorts for quick inspection. The CSV preserves the records for later analysis.

text:
What Does main() Make Visible?
def main():
    literary_characters = ...
    adaptation_characters = ...
    all_characters = literary_characters + adaptation_characters

    results = []
    for character in all_characters:
        results.append(analyze_character(character))

    print_results_table(results)
    save_csv(results, RESULTS_OUTPUT)

The usual entry-point pattern is:

    main()

The complete orchestration code from the lesson is:
def main():
    console.print("[cyan]Finding The Lord of the Rings characters...[/cyan]")
    literary_page = fetch_soup(LITERARY_CATEGORY_URL)
    literary_characters = scrape_characters(
        literary_page,
        LITERARY_CATEGORY_URL,
    )

    console.print("[cyan]Finding The Rings of Power characters...[/cyan]")
    adaptation_page = fetch_soup(ADAPTATION_CATEGORY_URL)
    adaptation_characters = scrape_characters(
        adaptation_page,
        ADAPTATION_CATEGORY_URL,
    )

    all_characters = literary_characters + adaptation_characters
    console.print(f"[green]Found {len(all_characters)} character pages.[/green]")

    results = []
    for number, character in enumerate(all_characters, start=1):
        console.print(
            f"Processing {number}/{len(all_characters)}: {character['character']}"
        )
        results.append(analyze_character(character))

    print_results_table(results)
    save_csv(results, RESULTS_OUTPUT)
    console.print(
        f"[green]Saved {len(results)} analyzed character pages "
        f"to {RESULTS_OUTPUT}[/green]"
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

text:
What is an API?

API Workflow
A browser or script sends an HTTP request to a server. The server processes it, often retrieves data from a database, and returns a response. A webpage request usually returns HTML for people to view. An API usually returns structured data for another program to process.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
What is a database?



History of Databases


How do tabulating machines, spreadsheets, databases, and APIs connect?

https://www.ibm.com/history/relational-database Recall Hollerith’s census machines and our discussion of tabulation. In 1970, Edgar F. Codd proposed the relational model. Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce developed SEQUEL, later SQL, for querying related tables. VisiCalc made a visible grid interactive in 1979. An API often sits in front of a database and determines which queries outsiders may make. None of these systems removes the earlier decision about what becomes a row, field, category, or identifier.
Recall our earlier discussion of tabulating machines. Hollerith’s punched-card machines helped the 1890 U.S. Census sort and count information about millions of people. These machines made tabulation faster, but people still had to decide which categories to record and punch onto the cards.
By the 1970s, computers were being used to store much larger collections of information. In 1970, IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd proposed the relational database model, which organized related data into tables. Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce then developed a language called SEQUEL, later renamed SQL, for asking questions of those tables. Instead of manually searching every record, someone could request particular rows, combine related tables, or calculate a result. You can read more through IBM’s histories of Edgar Codd and the relational database.
Spreadsheets developed alongside databases but served a somewhat different purpose. VisiCalc, released in 1979, let people directly edit information and formulas in a visible grid on a personal computer. A spreadsheet is useful for working directly with a table, while a database is better suited to managing and searching larger sets of related tables. Both continue the history of organizing information into rows, columns, and categories.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: Where do web APIs come from?
text:
Where do web APIs come from?



Salesforce API



Web APIs became prominent around 2000. Salesforce and eBay opened interfaces that let developers access platform data and build applications. Early APIs often returned XML. JSON later became a common format for exchanging structured data.
According to Lane, one of the first APIs was developed by Salesforce in 2000, which allowed developers to access data from their databases and to build applications for customer relationship management. This initial API provided access to XML data, which is a type of markup language similar to HTML (remember TEI?). This was followed by eBay, which also developed an API in 2000. As web APIs expanded during the decade, JSON increasingly joined and often replaced XML as a common format for returning structured data.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: Why are we in the Post-API Age? What has happened to APIs since 2010?
text:
Why are we in the Post-API Age? What has happened to APIs since 2010?





History of APIs






The rise of participatory platforms created large databases of user activity. APIs supported mashups and third-party applications built around Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, and other services. They also turned cultural activity into platform data governed by corporate interfaces. The Cambridge Analytica scandal revealed that Facebook had allowed a third-party app to collect data on millions of users. The resulting public outcry led to stricter data privacy regulations and changes in how social media platforms handle user data. Many platforms restricted API access, limiting the ability of researchers and developers to collect data. This has created a more challenging environment for studying social media and other online platforms, as researchers must navigate new restrictions and find alternative methods for data collection.
https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00027162251372557
TweetDeck shows how APIs supported third-party interfaces before Twitter bought it in 2011. Platforms retained the power to change access rules and rate limits. After the Cambridge Analytica revelations, many restricted access further. Deen Freelon calls the resulting research environment a post-API age.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: Where is the Web going? What is decentralized web infrastructure?
text:
Where is the Web going? What is decentralized web infrastructure?

Anyone Use Bluesky or Mastodon?
Bluesky and Mastodon are examples of federated social networks. They use the ActivityPub protocol to allow users on different servers to interact. This decentralization gives communities more control over their data and governance, but it also creates challenges for researchers trying to collect and analyze data across multiple instances.

What changes when we use an API? Why might we use an API over scraping?





Workflow
Response
Select data with




Web scraping
HTML
BeautifulSoup and elements


API request
Usually JSON
Keys and list indexes



Both begin with HTTP requests. Scraping recovers data from a document designed for people. An API returns data through an interface designed for programs. Structured access does not guarantee complete or neutral data.
/wiki/Main_Page may return 403 Forbidden

/api.php returns structured data with 200 OK
Fandom may block automated requests for rendered pages while supporting requests to its MediaWiki API. The same server offers a different door with different expectations. We still provide a descriptive User-Agent and follow the site’s policies.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: What happens if we try to scrape LOTR Fandom?
text:
What happens if we try to scrape LOTR Fandom?


Use the same basic workflow that succeeded with Tolkien Gateway:
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup


LOTR_FANDOM_URL = "https://lotr.fandom.com/wiki/Main_Page"
HEADERS = {
    "User-Agent": "is310-course-scraper/1.0 "
    "(student project; netid@illinois.edu)"
}

response = requests.get(
    LOTR_FANDOM_URL,
    headers=HEADERS,
    timeout=30,
)

print("Status:", response.status_code)
print("Content type:", response.headers.get("content-type"))
print("Final URL:", response.url)
print("Response preview:")
print(response.text[:500])
The diagnostic output matters more than immediately parsing the response. Depending on Fandom’s current bot protection, the request may return 403 Forbidden, another non-200 response, or HTML for a challenge page rather than the wiki article we expected.
I can then show why checking only for some returned text is insufficient. If the request succeeds, this code tries the same article selector pattern:
if response.status_code == 200:
    soup = BeautifulSoup(response.text, "html.parser")
    page_title = soup.find("h1")
    article = soup.select_one(".mw-parser-output")

    print("Page title:", page_title.get_text(" ", strip=True) if page_title else None)
    print("Article content found:", article is not None)
else:
    print("Stop here. Do not try to bypass the site's bot protection.")
The point of this demo is to inspect the response and respect what the server tells us. We should not switch to an evasion library or disguise the scraper. Instead, the next step is to look for a supported interface. Because Fandom runs MediaWiki, the site provides structured access through https://lotr.fandom.com/api.php, which leads directly into the following API slides.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
What is the MediaWiki API?



Click the image to visit the API documentation



Wikipedia launched in 2001 as an experiment connected to Nupedia. It first ran on UseModWiki, Perl software that stored pages as text files. Rapid growth prompted contributors to create a PHP and MySQL CMS. Wikipedia adopted it in 2002 and named it MediaWiki in 2003. The database-backed system supported namespaces, talk pages, histories, and watchlists. MediaWiki is the software. Wikimedia is the foundation and movement supporting Wikipedia and related projects.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
Where is the Action API?



LOTR API Sandbox



MediaWiki sites commonly expose /w/api.php or /api.php. The sandbox lets us build requests before writing Python. Site-specific help matters because installations may use different versions and extensions.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
What are endpoints and parameters?

Anatomy of URL parameters
The endpoint receives the request. Parameters describe what we want. A question mark starts the query string and ampersands separate options. Passing a dictionary to params= lets requests construct and encode the URL safely.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
What does action=query mean?
https://lotr.fandom.com/api.php?action=query&format=json

action=query retrieves structured information. It does not mean SQL or our complete research question. Within it, prop retrieves page properties, list produces lists, and meta describes the wiki or user. We use list=categorymembers; its settings use the cm prefix.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs

How do we query a category?

params = {
    "action": "query",
    "list": "categorymembers",

    "format": "json",
}
response = requests.get(API_URL, params=params, headers=HEADERS, timeout=15)


Demo this in first_api_script.py. Print the URL and status code. Then inspect data["query"]["categorymembers"] and print each page title. This is the API equivalent of inspecting HTML before writing selectors.
Complete first API request for the live demo:
import requests


API_URL = "https://lotr.fandom.com/api.php"
HEADERS = {
    "User-Agent": "is310-course/1.0 "
    "(https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io; YOUR_NETID@illinois.edu)"
}

params = {
    "action": "query",
    "list": "categorymembers",
    "cmtitle": "Category:Canon_characters_in_The_Rings_of_Power",
    "cmtype": "page",
    "cmlimit": "max",
    "format": "json",
}

response = requests.get(
    API_URL,
    params=params,
    headers=HEADERS,
    timeout=15,
)

print("Requested URL:", response.url)
print("Status:", response.status_code)

if response.status_code == 200:
    data = response.json()
    for page in data["query"]["categorymembers"]:
        print(page["title"])
else:
    print(response.text[:500])
Pause after printing response.url so students can identify the endpoint, question mark, and encoded parameters in the URL that requests constructed.

text:
What counts as editorial attention?



Metric
What we count




Words and characters
Visible article text


All and unique links
Connections within the wiki


Language links
Corresponding pages reported by MediaWiki




These parallel our Tolkien Gateway measures and add structured language links. They describe editorial work, not popularity itself.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
What does action=parse return?



Parse documentation


"action": "parse",
"page": title,
"prop": "text|links|langlinks",
"format": "json",

action=parse processes one page. The pipe separates three requested properties. text is rendered HTML, links contains internal references, and langlinks contains corresponding language pages. The site-specific documentation is available through api.php?action=help&modules=parse.
Build the complete function in first_api_script.py after the category query:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup


def analyze_fandom_page(title):
    response = requests.get(
        API_URL,
        params={
            "action": "parse",
            "page": title,
            "prop": "text|links|langlinks",
            "format": "json",
        },
        headers=HEADERS,
        timeout=15,
    )

    if response.status_code != 200:
        print(f"Could not retrieve {title}: {response.status_code}")
        return None

    data = response.json()
    if "error" in data:
        print(f"Could not parse {title}: {data['error']['info']}")
        return None

    page = data["parse"]
    html = page["text"]["*"]
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
    article_text = soup.get_text(" ", strip=True)

    internal_links = []
    for link in soup.find_all("a", href=True):
        href = link["href"]
        if href.startswith("/wiki/") and "#" not in href:
            internal_links.append(href)

    unique_internal_links = []
    for href in internal_links:
        if href not in unique_internal_links:
            unique_internal_links.append(href)

    return {
        "character": page["title"],
        "word_count": len(article_text.split()),
        "character_count": len(article_text),
        "internal_link_count": len(internal_links),
        "unique_internal_link_count": len(unique_internal_links),
        "language_link_count": len(page.get("langlinks", [])),
    }
Test the function with the same four records used in the lesson:
characters = ["Galadriel", "Arondir", "Halbrand", "Disa"]

for character in characters:
    result = analyze_fandom_page(character)
    if result is not None:
        print(result)

data = response.json()

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: Can we get all the data? What happens if we try to get characters?
text:
Can we get all the data? What happens if we try to get characters?



We have already confirmed that the public /book endpoint works without credentials. Now try the restricted /character endpoint without an Authorization header:
import requests


characters_url = "https://the-one-api.dev/v2/character"

response = requests.get(
    characters_url,
    timeout=15,
)

print("Requested URL:", response.url)
print("Status:", response.status_code)
print("Content type:", response.headers.get("content-type"))
print("Response body:")
print(response.text[:500])
Unlike the public books request, this should return an authentication error rather than character records. The exact status or wording could change, so I should interpret the response actually returned instead of promising one fixed message.
If the response identifies itself as JSON, we can inspect the structured error too:
content_type = response.headers.get("content-type", "")

if "application/json" in content_type:
    print(response.json())
else:
    print(response.text[:500])
For a quick comparison, run both endpoints one after another:
endpoints = [
    "https://the-one-api.dev/v2/book",
    "https://the-one-api.dev/v2/character",
]

for endpoint in endpoints:
    response = requests.get(endpoint, timeout=15)
    print(endpoint, response.status_code)
This demonstrates that authentication rules can differ across endpoints within the same API. The API is not simply open or closed as a whole. Its maintainers decide which resources can be retrieved anonymously and which require an account and token.
The next slide adds the API key through the Authorization header and repeats the character request.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: How Can We Get an API Key?
text:
How Can We Get an API Key?




The One API Key

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: How should we store API keys? What is the danger of committing credentials?
text:
How should we store API keys? What is the danger of committing credentials?

import apikey

the_one_api_key = apikey.load("THE_ONE_API_KEY")
authorization_headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {the_one_api_key}"
}

Never commit credentials. The Authorization header proves that a request belongs to an account. It differs from a descriptive User-Agent, which identifies a script and contact information rather than carrying a private credential.
An environment variable is a named value made available to programs running in a particular operating-system or shell environment. It lets the script retrieve a credential at runtime rather than storing the secret directly in the Python file.
For macOS, Linux, or WSL, set the variable in the active shell with:
export THE_ONE_API_KEY="YOUR_API_KEY_HERE"
For Windows PowerShell, use:
$env:THE_ONE_API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY_HERE"
These commands apply only to the current terminal session. If I close the terminal and open another one, I need to set the variable again. That temporary scope is useful in class because it avoids permanently modifying anyone’s shell configuration.
Python can read the value through its built-in os module:
import os


the_one_api_key = os.environ["THE_ONE_API_KEY"]

authorization_headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {the_one_api_key}"
}
os.environ behaves like a dictionary containing environment variables. Using square brackets makes Python raise a KeyError if the variable has not been set. That is often preferable to silently sending an empty credential.
For a friendlier check during the demo, I can use os.getenv() instead:
import os


the_one_api_key = os.getenv("THE_ONE_API_KEY")

if the_one_api_key is None:
    print("THE_ONE_API_KEY is not set in this terminal.")
else:
    authorization_headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {the_one_api_key}"
    }
Do not run print(the_one_api_key) while demonstrating. Terminal output can appear in screenshots, recordings, logs, or copied error reports.
Students may encounter tutorials that store secrets in a .env file. A .env file is still a plain-text file, so it must be listed in .gitignore before any key is added. If a credential has already been committed, adding the file to .gitignore afterward does not remove the secret from Git history. The key should be revoked and replaced. https://github.com/ulf1/apikey For this course, the apikey library gives us a simpler credential store that persists beyond one terminal session:
python -m pip install "apikey>=0.2.4"
Save the key once from a private terminal session:
import apikey


apikey.save("THE_ONE_API_KEY", "YOUR_API_KEY_HERE")
Then load it in the assignment script without including the secret itself:
import apikey


the_one_api_key = apikey.load("THE_ONE_API_KEY")
The distinction I want students to remember is:

A hard-coded key travels with the source file and can be committed accidentally.
A session environment variable stays outside the script but must be reset in each new terminal.
The apikey library stores the credential outside the repository and retrieves it by name across sessions.

None of these methods makes it appropriate to share or print the key. They reduce accidental exposure by separating credentials from source code.
After loading the key, test one restricted endpoint and inspect its structure:
characters_url = "https://the-one-api.dev/v2/character"
characters_response = requests.get(
    characters_url,
    headers=authorization_headers,
    timeout=15,
)

print("Status:", characters_response.status_code)

if characters_response.status_code == 200:
    characters_data = characters_response.json()
    print("Response keys:", characters_data.keys())
    print("Total characters:", characters_data["total"])
else:
    print(characters_response.text[:500])
If this returns 401, check that the key name passed to apikey.load() matches the name used when saving it and that the Authorization value begins with Bearer.

section: How do parameters filter the data?
text:
How do parameters filter the data?
params = {"name": "Galadriel"}
response = requests.get(
    "https://the-one-api.dev/v2/character",
    headers=authorization_headers,
    params=params,
)
print(response.url)

Requests constructs ?name=Galadriel. Filtering on the server retrieves one relevant record rather than downloading all characters and filtering locally. The API also supports sorting and pagination. Collecting everything is not always the best research strategy.
Complete filter and comparison code:
params = {"name": "Galadriel"}
response = requests.get(
    characters_url,
    headers=authorization_headers,
    params=params,
    timeout=15,
)

if response.status_code == 200:
    galadriel_data = response.json()
    print("Requested URL:", response.url)
    print(galadriel_data["docs"][0])

params = {
    "name!": "Galadriel",
    "race": "Elf",
}
response = requests.get(
    characters_url,
    headers=authorization_headers,
    params=params,
    timeout=15,
)

if response.status_code == 200:
    print("Requested URL:", response.url)
    print("Elves besides Galadriel:", response.json()["total"])

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: How do identifiers connect records? Why do we need to use time.sleep()?
text:
How do identifiers connect records? Why do we need to use time.sleep()?
galadriel_id = response.json()["docs"][0]["_id"]
quote_url = f"https://the-one-api.dev/v2/character/{galadriel_id}/quote"
quote_response = requests.get(quote_url, headers=authorization_headers)

Identifiers connect records even when names are duplicated or change. This resembles relationships in a database. Review current rate limits and pause between repeated requests; limits indicate the scale and type of use maintainers expect.
Copyable version with checks and a delay:
import time


galadriel_response = requests.get(
    characters_url,
    headers=authorization_headers,
    params={"name": "Galadriel"},
    timeout=15,
)

if galadriel_response.status_code == 200:
    galadriel = galadriel_response.json()["docs"][0]
    galadriel_id = galadriel["_id"]
    quote_url = (
        f"https://the-one-api.dev/v2/character/"
        f"{galadriel_id}/quote"
    )

    quote_response = requests.get(
        quote_url,
        headers=authorization_headers,
        timeout=15,
    )

    if quote_response.status_code == 200:
        print(quote_response.json())

time.sleep(10)
Finally, let’s use the time library in Python so that we don’t exceed the 100 requests every 10 minutes limit.
import time

url = 'https://the-one-api.dev/v2/character?name=Galadriel'
response = requests.get(url, headers=authorization_headers)
galadriel_id = response.json()['docs'][0]['_id']
quote_url = f'https://the-one-api.dev/v2/character/{galadriel_id}/quote'
response = requests.get(quote_url, headers=authorization_headers)
print(response.json())
time.sleep(10)

text: nrh-lotr: A small third-party wrapper

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
What does a wrapper change?
from lotr import LOTR

lotr = LOTR(the_one_api_key)
quotes = lotr.quotes(limit=5)

A wrapper packages endpoints, authentication, requests, and parsing into Python classes and methods. It reduces repeated code but adds another developer’s assumptions between us and the API. Install this example with python -m pip install nrh-lotr==0.0.3.
Terminal setup and complete working example:
python -m pip install nrh-lotr==0.0.3
import apikey
from lotr import LOTR


the_one_api_key = apikey.load("THE_ONE_API_KEY")
lotr = LOTR(the_one_api_key)

quotes = lotr.quotes(limit=5)
for quote in quotes:
    print(quote)
Then demonstrate the failing wrapper method separately:
movies = lotr.movies(limit=5)
print(movies)
The validation error is evidence about the wrapper’s model, not proof that The One API returned no movie data.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: What happens when the wrapper is wrong?
text:
What happens when the wrapper is wrong?

Pydantic validation error
The wrapper’s movies() method expects an integer Rotten Tomatoes score, but the live API returns decimals. Pydantic rejects the mismatch. A real fix requires updating the package model to use a float, maintaining a fork, or bypassing the method with requests. Defining a new Movie class in our script would not alter the installed wrapper.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
What does the wrapper omit?
/movie
/movie/{id}
/movie/{id}/quote
/quote
/quote/{id}

The wrapper covers only selected endpoints and omits books and characters. Wrappers reflect their developers’ priorities, can become outdated, and must be tested against live data rather than trusted automatically.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: How does the Internet Archive organize culture?
text:
How does the Internet Archive organize culture?



Internet Archive



The maintained internetarchive library offers a contrast with a small third-party wrapper. It supports a cultural institution and its collections. Install it with python -m pip install internetarchive.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
text:
Search result, item, or file?


Search result
Compact match

Item
Metadata and materials

File
One representation


An identifier connects a compact search result to an item. An item may represent a book, recording, film, software program, or captured website. Its files may include an original upload, OCR, thumbnails, metadata, and platform-generated derivatives.

title: GETting Cultural Data From APIs
section: How do we inspect one item?
text:
How do we inspect one item?

import internetarchive

search = internetarchive.search_items(
    'title:"Lord of the Rings" AND mediatype:texts',
    fields=["identifier", "title", "date"],
)

results = []
for result in search:
    results.append(result)
    if len(results) == 3:
        break

item = internetarchive.get_item(results[0]["identifier"])


We limit the test rather than retrieving thousands of matches. Use .get() for metadata because contributed records do not share every field. Missing metadata does not prove that a creator or rights holder does not exist; it means the field does not represent that information.
Complete copyable demonstration:
python -m pip install internetarchive
import internetarchive
from rich.console import Console

console = Console()
INTERNET_ARCHIVE_QUERY = 'title:"Lord of the Rings" AND mediatype:texts'

search = internetarchive.search_items(
    INTERNET_ARCHIVE_QUERY,
    fields=["identifier", "title", "date"],
)

results = []
for result in search:
    results.append(result)
    if len(results) == 3:
        break

for result in results:
    console.print(result.get("identifier"), result.get("title"))

first_identifier = results[0]["identifier"]
item = internetarchive.get_item(first_identifier)

metadata = item.metadata
console.print("Title:", metadata.get("title"))
console.print("Creator:", metadata.get("creator"))
console.print("Date:", metadata.get("date"))
console.print("Media type:", metadata.get("mediatype"))
console.print("Collection:", metadata.get("collection"))
console.print("License:", metadata.get("licenseurl"))

for file in list(item.files)[:10]:
    console.print(file.get("name"), file.get("format"))
The search result, item, and file hierarchy should be visible in the output. I can ask students which level they would save for a specific research question.
We could even use the https://akamhy.github.io/waybackpy/ to get snapshots of teh websites for instance!

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
Today’s agenda

Review introduction to Jupyter notebooks lesson
Review web scraping homework
Time permitting work in breakout groups

Any questions?

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: How have we run Python so far?
text:
How have we run Python so far?


python
Interpreter / REPL

python script.py
Python script


What might we want from a third way of working?

Recall the two workflows students already know. The interpreter gives immediate feedback but does not naturally preserve an extended argument. A script preserves an ordered procedure but usually requires us to rerun the file and explicitly print what we want to inspect.
Ask students what they would want to combine from both approaches: immediate feedback, saved code, explanatory prose, visible results, and the ability to revise one part of an analysis.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
What is a Jupyter notebook?


A Jupyter notebook is a computational notebook: a document that combines executable code, formatted text, images, equations, and the outputs produced by code.
Unlike a script, a notebook displays an expression’s result directly beneath a code cell. Unlike a terminal session, it can preserve the code, Markdown explanation, and selected outputs in one shareable .ipynb file.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
Python was interactive before Jupyter


Guido van Rossum began developing Python around 1989 and released it publicly in 1991. Python could be used interactively from the beginning: a user could enter one statement, have Python read and evaluate it, and immediately inspect the result.
This read-evaluate-print loop, or REPL, matters to the history of notebooks. Jupyter did not invent interactive Python. It reorganized an existing interactive practice into a persistent, browser-based document.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: What did IPython add to Python?
text:
What did IPython add to Python?


Fernando Perez began IPython in 2001 as a more powerful interactive environment around Python. IPython did not create a new language. It extended Python’s interpreter with richer output, command history, tab completion, object inspection, and easier connections to a computer’s shell.
The name originally meant Interactive Python. The IPython Notebook appeared in 2011 and moved this workflow into the browser. IPython remains the Python kernel most commonly used underneath Jupyter today.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: Should programs explain themselves to people?
text:
Should programs explain themselves to people?


Donald Knuth introduced the idea of literate programming in the 1980s. He argued that a program should be written for human readers, not only arranged for a computer to execute. Code and explanation should be intertwined so a reader can follow the author’s reasoning.
Knuth also created TeX; Leslie Lamport later built LaTeX on top of it. Jupyter is not identical to Knuth’s literate programming system, but it inherits the aspiration to place computation and explanation in the same document.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
What connected notebooks to Champaign?


Wolfram Research was founded by Stephen Wolfram in Champaign in 1987. Mathematica combined symbolic and numerical computation with a notebook interface containing code, text, and visualizations.
It also helped establish a useful architectural distinction. The visible notebook is a front end, while a separate kernel performs the computation. Later notebook systems could preserve this division while making the interface and communication protocol open source.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: What is the difference between Jupyter and a kernel?
text:
What is the difference between Jupyter and a kernel?


The notebook interface displays cells and sends code for execution. The kernel is the running process that executes the code, stores variables in memory, and sends results back.
This distinction explains why selecting the correct kernel matters. The notebook file does not contain a complete Python environment or a live session. It contains code, Markdown, metadata, and possibly saved outputs. The selected kernel determines which Python interpreter and installed libraries actually run the code.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
Why is it called Jupyter?


Project Jupyter separated from IPython in 2014 as the notebook architecture expanded beyond Python. Its name combines three languages important to its early development: Julia, Python, and R. It also invokes Galileo’s notebooks and observations of Jupiter’s moons.
The same notebook interface can communicate with different kernels. We will use a Python kernel, but Jupyter is not itself a programming language and is not limited to Python.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: How did notebooks become research infrastructure?
text:
How did notebooks become research infrastructure?







Notebooks became important infrastructure for data science, research, and teaching because they made it possible to place evidence, code, interpretation, and output together.
Melanie Walsh’s Introduction to Cultural Analytics & Python grew from notebooks. The Journal of Digital History publishes notebook-based scholarship. These examples also raise questions about reproducibility: does the saved notebook actually run, are its data still available, and can a reader distinguish a saved output from a freshly computed result?

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: Are Jupyter notebooks the end of this history?
text:
Are Jupyter notebooks the end of this history?







Jupyter is part of a changing ecosystem rather than the inevitable final form of computational writing. Posit developed Quarto to publish documents that can execute code through Jupyter kernels or R’s Knitr system. This course website is built with Quarto.
Newer systems such as Marimo rethink notebook state and reproducibility. We are learning Jupyter because it remains widely used and because its strengths and limitations teach us broader lessons about computational documents.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: What should we do before installing Jupyter?
text:
What should we do before installing Jupyter?

Activate the course virtual environment.
python -m pip install notebook ipykernel pandas

Have students activate the virtual environment used for their course repository. The command is the same in macOS, Linux, and PowerShell once the environment is active.
Using python -m pip makes explicit that pip belongs to the same Python interpreter that should run the notebook. We install the notebook application, the Python kernel integration, and Pandas.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: Where should we open the notebook?
text:
Where should we open the notebook?


The recommended workflow is to open the entire is310-coding-assignments folder in VS Code, not only an isolated notebook file. Students need both the Python and Jupyter VS Code extensions.
They can open the downloaded 01-intro-notebooks.ipynb or create a new .ipynb file. In the Command Palette, the relevant command is Create: New Jupyter Notebook.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: Which Python is actually running this notebook?
text:
Which Python is actually running this notebook?
Select Kernel → course virtual environment

import sys

sys.executable

Ask students to use Select Kernel in the upper-right corner and choose the interpreter inside their course virtual environment. If Pandas appears missing even after installation, a mismatched kernel is usually the cause.
sys.executable reveals the exact Python executable running the current kernel. Its path should point into the intended environment. This is more reliable than inferring the environment from the notebook filename or folder.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
What is inside an .ipynb file?


A notebook is stored as JSON. The file records cells, source text, metadata, execution counts, and possibly outputs. It does not preserve the live kernel after that process stops.
Because outputs are embedded in the JSON, notebooks can generate large or confusing Git diffs. Save meaningful outputs that help a reader, but clear accidental debugging output and enormous tables before committing.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: Why should we only run notebooks we trust?
text:
Why should we only run notebooks we trust?






Warning


Notebook cells can change files, delete data, install software, or send information over the internet.




A notebook is not merely a static document. Its cells can execute arbitrary code with the permissions of the current user. Students should read unfamiliar code before running it and only trust a downloaded notebook when they understand its source.
The presence of prose or polished outputs does not make a notebook safe. This connects to our earlier discussion of evaluating scripts, packages, and repositories before executing them.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: What are the two main kinds of cells?
text:
What are the two main kinds of cells?


## Research Question

What patterns appear in this data?
Markdown cell

favorite_movies[0]
Code cell


Markdown cells explain the question, sources, methods, interpretation, and limitations. Code cells perform computation. Outputs appear beneath code cells after execution.
Demonstrate creating one Markdown title and one code cell. Students can use the cell-type menu or M and Y in command mode.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: Which shortcuts do we actually need today?
text:
Which shortcuts do we actually need today?








macOS
Windows
Action




Shift+Return
Shift+Enter
Run and move to next cell


Control+Return
Ctrl+Enter
Run and remain on cell


Option+Return
Alt+Enter
Run and add a cell below


Esc, then A or B
Esc, then A or B
Add a cell above or below


Esc, then M or Y
Esc, then M or Y
Change to Markdown or code




Students do not need to memorize every shortcut. Demonstrate the distinction between edit mode and command mode: Enter edits a cell and Esc returns to command mode. Toolbar buttons remain valid alternatives.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: What happens when we run this cell?
text:
What happens when we run this cell?
favorite_movies = [
    {"name": "The Matrix IV", "release_year": 2022},
    {"name": "Star Wars IV", "release_year": 1977},
    {"name": "The Fellowship of the Ring", "release_year": 2001},
]

favorite_movies

In a notebook, the final expression in a cell is displayed automatically. We do not need print() merely to inspect the value of favorite_movies.
This convenience is useful for exploration, but print() remains appropriate when output formatting or multiple intermediate messages are part of the program.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
What does the kernel remember?
def released_after(movie, year):
    return movie["release_year"] > year

[movie["name"] for movie in favorite_movies if released_after(movie, 2000)]

After the first cell runs, the kernel keeps the function in memory. A later cell can call it without redefining it.
This is the notebook’s central affordance and one of its central risks. What a later cell can do depends on which earlier cells were executed in this particular live session.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: Does the page show the order in which the code ran?
text:
Does the page show the order in which the code ran?


Not necessarily. Cells can be executed in any order. The execution number beside a code cell records when it ran within the current kernel, but the visible top-to-bottom order may differ.
After closing or restarting the notebook, variables disappear from memory even though old outputs may still be visible. A notebook can therefore look complete while failing from a fresh start.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: How do we test whether a notebook is reproducible?
text:
How do we test whether a notebook is reproducible?
Restart Kernel and Run All Cells


Put imports and definitions before their use.
Run cells from top to bottom.
Fix hidden dependencies on old state.
Save the resulting notebook.


Make this the normal final check. Restarting clears memory, and Run All tests the document in its visible order.
If this fails, the notebook depended on hidden state: perhaps a variable was created in a deleted cell, a function was defined later, or data was modified interactively without preserving the transformation.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
What is Pandas?


Pandas is a Python library for working with labeled and tabular data. It is particularly useful inside notebooks because we can load data, inspect transformations, and display tables incrementally.
Pandas does not turn a notebook into a spreadsheet. We still write explicit operations in Python, and those operations can be rerun and documented.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
Where did Pandas come from?







Wes McKinney began Pandas in 2008 while working with financial data. It became a general-purpose library and is now maintained through a community governance model by a large open-source contributor community.
This is a useful continuation of our discussion of packages and ecosystems. pandas is not built into Python; its behavior, documentation, and maintenance are products of a changing community.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: Why do we import pandas as pd?
text:
Why do we import pandas as pd?
import pandas as pd

pd.__version__

pd is the conventional alias for Pandas. The alias does not alter the library; it gives us a shorter name for accessing its functions and classes.
Checking pd.__version__ is useful when an example behaves differently across environments. The current lesson accounts for changes in recent Pandas versions, including the newer dedicated string data type.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: How do we turn a data file into a Python object?
text:
How do we turn a data file into a Python object?
parks_url = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/melaniewalsh/"
    "responsible-datasets-in-context/main/datasets/national-parks/"
    "US-National-Parks_RecreationVisits_1979-2023.csv"
)

parks_data_df = pd.read_csv(parks_url)

pd.read_csv() reads comma-separated data from a local path or URL and returns a DataFrame. We store the source URL separately so the source remains visible and the function call stays readable.
The _df suffix is a common, optional convention indicating that a variable contains a DataFrame.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
What is a DataFrame?


A DataFrame is Pandas’s primary two-dimensional data structure. It has labeled rows and columns and can hold different data types in different columns.
The documentation compares it to a spreadsheet, a SQL table, or an R data frame. Those comparisons describe its shape, not an identical workflow. A DataFrame lives in Python memory and is manipulated through code.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: What should we inspect before analyzing anything?
text:
What should we inspect before analyzing anything?
parks_data_df.head()
parks_data_df.sample(random_state=42)
parks_data_df.shape
parks_data_df.dtypes

Demonstrate these one at a time rather than running all four in a single cell, since a notebook automatically displays only its final expression.
head() shows the first five rows. sample(random_state=42) gives everyone the same reproducible random row. shape returns rows and columns. dtypes reports the type assigned to each column.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: What can summary methods reveal—and conceal?
text:
What can summary methods reveal—and conceal?
parks_data_df.info()
parks_data_df.describe()

info() reports column names, non-null counts, and data types. describe() gives summary statistics for numeric columns by default.
These methods help us inspect structure, but they cannot explain provenance or tell us whether a column represents a responsible category. A mathematically valid summary can still describe incomplete, historically produced, or conceptually misleading data.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: What basic data-quality checks should we run?
text:
What basic data-quality checks should we run?
parks_data_df.isna().sum()
parks_data_df.duplicated().sum()

isna() produces Boolean values indicating missingness, and sum() counts the True values in each column. duplicated() identifies exact duplicate rows.
A zero result does not prove the data is correct. Missing information can be encoded as an empty string or misleading placeholder, and two records can describe the same entity without being exact duplicates. These are first checks, not an audit by themselves.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: How can we sort without changing the source data?
text:
How can we sort without changing the source data?
parks_data_df.sort_values(
    by="RecreationVisits",
    ascending=False,
).head(10)

sort_values() returns a sorted DataFrame. Unless we assign that result to a variable, the original parks_data_df remains unchanged.
Ask what the top ten rows represent. Because the dataset contains park-year observations, this finds the largest annual visit counts, not necessarily the ten most visited parks across the whole period.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: Why do one and two pairs of brackets differ?
text:
Why do one and two pairs of brackets differ?
parks_data_df["Year"]
parks_data_df[["Year"]]

The first returns a one-dimensional Series. The second passes a list containing one column name and returns a two-dimensional DataFrame.
Demonstrate type() on both outputs. The visible values may look similar, but the returned class affects which methods are available and how subsequent operations behave.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
What is a Series?


A Series is a one-dimensional labeled data structure. A DataFrame can be understood as a collection of Series sharing an index.
Selecting one column usually returns a Series. Selecting a list of columns, even a list containing only one name, returns a DataFrame.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: What values actually occur in a column?
text:
What values actually occur in a column?
parks_data_df["Year"].unique()
parks_data_df["State"].value_counts()

unique() returns the distinct values in a Series. value_counts() reports how frequently each value occurs.
Frequency still requires interpretation. In this dataset, repeated state values reflect park-year rows, not simply a count of parks. Always return to the unit represented by each row.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: How do we filter rows with a condition?
text:
How do we filter rows with a condition?
california_parks_df = parks_data_df[
    parks_data_df["State"] == "CA"
]

california_parks_df.head()

The expression inside the brackets produces a Series of True and False values. Pandas retains rows where the condition is True.
Connect this to conditionals students already know. Instead of one if statement evaluating one dictionary, Pandas evaluates the condition across an entire labeled column.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: How do we filter for several possible values?
text:
How do we filter for several possible values?
western_parks_df = parks_data_df[
    parks_data_df["State"].isin(["CA", "AK"])
]

isin() tests whether each value belongs to a supplied list. It is clearer than joining many equality comparisons with | when we have several accepted values.
Have students inspect the resulting states with western_parks_df["State"].value_counts().

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
What does groupby() actually do?


groupby() implements a split-apply-combine process. It splits rows into groups defined by one or more column values, applies an operation to each group, and combines the results.
Grouping alone returns a GroupBy object. We must then choose what should be counted, summed, averaged, or otherwise aggregated.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: Are we counting parks or rows?
text:
Are we counting parks or rows?
parks_data_df.groupby("State").size()

parks_data_df.groupby("State")["ParkName"].nunique()

This distinction is central. size() counts rows. Since this dataset contains one row per park and year, that produces park-year observations rather than distinct parks.
Selecting ParkName and using nunique() counts distinct park names within each state. The correct operation depends on the research question and the unit of observation.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: How do we turn the grouped result back into a table?
text:
How do we turn the grouped result back into a table?
parks_by_state_df = (
    parks_data_df
    .groupby("State")["ParkName"]
    .nunique()
    .reset_index(name="park_count")
)

parks_by_state_df.sort_values("park_count", ascending=False)

The grouped result is a Series whose index contains state labels. reset_index() moves those labels into a normal column and returns a DataFrame. Naming the resulting count column makes the table easier to interpret.
The parentheses allow us to place each step on its own line. Read the chain from top to bottom: start with the data, group by state, select park names, count unique names, and restore a tabular index.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
section: What should explanation do alongside code?

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
In-class notebook check
Create or open NationalParksEDA.ipynb, then:

Add a Markdown title and research question.
Import Pandas and load the National Parks data.
Inspect its shape, columns, data types, and missing values.
Filter one subset that interests you.
Group and aggregate the data to answer one question.
Explain what your result can and cannot tell us.
Restart the kernel and run all cells.


This follows the current lesson exercise while keeping the goal manageable. Students should save the notebook in a pandas-eda folder inside is310-coding-assignments.
Circulate and check kernel selection first when code fails. Then check exact column names and whether cells were executed in top-to-bottom order.

title: (Re)Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks & Pandas
text:
What should we remember?

A notebook is a document connected to a live kernel.
Visible order and execution order can differ.
Restart and run all before sharing.
A DataFrame represents rows and columns, but their meaning comes from provenance.
Selecting, filtering, and grouping are interpretive choices.


End by returning to the central question. Notebooks make it easier to place computation next to interpretation, but they do not automatically make an analysis reproducible or responsible. That depends on how we order, document, verify, and interpret the work.

title: Introduction to Version and File Histories
text:
Recap: The Command Line
We’ve learned how to:

But what exactly are files?

title: Introduction to Version and File Histories
section: What is a File? A Somewhat Reductive Answer
text:
What is a File? A Somewhat Reductive Answer
A file is a collection of data stored in a single unit, identified by a filename.

Files can be:

Documents
Images
Videos
Audio
Any other collection of data

title: Introduction to Version and File Histories
text:
File Extensions
The file extension is the part of the file name after the period.




Extension
Type




.docx
Microsoft Word document


.jpg
Image file


.mp3
Audio file


.txt
Plain text file


.md
Markdown file

title: Introduction to Version and File Histories
text:
Proprietary vs Open Formats
Some file formats depend on particular software ecosystems.

For example, .docx files are designed for Microsoft Word and similar word processors.

title: Introduction to Version and File Histories
text:
What is this?



Strange characters?

title: Introduction to Version and File Histories
text:
Proprietary All the Way Down
To be clear, .doc was invented in 1983 along with the first version of the software for Microsoft Word which ran on MS-DOS, whereas .docx was only introduced in 2007 as part of an XML-based update to the software.



History of Word

title: Introduction to Version and File Histories
text:
Plain Text vs Formatted Text
A Word Document and a .txt file might look the same…

But Word contains hidden formatting that .txt does not.


In programming, we want to be explicit - so plain text is preferable.

title: Introduction to Version and File Histories
section: What is Plain Text? The Unicode Definition
text:
What is Plain Text? The Unicode Definition
According to the Unicode Standard:

Plain text is a pure sequence of character codes; plain Unicode-encoded text is therefore a sequence of Unicode character codes.


Key concept: Plain text shows if it is formatted or not (we call this markup), and usually contains no formatting.

title: Introduction to Version and File Histories
section: Who Decides What Counts as Text?
text:

Who has heard of the Unicode Consortium?

title: Introduction to Version and File Histories
text:

Portable - moves between programs easily
Manipulable - responds to programmatic operations
Sustainable - doesn’t require specific software


Edited in a text editor like VS Code

“The World Wide Web (WWW), commonly known as the Web, is an information system where documents and other web resources are identified by Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), which may be interlinked by hypertext, and are accessible over the Internet. Understanding What’s Happening
When you push your HTML files to GitHub, here’s what happens behind the scenes:

GitHub detects the push to your repository
GitHub Pages automatically builds your site
Your HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files are copied to a web server
Your site becomes accessible at your unique URL

Their browser sends an HTTP request to GitHub’s servers
GitHub’s servers respond with your HTML file
The browser renders the page

You’ve created content (HTML), version controlled it (Git), and deployed it to a live web server!

section: Why is data cleaning counter to how humanists think about data?
text:
Why is data cleaning counter to how humanists think about data?



“Yet the humanities cannot import paradigms and practices wholesale from other fields, whether from “technoscience” or the nearer “social” sciences, without risking the foreclosure of specific and valuable humanistic modes of producing knowledge. If we are interested in working with data, and we accept that there is something in our work with data that is like what other fields might call “data cleaning,” we have no choice but to try to articulate both what it is and what it means in terms of how humanists make knowledge.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 280)
“In other data-intensive fields in which researchers have long been explicit about their framing orders, the limits of results are often understood and articulated using specialized discourses. For example, in climate science, researchers confine their claims to the data they can work with and report results with margins of error. While humanities researchers do have discourses for limiting claims (acknowledging the choice of an archive or a particular intellectual tradition), the move into data-intensive research asks humanists to modify such discourses or develop new ones suitable for these projects.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 281)

title: Creating & Curating
text:
Scale & Menus



A menu describes what a restaurant serves—but a menu also describes who is being served. They reflect the class, gender, political, technological, and environmental shifts of history. The thousands of menus in this collection document a period of fundamental transformation – and the birth of the society and the restaurant we know today. (The Pudding, 2026)



“Making menus is a scalable process. Although menus are sometimes handwritten or elaborately printed on ribbon-sewn silk, the format of a menu is designed to be scalable. Menus are an efficient typographical vehicle for communicating a set of offerings for often low-margin dining enterprises. Part of the way that we know that menus are scalable is how alike they appear. “Eggs Benedict” or “caviar,” with their accompanying prices, may fit interchangeably into the “slots” of the menu’s layout.” (Rawson and Muñoz, 2019, p. 285)
